definitions.definition: Abetment, as used in Section 84B of the Information Technology Act, 2000, means the act of instigating, engaging in a conspiracy, or rendering aid that causes or facilitates the commission of an offence under the Act. An act or offence is said to be committed in consequence of abetment when it is committed in consequence of instigation, or in pursuance of a conspiracy, or with the aid which constitutes the abetment.
definitions.plain_english: Abetment means helping, encouraging, or conspiring with someone to commit a crime under this law. If a person pushes another to do something illegal, plans it with them, or actively assists them in carrying it out, that person is said to have 'abetted' the offence. Even if the helper did not personally commit the illegal act, they can still be punished just as if they had committed it themselves.
real_world_examples: A cybercriminal in Delhi instructs a younger associate in Mumbai on exactly how to hack into a bank's computer system and provides hacking tools; even though only the associate executes the attack, the Delhi individual is liable for abetment of unauthorised access under the IT Act.

A group of individuals in Bengaluru conspire together to spread morphed obscene images of a woman online; those who planned the act and sourced the images, even if they did not personally upload them, are guilty of abetment of the offence of publishing obscene material.

A tech support scammer based in Hyderabad trains and coaches junior operators on how to deceive elderly victims into installing malware on their computers; the trainer is liable for abetting the offence of computer fraud under the Act.

An employee of an e-commerce company in Chennai deliberately provides login credentials of the company's secure database to an external hacker friend, enabling the hacker to steal customer data; the employee is guilty of abetting the data theft offence even though they did not personally extract the data.

A social media group administrator in Kolkata knowingly allows and encourages members to share child sexually abusive material on the platform and provides technical guidance on how to evade detection; the administrator is liable for abetting the publication of such material under the IT Act.
what_it_covers: A person who instigates another to commit an offence under the IT Act, such as urging someone to hack into a competitor's computer system.
A person who enters into a conspiracy with others to commit an IT Act offence, such as jointly planning a phishing campaign targeting Indian bank customers.

A person who provides active aid — such as tools, credentials, or technical assistance — that enables another to commit an IT Act offence, even if the aider is not physically present at the time of commission.
An individual who coaches or trains others to carry out cyberattacks or digital frauds, thereby instigating the offence through direction and instruction.
Any act of facilitation that directly results in the commission of an offence under the Act, where no separate express punishment for abetment is provided.
what_it_excludes: Mere knowledge or awareness of another person's intent to commit an IT Act offence, without any active instigation, conspiracy, or aid.
Inadvertent or passive facilitation, such as an internet service provider unknowingly routing traffic used by a cybercriminal, where there is no deliberate assistance or conspiracy.
Acts that independently constitute a separately punishable offence under the IT Act with an express abetment provision, as Section 84B applies only where no such express provision exists.
Persons who are victims or unwitting instruments of the primary offender and who had no intent or knowledge of their role in enabling the offence.
General presence at the scene of an IT offence without any prior conspiracy, instigation, or provision of assistance.
definitions.why_it_matters: Section 84B extends criminal liability to persons who instigate, conspire, or aid in the commission of any IT Act offence, ensuring that accomplices and facilitators face the same punishment as the primary offender. This provision is critical because it prevents indirect participants — such as planners, trainers, or tool-providers — from escaping liability by arguing they did not personally commit the act, thereby closing a significant loophole in cybercrime prosecution.

definitions.definition: 'access' with its grammatical variations and cognate expressions means gaining entry into, instructing or communicating with the logical, arithmetical, or memory function resources of a computer, computer system or computer network.
definitions.plain_english: Access means any way of getting into, giving instructions to, or exchanging information with a computer or a network of computers. This includes logging into a system, running a program, reading stored data, or sending commands to a remote machine. It covers both physical and remote forms of interaction with computing resources.
real_world_examples: A hacker in Mumbai remotely logs into a Bengaluru-based company's server without permission and reads confidential employee records — this constitutes unauthorised access under the IT Act.

A bank employee in Delhi uses her official login credentials to query a customer's account balance through the bank's internal computer system — this is a legitimate, authorised access to a computer network.

A student in Hyderabad uses a cyber cafe computer to log into a government scholarship portal and submit an application — accessing the government's computer system via the internet qualifies as access.

A cybercriminal sends a specially crafted SQL injection request to an e-commerce website's database server in Chennai, causing the server to execute unintended commands and reveal customer payment data — instructing a computer system through malicious input constitutes access.

A corporate IT administrator in Pune connects remotely via VPN to a colleague's workstation to troubleshoot a software issue — remotely communicating with the memory and logical functions of another computer is access.

A phishing victim in Kolkata unknowingly provides OTP details to a fraudster who then uses those credentials to instruct the victim's net-banking system to transfer funds — the fraudster's use of the banking system constitutes access.
what_it_covers: Logging into a computer system remotely over the internet, including via SSH, RDP, or VPN connections.
Sending commands or instructions to a computer's processor or memory, such as executing a script or running malware on a target system.
Communicating with a computer network by transmitting data packets, queries, or requests to servers or connected devices.
Physically using a terminal or keyboard to interact with a computer's logical and arithmetical functions.
Automated or programmatic access such as API calls or bot-driven queries that instruct a computer system to perform operations.
what_it_excludes: Merely being in physical proximity to a computer without interacting with its logical, arithmetical, or memory functions — for example, standing next to a switched-off server.
Reading a printed computer-generated report or document, as this does not involve gaining entry into or instructing the computer's functional resources.

Using a non-programmable calculator, since the definition of 'computer' under the Act explicitly excludes calculators that are not programmable, meaning interacting with such a device is not access within this Act.
Viewing a publicly broadcast signal or traditional telephone communication that does not involve instructing or communicating with a computer system or network's internal resources.
Passive observation of a computer screen by a bystander who does not interact with the system in any way.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person's interaction with a computer qualifies as 'access' is the threshold question for nearly every cyber offence under the IT Act — in particular, unauthorised access triggers liability under Section 43 (penalty for damage to computer resources) and Section 66 (computer-related offences), meaning that without satisfying this definition, those penal and compensatory provisions cannot be invoked. It equally determines the scope of lawful authorisation defences, since access that is permitted by the owner falls outside the mischief targeted by the Act.

definitions.definition: 'Addressee' means a person who is intended by the originator to receive the electronic record but does not include any intermediary.
definitions.plain_english: An addressee is the specific person that the sender (originator) deliberately targets to receive a digital message or document — such as an email, e-contract, or digital notice. The key idea is that the person must be the intended recipient, not just someone who happens to handle or pass on the message. A courier company or email server that merely relays the message is not an addressee.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based company sends a digitally signed purchase order via email to a supplier in Pune — the supplier is the 'addressee' because the originator (the company) specifically intends the supplier to receive that electronic record.

The Income Tax Department sends an e-notice through the IT portal to a taxpayer's registered email address — the taxpayer is the addressee, while the email service provider (e.g., Gmail) that routes the notice is not.

A bank in Delhi sends a loan sanction letter as a PDF attachment over secure email to a borrower — the borrower is the addressee, whereas the bank's internal mail server or any internet service provider involved in transmission is excluded.

An advocate in Chennai sends a legal notice in electronic form under Section 80 CPC to an opposing party via registered email — the opposing party is the addressee, and any intermediary platform (such as WhatsApp infrastructure or SMTP relay server) used to deliver the message is not.

A government ministry issues an electronic circular through the National Informatics Centre portal addressed to a specific state department — the state department official who is the designated recipient is the addressee, not NIC which merely hosts and transmits the record.
what_it_covers: A customer who is the designated recipient of an e-invoice sent by a seller via email or electronic platform.
A government official or department specifically named to receive an official electronic communication or digital notification.
A contracting party who is intended to receive and act upon a digitally signed electronic contract or agreement.
An individual taxpayer to whom the tax authority directs an electronic assessment order through the designated e-filing portal.
A borrower who receives an electronic loan agreement or repayment notice directly addressed by the lending institution.
what_it_excludes: Intermediaries such as internet service providers, telecom service providers, or network service providers who merely transmit or route the electronic record without being its intended recipients.
Web-hosting service providers or cloud storage platforms that store the electronic record on behalf of the originator or addressee but are not the intended recipient of the communication.
Email gateway servers or SMTP relay services that handle the technical delivery of the electronic record without being the person the originator intends to receive it.
Third parties who inadvertently receive or access an electronic record not intended for them, such as someone who receives a misdirected email.
An aggregator or digital platform that processes electronic records on behalf of both the originator and the true addressee without itself being the intended final recipient.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identity of the 'addressee' is legally critical under Sections 12 and 13 of the IT Act, which govern when an electronic record is deemed dispatched and received — the time and place of receipt are determined with reference to the addressee's computer resource, directly affecting contract formation, legal notice validity, and enforcement timelines. Misidentifying an intermediary as an addressee could incorrectly trigger or negate obligations related to acknowledgment of receipt, attribution of electronic records, and liability under the Act.

definitions.definition: 'Adjudicating officer' means an adjudicating officer appointed under sub-section (1) of section 46 of the Information Technology Act, 2000.
definitions.plain_english: An adjudicating officer is a government-appointed official who has the authority to hear and decide complaints and disputes arising under the IT Act, particularly those involving financial penalties for contraventions. They function like a quasi-judicial authority — not a court, but empowered to investigate, hear parties, and impose compensation or penalties. Their role is similar to a referee or tribunal officer who resolves IT-related civil disputes without requiring parties to go to a full court.
real_world_examples: A customer complains that an e-commerce company based in Bengaluru leaked her personal data due to poor security practices; the adjudicating officer appointed under Section 46 hears the case and orders the company to pay compensation under Section 43.

A Mumbai-based bank fails to protect sensitive financial data of its customers, resulting in unauthorized access; the affected customers file a complaint before the adjudicating officer who adjudicates the claim and imposes a penalty on the bank.

A Delhi resident's identity is stolen through phishing, and the fraudster used the victim's credentials to access his net banking; the victim approaches the adjudicating officer seeking compensation from the internet service provider for failure to maintain due diligence.

A Hyderabad software firm is accused of unauthorised copying and use of a competitor's computer database; the competitor files a complaint before the adjudicating officer under the IT Act seeking adjudication of the contravention and award of damages.

A cyber cafe owner in Chennai is alleged to have knowingly allowed users to access obscene material in violation of the IT Act; the adjudicating officer is approached to determine liability and impose appropriate penalties.
what_it_covers: An officer of the Indian government with the rank of not below Director, appointed by the Central Government under Section 46(1) to adjudicate IT Act contraventions.
Any person duly notified and empowered to hold inquiries, summon parties, receive evidence, and impose compensation or penalties for contraventions under Sections 43, 43A, and related provisions.
The authority presiding over proceedings where individuals or bodies corporate are alleged to have caused loss or damage through unauthorised access, data theft, or other IT-related contraventions.
An officer whose decisions are subject to appeal before the Appellate Tribunal under Section 57 of the IT Act.
what_it_excludes: Judges of civil courts or criminal courts who handle offences under the IT Act — they operate under separate judicial proceedings and are not adjudicating officers.
The Appellate Tribunal constituted under Section 48, which is a distinct appellate body and not an adjudicating officer.
Police officers or investigating agencies (such as the Cyber Crime Cell) who investigate IT offences under penal provisions — their role is investigative, not adjudicatory under Section 46.
Arbitrators appointed under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act for IT-related commercial disputes, as they derive authority from contract rather than statutory appointment under Section 46.
The Controller of Certifying Authorities, whose functions relate to licensing and regulation of certifying authorities, not adjudication of contraventions.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as an 'adjudicating officer' determines who has the legal competence to impose compensation and penalties for contraventions under Sections 43 and 43A, and any order passed by a person not properly appointed under Section 46(1) would be without jurisdiction and void. This definition also governs the right of appeal under Section 57 — only orders made by an adjudicating officer can be challenged before the Appellate Tribunal, distinguishing such proceedings from criminal prosecutions before a court.

definitions.definition: ‗affixing electronic signature' with its grammatical variations and cognate expressions means adoption of any methodology or procedure by a person for the purpose of authenticating an electronic record by means of digital signature.
definitions.plain_english: Affixing an electronic signature means the act of applying or attaching a digital signature to an electronic document to prove that you are the one who created or approved it. It is the digital equivalent of physically signing a paper document. The process involves using a specific technical method or procedure that ties the signer's identity to the electronic record.
real_world_examples: A company director in Mumbai uses his digital signature certificate issued by a licensed Certifying Authority to digitally sign the annual financial statements before filing them on the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA21) portal.
A taxpayer in Delhi affixes their digital signature on their Income Tax Return (ITR) uploaded to the Income Tax Department's e-filing portal, thereby authenticating the electronic submission.

A lawyer in Chennai uses a USB-token-based digital signature certificate to sign and submit court pleadings electronically on the eCourts platform, authenticating the electronic records filed before the tribunal.
A government officer in Hyderabad affixes their electronic signature on an e-tender document published on the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) portal to authenticate the official procurement notice.
A borrower and a bank representative in Bengaluru both affix their digital signatures on an electronic loan agreement, making it a legally authenticated electronic record under the IT Act, 2000.
A registered medical practitioner affixes their digital signature on an electronic prescription sent via a telemedicine platform, authenticating the document as genuinely issued by them.
what_it_covers: Using a DSC (Digital Signature Certificate) issued by a licensed Certifying Authority to sign an electronic document, thereby completing the act of affixing an electronic signature.
Any technical procedure or methodology adopted by a person — such as using a private key with an asymmetric crypto system — to authenticate an electronic record.
Signing electronic contracts, forms, returns, or certificates on government portals like MCA21, GSTN, or Income Tax e-filing using a valid digital signature.
The act of a subscriber applying their digital signature to authenticate electronic records in any transaction governed by the IT Act, 2000.
what_it_excludes: Scanned images of handwritten signatures pasted into a PDF document, as these do not constitute adoption of a recognised methodology or procedure for authentication under the Act.
Typing one's name at the end of an email or electronic message, which is not a methodology or procedure for authenticating an electronic record as required by the definition.

Biometric-based or other electronic techniques that may constitute electronic signatures under the Second Schedule but are not specifically covered by the narrower concept of digital signature-based affixation referred to in this definition.
Passwords or PINs used for logging into a system, which serve as access credentials rather than as a methodology for authenticating a specific electronic record.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person has 'affixed an electronic signature' determines whether an electronic record is legally authenticated and enforceable under the IT Act, 2000, including for purposes of contract formation and evidentiary validity. It also determines liability and obligations under the Act — for instance, any unauthorised or fraudulent affixation of another person's electronic signature can attract criminal liability under sections dealing with fraud and impersonation.

definitions.definition: 'Appellate Tribunal' means the Appellate Tribunal referred to in sub-section (1) of section 48.
definitions.plain_english: The Appellate Tribunal is a specialised quasi-judicial body set up under the IT Act, 2000 to hear and decide appeals against orders passed by the Adjudicating Officer. It functions like a court for disputes arising under the IT Act, giving aggrieved parties a formal avenue to challenge decisions before approaching a High Court. In practice, the Cyber Appellate Tribunal (CyAT) has been designated to perform this role.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based e-commerce company penalised by the Adjudicating Officer under Section 43 for unauthorised data access files an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal challenging the quantum of compensation awarded.
An individual from Bengaluru whose digital signature certificate was suspended by a Certifying Authority appeals to the Appellate Tribunal under Section 57 seeking reinstatement of the certificate.

A Delhi-based internet service provider aggrieved by an order passed by the Adjudicating Officer directing it to pay damages for failure to exercise due diligence under Section 79 approaches the Appellate Tribunal for relief.
A Certifying Authority in Chennai whose licence was revoked by the Controller of Certifying Authorities files an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal contesting the revocation order under the IT Act.

A fintech startup penalised for contravention of data protection directions issued under the IT Act challenges the penalty order before the Appellate Tribunal, staying the enforcement of the original order pending the appeal.

Proceedings where the Appellate Tribunal exercises powers of a civil court in accordance with Section 58 of the IT Act.
Orders passed by the Appellate Tribunal that are binding on parties and enforceable as decrees of a civil court.
what_it_excludes: Original complaints or first-instance adjudication — the Appellate Tribunal does not hear matters that have not first been decided by the Adjudicating Officer or Controller.

Criminal proceedings under the IT Act — matters involving prosecution for offences such as hacking or cyber fraud are outside the Appellate Tribunal's jurisdiction and are tried by competent criminal courts.
Appeals against orders of the Appellate Tribunal itself — further appeals lie to the High Court under Section 62, not back to the Tribunal.
Disputes between private parties that do not arise from an order or decision under the IT Act, 2000, such as purely contractual or tortious claims unrelated to the Act.
Matters falling under the jurisdiction of any other statutory tribunal or regulatory body established under a separate law, such as TRAI or SEBI.

It also triggers the procedural powers and obligations set out in Sections 55–59 and 62.

definitions.definition: "appropriate Government" means as respects any matter enumerated in List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, the State Government; and relating to any State law enacted under List III of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, the State Government; and in any other case, the Central Government.
definitions.plain_english: The term 'appropriate Government' tells us which level of government — Central or State — has the authority to act on a particular matter under the IT Act. If the subject falls under the State List (List II) or a State law under the Concurrent List (List III) of the Indian Constitution, it is the State Government. For everything else, it is the Central Government. This distinction determines who is responsible for issuing orders, framing rules, or taking action in a given situation.
real_world_examples: When the Maharashtra State Government issues a notification directing its departments to use electronic records for land registration under Section 6, it acts as the 'appropriate Government' because land registration falls under List II (State List) of the Seventh Schedule.

When the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) at the Centre designates certain power grid computer systems as 'protected systems' under Section 70, the Central Government acts as the 'appropriate Government' since national critical infrastructure is a Union subject.

When the Telangana State Government sets up a State-level portal for delivery of services electronically under Section 6A, it functions as the 'appropriate Government' for matters relating to State services enumerated in the State List.

When rules are framed for regulating cyber cafes or directing service providers operating under a State law, the respective State Government (e.g., Karnataka or Tamil Nadu) is the 'appropriate Government' responsible for issuing those directions.

When the Central Government issues directions to block certain websites or online content that threaten national security under Section 69A, it acts as the 'appropriate Government' since public order and national security are Union subjects.

If a State enacts a law under List III (Concurrent List) regarding electronic contracts for agricultural produce trading within that State, the State Government is the 'appropriate Government' for matters arising under that State law.
what_it_covers: The Central Government, for all matters not specifically enumerated in List II or not relating to a State law under List III — such as national cybersecurity policy, Union-level electronic governance, and designation of protected systems.

The State Government, for matters enumerated in List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution — such as public health, land records, police, local government, and other State subjects where electronic governance is being implemented.

The State Government, for matters relating to any State law enacted under List III (Concurrent List) of the Seventh Schedule — such as a State-specific electronic commerce regulation or a State law governing electronic contracts in concurrent domains.
State Governments when directing their own departments to adopt electronic records or digital service delivery under Sections 6 and 6A for State-subject services.
The Central Government when notifying rules, exercising powers, or issuing directions under the IT Act on subjects that fall exclusively within Union jurisdiction.
what_it_excludes: Local bodies such as municipal corporations, panchayats, or district authorities — they are not 'appropriate Government' under the IT Act even if they exercise statutory functions.

Statutory regulators or autonomous bodies such as TRAI, SEBI, or RBI — even if they exercise regulatory power in technology-related matters, they do not qualify as 'appropriate Government' under this definition.

Union Territories without legislature, which are administered by the Central Government and therefore the Central Government acts in their place — the UT administration itself is not the 'appropriate Government' for IT Act purposes.
Private entities, industry associations, or self-regulatory organisations, regardless of their role in internet governance or cybersecurity — they are entirely outside the scope of this definition.

State Governments acting on matters that exclusively fall under List I (Union List) of the Seventh Schedule — in such cases, the State Government is not the 'appropriate Government' even if the matter has local ramifications.
definitions.why_it_matters: Identifying the 'appropriate Government' is critical because it determines which government body has the legal authority to issue notifications, frame rules, designate protected systems, or grant permissions under the IT Act — an action taken by the wrong level of government would be without jurisdiction and legally void. It also determines accountability and enforcement: obligations under Sections 6, 6A, and 70 attach to whichever government entity is 'appropriate', and failure by that entity to act or improper action by it could be challenged in a court of law.

definitions.definition: An Assistant Controller is an officer appointed by the Central Government under Section 17 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, to assist in the administration of the Act under the general superintendence and control of the Controller of Certifying Authorities, and may be authorised in writing by the Controller to exercise any of the Controller's powers under Chapter VI. An Assistant Controller is deemed to be a public servant within the meaning of Section 21 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
definitions.plain_english: An Assistant Controller is a government-appointed official who works under the Controller of Certifying Authorities to help manage and regulate digital signature and certifying authority-related functions under India's IT law. They can be given specific powers by the Controller to act on his behalf. Because they hold a government office, they are treated as public servants, which means they enjoy certain legal protections and are also held to strict standards of conduct.
real_world_examples: An Assistant Controller at the Office of the Controller of Certifying Authorities in New Delhi is delegated in writing by the Controller to inspect the premises and records of a licensed Certifying Authority such as eMudhra or (n)Code Solutions during a compliance audit.

When a complaint is filed against a Certifying Authority for improperly issuing a Digital Signature Certificate to an applicant who did not meet eligibility criteria, an Assistant Controller is authorised by the Controller to conduct the investigation and gather evidence under Chapter VI of the IT Act.

An Assistant Controller is assigned to review and process licence renewal applications submitted by Certifying Authorities operating in India, exercising delegated powers under Section 27 to ensure all prescribed documentation and fees are in order before forwarding recommendations to the Controller.

During a cyber security incident involving a compromised Certifying Authority's root certificate, an Assistant Controller acts under delegated authority to issue directions to the Certifying Authority to suspend issuance of new certificates pending inquiry, thereby protecting the integrity of the public key infrastructure in India.

A complainant files a case alleging that an Assistant Controller accepted a bribe to overlook irregularities in a Certifying Authority's operations; because the Assistant Controller is a public servant under Section 82 of the IT Act, the matter is referred to the CBI under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.

what_it_covers: An officer formally appointed by the Central Government via notification in the Official Gazette specifically for the purposes of the IT Act, 2000.

A person who performs functions assigned by the Controller under the Controller's general superintendence and control, including exercising delegated powers over Certifying Authorities under Chapter VI.
An individual who is deemed a public servant under Section 21 of the Indian Penal Code, attracting both the protections and liabilities associated with that status.
An officer whose qualifications, experience, and terms of service are prescribed by the Central Government under rules framed pursuant to Section 87 of the IT Act.
A person who can be specifically authorised in writing by the Controller under Section 27 to exercise any of the Controller's statutory powers under Chapter VI.
what_it_excludes: The Controller of Certifying Authorities himself, who is a separately defined and superior authority appointed under Section 17 and governed by distinct provisions.
Deputy Controllers, who are a distinct and hierarchically higher category of officer also appointed under Section 17 and separately named throughout the Act.
Private employees or contractual consultants engaged by the Office of the Controller who are not formally notified as Assistant Controllers by the Central Government in the Official Gazette.
Officers of licensed Certifying Authorities such as eMudhra or SafeScrypt, who operate in the private or quasi-government sector and are not part of the regulatory hierarchy under Section 17.
Adjudicating Officers appointed under Section 46 of the IT Act, who form a separate and independent quasi-judicial authority with distinct powers and appointment procedures.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of an individual as an Assistant Controller determines whether they can lawfully exercise delegated regulatory powers over Certifying Authorities under Chapter VI of the IT Act, making their actions in granting, suspending, or revoking licences legally valid. Additionally, their status as a public servant under Section 82 means that any obstruction, bribery, or dishonest conduct in relation to them attracts criminal liability under the Indian Penal Code and the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.

definitions.definition: "Asymmetric crypto system" means a system of a secure key pair consisting of a private key for creating a digital signature and a public key to verify the digital signature.
definitions.plain_english: An asymmetric crypto system is a two-key security setup where one key (private key) is kept secret by the owner and used to sign documents digitally, while the other key (public key) is shared openly and used by anyone to confirm the authenticity of that digital signature. The two keys are mathematically linked so that what one key locks, only the other can unlock or verify. This system ensures that only the genuine owner could have signed the document, since only they hold the private key.
real_world_examples: A taxpayer in India uses their private key issued by a licensed Certifying Authority to digitally sign their income tax return filed on the Income Tax e-filing portal; the Income Tax Department uses the corresponding public key to verify the authenticity of the signature.

A company director in Mumbai uses an asymmetric crypto system to sign Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA21) filings such as annual returns and financial statements, with the public key embedded in their Digital Signature Certificate allowing the Registrar of Companies to validate the filing.

A doctor registered on the NHA Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission platform uses their private key to digitally sign electronic prescriptions, and patients or pharmacies use the doctor's public key to confirm the prescription has not been tampered with.

A government officer in the Central Secretariat uses a Class 3 Digital Signature Certificate based on an asymmetric crypto system to sign e-procurement tender documents on the Government e-Marketplace (GeM), enabling vendors to verify the document's authenticity using the officer's public key.

An advocate filing a petition before the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) through the e-filing portal applies their private key to sign the petition electronically, and the tribunal's system uses the advocate's public key (from their DSC) to authenticate the submission before accepting it.
what_it_covers: A paired set of mathematically linked cryptographic keys where the private key is exclusively used to create a digital signature on an electronic record.

The public key component of the pair, which is made available to recipients or verifying parties to authenticate that the digital signature was indeed created by the holder of the corresponding private key.
Any secure key pair system issued by a licensed Certifying Authority in India (such as eMudhra, NIC, or Sify) and used for signing and verifying electronic records under the IT Act, 2000.
The underlying cryptographic infrastructure enabling Digital Signature Certificates issued under Section 35 of the IT Act, since such certificates are inherently based on asymmetric crypto systems.
what_it_excludes: Symmetric encryption systems where a single shared secret key is used by both parties for both encryption and decryption, as these do not involve separate private and public keys.
Simple password-based or PIN-based authentication mechanisms that do not involve a mathematically linked key pair for signature creation and verification.
Hash functions used standalone (without an associated key pair) for data integrity verification, as they do not constitute a key pair system for creating or verifying digital signatures.
Biometric authentication systems (such as fingerprint or iris scans) used for identity verification, which are not based on a cryptographic key pair structure.
Manual or wet-ink handwritten signatures and their authentication processes, which fall entirely outside the scope of any cryptographic system.
definitions.why_it_matters: The legal validity of a digital signature under Section 3 of the IT Act, 2000 is entirely predicated on the use of an asymmetric crypto system, meaning that any purported digital signature not generated through such a system cannot be accorded legal recognition as a valid digital signature under the Act. Whether a document is considered legally authenticated — triggering enforceability of contracts, admissibility of electronic records as evidence, and compliance with e-governance mandates — depends directly on whether the signing mechanism qualifies as an asymmetric crypto system as defined.

definitions.definition: Authentication of any electronic record by a subscriber by means of an electronic technique or procedure, including digital signature, so as to establish the genuineness and integrity of the record and to identify the person who has signed or sent it. Under Section 5 of the Act, where any law provides that information or any other matter shall be authenticated by affixing the signature, such requirement shall be deemed to have been satisfied if such information or matter is authenticated by means of digital signature affixed in the manner prescribed by the Act.
definitions.plain_english: Authentication means verifying that an electronic document or message is genuine and that it was indeed created or sent by the person who claims to have sent it. It is the digital equivalent of signing your name on a paper document to confirm it is real and that it comes from you. Under Indian law, a digital signature is the primary way to authenticate electronic records, giving them the same legal standing as a handwritten signature.
real_world_examples: A taxpayer in Mumbai uses their digital signature certificate (DSC) issued by a licensed Certifying Authority to authenticate and file their Income Tax Return on the e-filing portal, thereby legally establishing that the return was submitted by them.

A company director in Bengaluru authenticates the Memorandum of Association submitted to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA21 portal) using a Class 3 DSC, fulfilling the statutory requirement of signature under the Companies Act.
A government officer in Delhi authenticates an official government notification before it is published in the Electronic Gazette, ensuring its legal validity under Section 8 of the IT Act.
A lawyer in Chennai uses an Aadhaar-based electronic signature (eSign) to authenticate an affidavit submitted to an e-court, which the court recognises as legally equivalent to a physical signature.

A bank in Hyderabad authenticates electronic fund transfer instructions sent through its secure system using asymmetric cryptography, ensuring that only the verified account holder can authorise transactions.
what_it_covers: Authentication of electronic records using a digital signature issued by a licensed Certifying Authority under Section 35 of the IT Act.
Authentication using any electronic technique specified in the Second Schedule to the IT Act, including Aadhaar-based eSign services.
Statutory satisfaction of signature requirements under other laws (e.g., Companies Act, Income Tax Act) when an electronic record is authenticated by digital signature as per Section 5.

definitions.definition: Authentication data means the data that is linked to the authenticator and used in the process of electronic authentication, which within the context of its use, is linked to the authenticator and to no other person, and was at the time of authentication under the control of the authenticator and of no other person, as described under Section 3A(2) of the Information Technology Act, 2000.
definitions.plain_english: Authentication data is the unique digital information or credentials that an individual uses to prove their identity when authenticating an electronic record. Think of it like a digital fingerprint or secret key that belongs exclusively to one person and is used to confirm that they are the one signing or approving a digital document. Just as a handwritten signature is unique to a person, authentication data is the digital equivalent that ties an electronic action specifically to the person who performed it.
real_world_examples: A taxpayer logging into the Income Tax e-filing portal using an Aadhaar-based OTP (One-Time Password) — the OTP and associated biometric or demographic data used in that session constitute authentication data linking the filing to that specific taxpayer.

A government employee of a State Secretariat using a USB-based cryptographic token (hardware security module) to digitally sign official government orders on the e-Office platform — the PIN and cryptographic keys stored within the token serve as authentication data.

A customer of HDFC Bank authenticating a high-value NEFT transfer using their registered mobile number OTP combined with a grid-card value — the combination of these credentials forms authentication data for that specific transaction.

A doctor registered on the National Medical Commission portal using their NMC-issued digital certificate and associated private key to authenticate medical prescriptions issued via telemedicine — the private key and certificate data are the authentication data.

An advocate filing a petition on the Supreme Court of India's e-filing system using their Bar Council digital signature certificate — the cryptographic data embedded in the certificate and used during the signing process constitutes authentication data.

A company director authenticating the filing of annual returns on the Ministry of Corporate Affairs MCA21 portal using a Class 3 Digital Signature Certificate issued by a licensed Certifying Authority — the authentication data is the private key and digital certificate used during that signing event.
what_it_covers: Cryptographic private keys used exclusively by an authenticator to authenticate an electronic record under a recognised electronic authentication technique listed in the Second Schedule.
Biometric data such as fingerprints or iris scans linked to an individual and used through an Aadhaar-based e-KYC system to authenticate electronic documents.
One-Time Passwords (OTPs) or PINs that are dynamically generated and exclusively controlled by the authenticator at the moment of authentication of an electronic record.
Digital certificate-based credentials stored in hardware security tokens (USB dongles) issued by a licensed Certifying Authority, used by a subscriber to authenticate government filings.

Any other data element forming part of an electronic authentication technique specified in the Second Schedule that is uniquely linked to the authenticator and under their sole control at the time of authentication.
what_it_excludes: Signature creation data used by a signatory for the purpose of creating a digital signature under Section 3, which is a distinct concept from authentication data used under Section 3A.

Shared or common credentials such as generic departmental login passwords used by multiple officials, since authentication data must be linked to one and only one authenticator and under their exclusive control.
Data used merely to verify an already-authenticated electronic record (verification data or public keys), rather than data used in the act of authentication itself.

Physical identity documents such as Aadhaar cards, PAN cards, or passports presented offline, as these are not electronic data used in the process of electronic authentication of an electronic record.

Authentication attempts made using credentials that have been compromised, shared, or are no longer under the exclusive control of the authenticator, as such data would not satisfy the reliability conditions of Section 3A(2).
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether data qualifies as valid 'authentication data' under Section 3A determines whether an electronic authentication technique is deemed reliable, which in turn decides the legal enforceability and evidentiary validity of the authenticated electronic record in judicial and administrative proceedings. If the authentication data does not meet the conditions of Section 3A(2) — particularly exclusive linkage and control — the electronic signature or authentication technique fails the reliability test, rendering the electronic record legally unauthenticated and potentially inadmissible or unenforceable.

definitions.definition: "Authorised access" is not explicitly defined in Section 2 of the Information Technology Act, 2000; however, as used in Section 66F (cyber terrorism), it refers to access to a computer resource that is permitted, sanctioned, or granted by the owner or administrator of that resource, whether through credentials, contractual arrangement, or lawful authority, as distinguished from unauthorised access which is prohibited under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: Authorised access means that a person has been given proper permission to enter or use a computer system, network, or data by whoever owns or controls it. Think of it like having a valid key to a building — you are allowed to be there. In contrast, someone who breaks in without permission has unauthorised access. Under the IT Act, whether your access is authorised or not can determine whether you have committed a serious crime like cyber terrorism.
real_world_examples: A network administrator at a Mumbai-based bank who uses her login credentials to access the bank's core banking servers during routine maintenance is exercising authorised access — she has been explicitly granted permission by her employer to enter those systems.

A CERT-In empanelled cybersecurity auditor hired by a Bengaluru software firm to conduct a penetration test has authorised access to that firm's servers because the client has signed a formal agreement permitting the auditor to probe the systems.

A government employee in Delhi who uses his official NICNET credentials to access the National Informatics Centre's internal databases for performing his assigned duties is considered to have authorised access to those specific resources.

A telecom engineer at a BSNL facility in Chennai who is granted temporary system-level access by her supervisor to diagnose a network fault has authorised access for the duration and scope defined by that permission, even if she would not normally have such elevated privileges.

An ethical hacker engaged by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under a bug bounty programme to identify vulnerabilities in the government's digital infrastructure is exercising authorised access within the boundaries defined by the programme's rules of engagement.

A software developer at an IT company in Hyderabad who uses his role-based access control (RBAC) credentials to retrieve source code from the company's version control repository is exercising authorised access as defined by his employment contract and company policy.
what_it_covers: Access by an employee to employer-owned computer systems using credentials issued as part of their employment contract or job role.
Access by a third-party vendor, auditor, or contractor to a client's computer network pursuant to a written agreement or formal work order explicitly granting such permission.
Access by a government official or law enforcement agency to computer resources under a lawful order, warrant, or statutory authority granted by a competent authority.
Access by a system owner or administrator to their own computer resource, network, or database for management, maintenance, or operational purposes.
Access granted through technical mechanisms such as username-password authentication, digital certificates, API keys, or biometric authentication set up by the resource owner.
what_it_excludes: Access to a computer system by exploiting vulnerabilities, malware, or hacking techniques without the knowledge or consent of the system owner, even if the intruder believes the information is publicly important.
Access that exceeds the scope of granted permission — for example, an employee who uses their legitimate login to access databases or files outside their designated role or authorisation level.
Access obtained through deception, phishing, social engineering, or impersonation of an authorised user, since the underlying permission was never genuinely granted.
Access by a former employee using old, revoked credentials after their employment has been terminated, as the authorisation no longer exists.
Access by one person using another person's credentials without that person's explicit, current consent, even if the two individuals are colleagues within the same organisation.
definitions.why_it_matters: Under Section 66F of the IT Act, cyber terrorism offences specifically involve acts committed through 'authorised or unauthorised access' to computer resources with intent to threaten India's unity, security, or cause terror — meaning that even a person with legitimate access credentials can be prosecuted for cyber terrorism if they misuse that access with the requisite criminal intent. Conversely, establishing that access was genuinely authorised and used within its permitted scope is a critical defence that can negate liability not only under Section 66F but also under related offences such as Sections 43, 66, and 70 of the Act.

definitions.definition: An offence is 'bailable' under the Information Technology Act, 2000, where the punishment prescribed is imprisonment of three years (and not above three years), entitling the accused as a matter of right to be released on bail upon furnishing the required surety or bond, notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
definitions.plain_english: A 'bailable' offence is one where a person who is arrested has a legal right to get bail — meaning they can be released from custody by paying a security amount or giving a guarantee, and the police or court cannot refuse bail. Under the IT Act, this applies to offences where the maximum punishment is exactly three years of imprisonment. This is different from more serious offences where bail is not automatic and the court must decide whether to grant it.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai is arrested for sending repeated offensive electronic messages under Section 66A (before it was struck down) carrying a punishment of three years — being a bailable offence, the accused can walk out of the police station upon furnishing a bail bond without needing a court hearing.

An individual in Bengaluru accused of breach of confidentiality and privacy under Section 72 of the IT Act, which carries imprisonment up to two years, is entitled to bail as a matter of right since the offence is bailable.

A small business owner in Delhi is arrested for failure to protect sensitive personal data leading to a data breach, where the prescribed punishment does not exceed three years — the accused can secure bail at the police station itself without approaching a magistrate.

A cybercafe operator in Hyderabad charged under a provision of the IT Act carrying a three-year sentence is entitled to bailable status, meaning the police must release them on bail once the required surety is produced, unlike more serious cybercrime offences that are non-bailable.

A young engineer in Pune arrested for computer-related impersonation under Section 66D (punishable with imprisonment up to three years) is entitled to bail as a right under Section 77B, and the arresting officer must facilitate the bail process at the station level itself.
what_it_covers: Offences under the IT Act, 2000 where the maximum prescribed punishment is imprisonment of exactly three years, entitling the accused to bail as a matter of right.
Situations where an accused arrested by police for a three-year IT Act offence can demand release on bail at the police station itself without requiring a court order.
IT Act offences carrying a punishment of less than three years imprisonment, which are similarly bailable and permit the accused to secure release upon furnishing the required bond or surety.

Cases where the overriding provision in Section 77B displaces the default categorisation under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, making certain IT Act offences bailable despite CrPC classifications.
what_it_excludes: Offences under the IT Act punishable with imprisonment of more than three years, which are classified as cognizable and non-bailable, and for which the accused must apply to a court for bail.
Serious cybercrimes such as offences against critical information infrastructure or those involving child pornography that carry punishments exceeding three years and are therefore non-bailable.

Offences under other laws (e.g., Indian Penal Code, POCSO Act) that may be invoked alongside IT Act charges — the bailable classification under Section 77B applies only to the specific IT Act provision in question and not automatically to charges under other statutes.

Situations where the accused is charged under a provision carrying a punishment higher than three years — even if the actual sentence awarded is three years or less, the offence itself remains non-bailable at the stage of arrest.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an offence is classified as 'bailable' under Section 77B directly determines whether an accused has an enforceable right to immediate release upon arrest or must remain in custody pending a court's discretionary bail order; it therefore governs personal liberty, the burden on courts, and the leverage available to investigating agencies during the investigation of IT Act offences.

definitions.definition: A 'Bench' means a sitting or panel of one or more Members of the Appellate Tribunal constituted to hear and decide appeals or matters before it; where a Bench consists of two Members and they differ in opinion on any point, the point of difference is referred to the Chairperson who hears it and the matter is decided according to the opinion of the majority of all Members who have heard the case.
definitions.plain_english: A Bench is a group of one or more judges (called Members) of the Cyber Appellate Tribunal who sit together to hear and decide a case. If two Members on a Bench disagree on a legal point, that disagreement is sent to the head of the Tribunal (the Chairperson) to resolve. The final answer is whatever the majority of all Members who heard the case agree on.
real_world_examples: A company appeals against an adjudicating officer's penalty order for a data breach under Section 43; a Bench of two Members of the Cyber Appellate Tribunal is constituted to hear the appeal and pronounce judgment.

Two Members of the Appellate Tribunal hearing an appeal filed by a Certifying Authority against cancellation of its licence disagree on whether due process was followed; they state the point of difference and refer it to the Chairperson, who then hears that specific issue along with both Members to arrive at a majority decision.

A single-Member Bench of the Appellate Tribunal in New Delhi hears and disposes of a preliminary objection regarding jurisdiction in a case involving an intermediary based in Mumbai who failed to observe due diligence obligations.

A Bench is specially constituted by the Chairperson to hear an urgent appeal challenging a government order declaring a private computer resource a 'protected system', with the Bench required to deliver its decision expeditiously to prevent irreparable harm.

In a case where an individual challenges an adjudicating officer's compensation award for unauthorised access to a computer database, a two-Member Bench hears both parties; on the quantum of compensation the Members differ, and the Chairperson is brought in to form a majority opinion.
what_it_covers: A panel of two Members of the Cyber Appellate Tribunal constituted to hear an appeal and differing on a point of law or fact, thereby triggering the majority-decision mechanism under Section 52D.
A single-Member sitting of the Appellate Tribunal assigned to hear and decide a specific appeal or interlocutory matter before the Tribunal.
A multi-Member Bench including the Chairperson who joins to resolve a referred point of difference, forming the enlarged panel whose majority opinion becomes the binding decision.
Any Bench specially constituted by the Chairperson to hear urgent or complex matters arising under the Information Technology Act, 2000.
what_it_excludes: An adjudicating officer appointed under Section 46 of the Act, who is not a Member of the Appellate Tribunal and does not constitute a Bench.
Courts of civil jurisdiction, High Courts, or the Supreme Court of India, which are separate constitutional or statutory bodies and are not Benches of the Cyber Appellate Tribunal.

A single official or government functionary exercising administrative or executive powers under the Act (such as the Controller of Certifying Authorities) who hears representations but is not constituted as a Bench.
Committees such as the Cyber Regulations Advisory Committee, which advise on policy matters and do not adjudicate disputes as a Bench.
definitions.why_it_matters: The constitution and functioning of a Bench directly determines the validity of appellate decisions made by the Cyber Appellate Tribunal — an improperly constituted Bench could render its orders void or challengeable. The majority-decision mechanism under Section 52D ensures that every point of legal difference is conclusively resolved, thereby determining whether a penalty, compensation award, or licensing decision is upheld or set aside.

definitions.definition: "Body corporate" means any company and includes a firm, sole proprietorship or other association of individuals engaged in commercial or professional activities. [Section 43A(b)(i), Information Technology Act, 2000]
definitions.plain_english: A 'body corporate' is any organised business or commercial entity — it covers not just registered companies but also partnerships, sole proprietors, and any group of people working together for business or professional purposes. Essentially, if an organisation handles data or provides services for commercial gain, it likely qualifies as a body corporate under this law. This matters because such entities have legal duties to protect personal data and must follow directions from agencies like CERT-In.
real_world_examples: A Bengaluru-based IT services company like Infosys or Wipro that stores employee and client data on its servers is a body corporate and must maintain reasonable security practices to protect that sensitive information under Section 43A.

A sole proprietorship running an online tutoring platform in Mumbai that collects students' Aadhaar numbers and payment details qualifies as a body corporate and can be held liable for compensation if it fails to secure that data and a breach occurs.

A chartered accountancy firm (partnership) in Delhi that handles clients' financial records and tax information digitally is a body corporate and must comply with CERT-In's directions under Section 70B when a cyber incident is reported.

A private hospital chain operating as a company across multiple cities in India that maintains electronic health records of patients is a body corporate and is liable to pay damages if patient data is exposed due to negligent security practices.

A startup registered as a Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) in Hyderabad that operates an e-commerce marketplace and processes customer personal data is treated as a body corporate, making it subject to both data protection obligations and CERT-In compliance requirements.

A cooperative society of professionals offering legal services digitally and collecting client information through an online portal would be considered an association of individuals engaged in professional activities and thus fall within the definition of body corporate.

A sole proprietorship running an online business, e-commerce store, or digital service that collects and processes customer data.
An association of individuals — such as a society or trust — engaged in professional or commercial activities involving digital data.
Data centres and service providers operating as any of the above entity forms that handle third-party personal data as part of their business operations.
what_it_excludes: Government departments and ministries acting in a purely sovereign or administrative capacity, as they are not engaged in 'commercial or professional activities' in the ordinary sense.
Individual natural persons acting in their personal capacity, even if they incidentally process some data, as they are not an 'association' or incorporated entity.
Non-profit charitable organisations or trusts that have no commercial or professional activity dimension and do not deal in sensitive personal data for business purposes.
Entities that are purely statutory bodies constituted under special legislation and not engaged in commercial activity, such as certain regulatory commissions.

An ad hoc informal group of individuals with no business purpose, structure, or continuity, as they do not constitute a legally recognisable 'association of individuals engaged in commercial or professional activities'.

definitions.definition: "Capture", with respect to an image, means to videotape, photograph, film or record by any means.
definitions.plain_english: "Capture" means to record a visual image of a person using any method or device, including taking a photograph, making a video, filming, or recording through any other technological means. It does not matter what device or technique is used — if a visual image is being recorded, it counts as capturing. This term is used specifically in the context of recording images of private body parts without a person's consent.
real_world_examples: A person uses a hidden smartphone camera placed in a changing room of a clothing store in Mumbai to secretly photograph customers while they are undressing, thereby capturing images of their private areas without consent.
An individual fixes a miniature spy camera underneath a desk or in a public restroom in Delhi to record the private areas of unsuspecting persons who use the facility.
Someone uses a camera concealed in spectacles or a watch to film a woman's private areas in a crowded local train in Chennai without her knowledge or consent.
A tenant secretly installs a recording device inside a rented flat in Bengaluru to videotape the private areas of another occupant while they change clothes or use the bathroom.
A person at a beach in Goa uses a drone equipped with a camera to zoom in and record close-up footage of individuals' private areas without their awareness or permission.
what_it_covers: Secretly photographing a person's private area using a smartphone camera without their consent.
Videotaping or filming a person's private area using any recording device, including spy cameras, drones, or wearable gadgets.
Recording a person's private area by any technological means, including analog film cameras, digital cameras, or CCTV systems used for voyeuristic purposes.
Using screen-recording software or any digital tool to record a live video feed showing a person's private area.
what_it_excludes: Merely viewing or observing a private area without making any recording — since 'capture' specifically requires the creation of a recorded image.
Transmitting or sharing an already-recorded image, which falls under 'transmit' or 'publishes' rather than 'capture'.
Accidental or incidental recording of a private area where there is no intentional or knowing act of capturing the image, as Section 66E requires the act to be intentional or knowing.
Capturing images of public areas or non-private body parts of a person, which does not fall within the scope of this definition as used in Section 66E.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'capture' under Section 66E determines whether the primary offence of violation of privacy is constituted — without a 'capture', there can be no subsequent publishing or transmission offence under this section. A finding that 'capture' occurred exposes the accused to imprisonment of up to three years and/or a fine of up to two lakh rupees.

definitions.definition: "Certification practice statement" means a statement issued by a Certifying Authority to specify the practices that the Certifying Authority employs in issuing electronic signature Certificates.
definitions.plain_english: A certification practice statement is an official document published by a licensed certificate-issuing authority that explains exactly how it verifies identities, issues digital certificates, and manages them. Think of it as a rulebook or policy manual that tells users what procedures the authority follows to ensure the certificates it issues are trustworthy. It helps the public and businesses understand the security standards and processes behind the digital certificates they rely on.
real_world_examples: eMudhra Limited, a licensed Certifying Authority in India, publishes its Certification Practice Statement detailing how it verifies the identity of an applicant before issuing a Class 3 Digital Signature Certificate used for income tax e-filing.

The National Informatics Centre (NIC), acting as a Certifying Authority for government entities, issues a CPS explaining its procedures for issuing digital certificates to Central and State Government employees for signing official electronic documents.

A private Certifying Authority registered with the Controller of Certifying Authorities under the IT Act publishes its CPS to specify its key generation ceremonies, subscriber authentication steps, and certificate revocation procedures used while issuing electronic signature certificates to banks for online transactions.

Safescrypt (a licensed CA in India) maintained a CPS describing its practices for issuing SSL and code-signing certificates, including how it validated company registration documents before certificate issuance, which was scrutinised during a compliance audit by the Controller of Certifying Authorities.

During a dispute over the authenticity of a digitally signed contract in a Bombay High Court proceeding, the court referred to the relevant Certifying Authority's certification practice statement under Section 34 of the IT Act to determine whether proper issuance procedures were followed.
what_it_covers: The identity verification and authentication procedures a Certifying Authority uses before issuing an Electronic Signature Certificate to a subscriber.
The key generation, storage, and protection practices employed by the Certifying Authority for its own root and intermediate certificates.
Certificate revocation and suspension procedures, including how and when the Certifying Authority will revoke an issued certificate.
Disclosure obligations and liability limitations that the Certifying Authority places on subscribers and relying parties.
Security controls, audit practices, and physical safeguards maintained by the Certifying Authority at its facilities.
what_it_excludes: General privacy policies or terms of service of the Certifying Authority that do not relate to certificate issuance practices.
Subscriber agreements or end-user licence agreements signed individually between a subscriber and the Certifying Authority, which are separate contractual documents.
Technical specifications or standards documents published by third-party bodies (such as BIS or ISO) that the CA may follow but did not itself issue as its own CPS.
Statements or policies issued by entities that are not licensed Certifying Authorities under Section 24 of the IT Act.
Informal internal operating procedures not officially published or notified as part of the formal CPS under Sections 22 and 34 of the IT Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Under Sections 22 and 34 of the IT Act, a Certifying Authority is legally required to include the certification practice statement in every Electronic Signature Certificate it issues, and must publish it in a recognised repository; failure to do so can result in suspension or revocation of the CA's licence under Section 25 and makes the Authority liable for damages to subscribers and relying parties under Section 43A. The CPS also serves as the primary evidentiary document in disputes over whether a certificate was issued in accordance with lawful procedures, directly affecting the certificate's legal validity.

definitions.definition: 'Certifying Authority' means a person who has been granted a licence to issue a Digital Signature Certificate under section 24.
definitions.plain_english: A Certifying Authority is an organisation or individual that has been officially licensed by the government to issue digital certificates that verify the identity of people using digital signatures online. Think of them like a trusted passport office, but for the digital world — they confirm that a digital signature truly belongs to the person who claims to own it. Only those who have received a formal licence under the IT Act can legally perform this role in India.
real_world_examples: eMudhra Limited, a licensed Certifying Authority in India, issues Digital Signature Certificates to chartered accountants filing income tax returns electronically on the Income Tax e-Filing portal.

The National Informatics Centre (NIC), acting as a licensed Certifying Authority, issues Digital Signature Certificates to government officials for signing e-tendering documents on the Government e-Marketplace (GeM).

SafeScrypt (a Sify Technologies company), as a licensed Certifying Authority, issues Class 3 Digital Signature Certificates to company directors for e-filing of documents with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA21 portal).

CDAC (Centre for Development of Advanced Computing) as a licensed Certifying Authority issues Digital Signature Certificates to users of the IRCTC platform to authenticate high-value railway procurement contracts.

A Certifying Authority such as (n)Code Solutions issues certificates to exporters for digitally signing shipping bills and customs documents filed on the ICEGATE portal of the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs.
what_it_covers: Any person or organisation that has been formally granted a licence under Section 24 of the IT Act, 2000 to issue Electronic Signature Certificates or Digital Signature Certificates.

Private companies such as eMudhra, SafeScrypt, and (n)Code Solutions that have obtained a licence from the Controller of Certifying Authorities and operate as recognised trust service providers in India.
Government entities such as NIC and CDAC that have been licensed by the Controller to issue Digital Signature Certificates to public authorities and government departments.
Any foreign certifying authority that has been recognised by the Controller under Section 19 of the IT Act as equivalent to a domestic Certifying Authority licensed under the Act.
what_it_excludes: Any person, company, or organisation that issues digital certificates without having obtained a formal licence under Section 24 of the IT Act, regardless of their technical capability.
The Controller of Certifying Authorities himself, who is the regulatory authority overseeing Certifying Authorities but is not a Certifying Authority issuing certificates to subscribers.
Subscribers who merely hold and use a Digital Signature Certificate issued by a licensed Certifying Authority — they receive the certificate but are not themselves authorised to issue certificates.
Technology vendors or software providers who supply public key infrastructure (PKI) software or hardware to Certifying Authorities but have not themselves obtained a licence to issue certificates.
Intermediaries such as Registration Authorities (RAs) that verify applicant identity on behalf of a Certifying Authority but are not themselves licensed to issue Digital Signature Certificates.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as a 'Certifying Authority' under the IT Act determines whether the Digital Signature Certificates it issues are legally valid and admissible as proof of authentication under the Act; only licenced Certifying Authorities can lawfully issue such certificates, and contravening this triggers penalties under Sections 44 and 68, while obligations related to maintaining security standards, disclosure of compromise, and suspension or revocation of certificates under Sections 31, 37, 38, and 39 apply exclusively to entities meeting this definition.

real_world_examples: eMudhra Limited, a licensed Certifying Authority in India, issues Digital Signature Certificates (DSCs) used by chartered accountants and company directors to file returns with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA21 portal).

The National Informatics Centre (NIC), operating as a Certifying Authority, issues DSCs to government employees and departments so that official electronic communications and e-tendering processes can be digitally authenticated.
Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), holding a Certifying Authority licence, issues Class 3 DSCs to individuals and organisations for use in income tax e-filing on the Income Tax Department's portal.

SafeScrypt (a Sify Technologies subsidiary), as a licensed Certifying Authority, provides DSCs to importers and exporters for use on the DGFT (Directorate General of Foreign Trade) e-platform for submitting trade-related documents electronically.

CDAC (Centre for Development of Advanced Computing), acting as a Certifying Authority, issues DSCs to academic institutions and research bodies for secure electronic correspondence and official digital transactions with government bodies.

A licensed Certifying Authority issues a DSC to a property owner in Maharashtra enabling them to execute and register e-agreements on the state's online document registration portal without visiting a sub-registrar office.
what_it_covers: A private company that has applied for and been granted a licence by the Controller of Certifying Authorities under section 24 to issue Electronic Signature Certificates, such as eMudhra Limited or SafeScrypt.
A government body or department that has been granted a Certifying Authority licence, such as NIC (National Informatics Centre) or CDAC, issuing DSCs for official and public use.

A person (legal or natural) operating under a valid, subsisting licence under section 24, complying with certification practice statement requirements and obligations under sections 30–34 of the IT Act.
An entity that issues both Digital Signature Certificates (a subset) and broader Electronic Signature Certificates, provided it holds the requisite licence.
A foreign Certifying Authority recognised by the Controller under the Act for issuing certificates valid within the Indian legal framework.
what_it_excludes: A person or organisation that merely applies for a licence but has not yet been granted one under section 24 — the licence grant is the operative condition.
An individual subscriber who holds and uses a Digital Signature Certificate issued by a Certifying Authority; the subscriber is not themselves a Certifying Authority.

A technology service provider or software vendor that supplies PKI software or cryptographic tools without holding an independent Certifying Authority licence under section 24.

definitions.plain_english: The Chairperson is the head of the Appellate Tribunal set up under the IT Act, appointed by the Central Government to oversee its functioning. When two members of the Tribunal disagree on a legal point, the Chairperson steps in to hear the matter and cast the deciding vote. The Chairperson's appointment is legally protected and cannot be challenged in any court or forum.
real_world_examples: Two Members of the IT Appellate Tribunal in New Delhi are hearing an appeal against a penalty imposed by an Adjudicating Officer for a data breach. They disagree on whether the company exercised 'due diligence'. The case is referred to the Chairperson, who hears both sides and gives the majority opinion that decides the outcome.

The Central Government issues a notification in the Official Gazette appointing a retired High Court judge as the Chairperson of the Cyber Appellate Tribunal. A losing party in an earlier case tries to challenge this appointment, but Section 55 bars any court from questioning such an order.

A company penalised under the IT Act appeals to the Cyber Appellate Tribunal. The Bench of two Members splits on the question of quantum of compensation. The Chairperson is called upon to hear the disputed point personally and resolve it by majority, ensuring the appeal is decided.

During a proceeding before the Cyber Appellate Tribunal challenging an order of the Controller of Certifying Authorities, an objection is raised that the Tribunal was not properly constituted. Section 55 protects the Tribunal's proceedings from being invalidated on this ground, a protection that directly rests on the validity of the Chairperson's appointment.

A telecom intermediary challenges a penalty order under the IT Act before the Appellate Tribunal. The Bench disagrees on whether the intermediary had knowledge of the unlawful content hosted on its platform. The Chairperson, acting under Section 52D, hears the referred point and gives the decisive opinion.

The Chairperson's vote as part of the majority opinion that finally determines the referred point in a split Bench decision.
what_it_excludes: An Adjudicating Officer appointed under Section 46, who is a separate quasi-judicial authority and not part of the Appellate Tribunal.
Ordinary Members of the Appellate Tribunal who sit on a Bench but do not carry the presiding and tie-breaking functions of the Chairperson.
The Controller of Certifying Authorities, who is an executive/regulatory authority under the Act, distinct from the judicial Chairperson of the Tribunal.
Any officer of the Central or State Government who may exercise administrative powers under the IT Act but does not preside over the Appellate Tribunal.
A presiding officer of any other tribunal or forum constituted under different legislation, such as TDSAT or SAT, even if they hold the title 'Chairperson'.
