definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 67B, 'children' means a person who has not completed the age of 18 years.
definitions.plain_english: Under the IT Act, a 'child' is any person who is below 18 years of age. This definition is specifically used when dealing with laws about protecting children from sexual exploitation online. Once a person turns 18, they are no longer considered a 'child' for the purposes of this section.
real_world_examples: A 15-year-old student from Mumbai whose photographs are downloaded and distributed by an adult in sexually explicit digital content would be considered a 'child' under this section, triggering criminal liability for the offender under Section 67B.

An operator of a Telegram group in Delhi who shares obscene digital images or videos depicting a 17-year-old is exploiting a 'child' as defined, and faces up to five years imprisonment on first conviction.

A person in Bengaluru who uses a social media platform to entice a 16-year-old into an online relationship for sexually explicit acts is targeting a 'child' under Section 67B, making the act a cognizable offence.

A website hosted on Indian servers that advertises or promotes digitally created indecent content depicting minors aged under 18 is dealing with material involving 'children' as defined, and its operators are liable under this section.

A school teacher in Chennai who records on a mobile phone sexually explicit acts involving a 14-year-old student and stores it in electronic form is committing an offence involving a 'child' under Section 67B of the IT Act.
what_it_covers: Any person below 18 years of age depicted in sexually explicit or obscene material in electronic form.
A 17-year-old who is enticed, induced, or cultivated into an online relationship for sexually explicit purposes.
A minor under 18 years whose abuse is recorded, distributed, advertised, or downloaded in any electronic form.
A child under 18 who is facilitated to be abused online, regardless of whether they appear to have consented.
what_it_excludes: Any person who has completed 18 years of age, who falls outside this definition for the purposes of Section 67B.
Adults aged 18 or above depicted in sexually explicit electronic content, whose material is governed by other provisions such as Section 67 or 67A rather than Section 67B.

Content depicting children that is maintained bona fide for heritage or religious purposes, or is justified as being in the public good in the interest of science, literature, art or learning, as carved out by the proviso to Section 67B.
Persons of unverified age where no material or context confirms they are below 18, though investigative agencies may still pursue based on apparent age.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a victim as a 'child' under Section 67B is the threshold that activates the specific and more stringent offences under that section, including punishment up to five years on first conviction and seven years on subsequent conviction, with fines up to ten lakh rupees. If the victim does not fall within this definition, the conduct may fall under the less specific provisions of Section 67 or 67A rather than the child-specific protections of Section 67B.

definitions.definition: An offence is 'cognizable' under the Information Technology Act, 2000 if it is punishable with imprisonment of three years and above, as provided under Section 77B, which states that such offences shall be cognizable notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. A cognizable offence is one in which a police officer may arrest a person without a warrant, investigate, and take other actions without prior permission of a Magistrate.
definitions.plain_english: A 'cognizable' offence is one serious enough that the police can arrest the accused person immediately without needing to get permission from a court first. Under the IT Act, any offence that carries a punishment of three years or more in jail is treated as cognizable. This means police have stronger powers to act quickly — they can arrest, search, and investigate without waiting for a warrant.
real_world_examples: A hacker in Mumbai breaches the servers of a nationalised bank and steals customer data; since the offence under Section 66 carries punishment exceeding three years, police can arrest him on the spot without a Magistrate's warrant.

Delhi Police receive a complaint that an individual has been sending obscene content to a minor through a social media platform; as the offence under Section 67B is punishable with five years imprisonment, it is cognizable and officers can take immediate action including arrest.

A cyber cell in Hyderabad discovers that a group is operating a phishing network that has defrauded thousands of citizens; the offence under Section 66C (identity theft, punishable with three years) is cognizable, enabling police to raid premises and detain suspects without prior judicial approval.

A Bengaluru-based employee leaks confidential data of a protected system to a foreign entity; the offence under Section 70 carries imprisonment up to ten years, making it cognizable — the Central Industrial Security Force and cyber police can arrest the accused without a warrant.

In Chennai, police intercept communications revealing that a person is planning a ransomware attack on critical information infrastructure; since the anticipated offence carries more than three years imprisonment, authorities can arrest and investigate the suspect immediately under their cognizable offence powers.
what_it_covers: Any offence under the IT Act that is punishable with imprisonment of three years and above, such as hacking under Section 66, identity theft under Section 66C, and cyber terrorism under Section 66F.
Offences involving obscene or sexually explicit material involving children under Section 67B, which carry imprisonment of five years on first conviction and seven years on subsequent convictions.
Offences relating to breach of confidentiality and privacy under Section 72 where the prescribed punishment meets or exceeds the three-year threshold.
Unauthorised access to or damage of a protected system under Section 70, punishable with imprisonment up to ten years, which clearly falls within the cognizable category.
what_it_excludes: Offences punishable with imprisonment of less than three years under the IT Act, which are not cognizable and require a Magistrate's permission before police can arrest.

Offences that are bailable under Section 77B — specifically those punishable with exactly three years imprisonment — which, while cognizable, are separately classified as bailable, distinguishing them from the more serious non-bailable cognizable offences.

Civil contraventions and penalty proceedings adjudicated by the Adjudicating Officer under Chapter IX of the IT Act, which are not criminal offences and therefore the concept of cognizability does not apply.

Offences under other laws (e.g., Indian Penal Code) that may be related to cyber incidents but are governed by their own classification under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, not Section 77B of the IT Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an offence is cognizable determines whether police can arrest the accused, search premises, and commence investigation without prior Magistrate approval — directly affecting the speed and manner of law enforcement response to cyber crimes. It also determines whether the accused can be detained during investigation or must be released, which has significant consequences for evidence preservation and public safety in cyber crime cases.

definitions.definition: 'communication device' means cell phones, personal digital assistance or combination of both or any other device used to communicate, send or transmit any text, video, audio or image.
definitions.plain_english: A communication device is any gadget that can send or receive messages, calls, videos, images, or audio — most commonly a mobile phone or a personal digital assistant (PDA). The definition is broad enough to include any modern device capable of transmitting digital content. It does not require the device to be a traditional computer.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai uses their Android smartphone to send threatening WhatsApp messages to a colleague — the smartphone qualifies as a communication device under Section 66A (prior to its striking down) for purposes of prosecution.

A cybercriminal in Bengaluru uses a stolen iPad to send fraudulent UPI payment links to victims — the iPad, being used to transmit text and images, qualifies as a communication device under Section 66D for cheating by personation.
A student in Delhi uses a feature phone to receive and forward obscene MMS clips to classmates — the feature phone is a communication device attracting liability under relevant IT Act provisions.

A business executive in Chennai uses a BlackBerry PDA to transmit confidential corporate data to a competitor — the BlackBerry PDA falls squarely within the definition of communication device under Section 2 of the IT Act.

A person in Hyderabad uses a smartwatch capable of sending voice messages and images to coordinate a cyberfraud scheme — the smartwatch, being used to transmit audio and images, may be classified as a communication device under the Act.
what_it_covers: Cell phones and smartphones (e.g., iPhones, Android devices) used to send texts, make calls, or transmit multimedia content
Personal Digital Assistants (PDAs) such as older BlackBerry devices or handheld organizers capable of sending or receiving data
Any hybrid or combination device that merges phone and PDA functionality, such as modern smartphones with advanced organizer features
Tablets or phablets that are primarily used to communicate, send audio, video, text, or images over a network
Feature phones or basic mobile handsets capable of sending SMS, MMS, or transmitting audio or images
what_it_excludes: Standalone desktop computers or laptops that are not primarily characterised as communication or transmission devices (these fall under the definition of 'computer' instead)
Landline telephones or PSTN-based fixed-line phones that transmit only voice and do not send text, video, audio files, or images in digital form
Storage devices such as USB drives, external hard disks, or memory cards that do not independently communicate, send, or transmit content
Calculators or non-programmable electronic devices that lack any communication or transmission functionality
Broadcasting equipment such as television transmitters or radio towers, which are governed by separate regulatory frameworks and are not personal devices
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a device qualifies as a 'communication device' under the IT Act determines whether offences under Sections 66A, 66B, and 66D can be invoked — for example, sending offensive messages, receiving stolen computer resources, or cheating by personation using electronic means. It also determines the scope of 'cyber security' obligations under Section 2, since that definition explicitly protects communication devices from unauthorised access, use, or destruction.

definitions.definition: As used in the Information Technology Act, 2000, 'company' means any body incorporated under the Companies Act and includes a firm or other association of individuals. In the context of Section 85, a company is a legal entity that can commit offences under the Act and whose directors, managers, secretaries, or other officers can be held personally liable for such offences.
definitions.plain_english: A 'company' in this Act refers to any legally registered business entity incorporated under Indian company law. When a company breaks any rule under the IT Act, the people who were in charge of and responsible for running the company at the time can also be personally held responsible and punished, not just the company itself. This ensures that individuals cannot hide behind the company structure to escape accountability for digital or cyber-related violations.
real_world_examples: A private limited company registered in Bengaluru operating an e-commerce platform is found to have allowed unauthorised access to customer data due to negligent security practices; the Managing Director and the Chief Technology Officer can be prosecuted under Section 85 along with the company.

A public limited company listed on the Bombay Stock Exchange sends unsolicited electronic communications (spam) in violation of the IT Act; both the company and its directors responsible for marketing decisions can face liability.

A Chennai-based fintech company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 fails to implement reasonable security practices and causes wrongful loss to users; the company and its officers in default become liable for compensation under Section 43A read with Section 85.

A Mumbai-registered IT services company acts as an intermediary and knowingly hosts illegal content on its servers; the company and the director responsible for content moderation can be held liable under Section 79 and Section 85 of the IT Act.

A Delhi-based company involved in digital signature certificate services violates the provisions governing Certifying Authorities; upon winding up or dissolution, the officers who were in charge at the time of the offence remain liable under Section 85.
what_it_covers: A private limited company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 that operates digital or online services in India.
A public limited company that processes, stores, or transmits electronic records and is subject to obligations under the IT Act.
A company that has been dissolved or wound up, with its officers remaining liable for offences committed during its active existence.
A company acting as an intermediary, service provider, or body corporate under the IT Act, including those handling sensitive personal data.
Foreign companies operating in India through a registered branch or subsidiary that are subject to IT Act provisions.
what_it_excludes: Sole proprietorship firms, which are not incorporated entities and are treated separately from companies under the Act.
Partnership firms that are not incorporated as Limited Liability Partnerships, as they lack separate legal personality as a 'company'.
Individual natural persons acting in their personal capacity, even if they are shareholders or founders of a company.
Government departments and statutory bodies that may be treated differently under specific provisions of the IT Act.
Unregistered associations or informal groups of individuals not constituted as a company under any applicable law.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'company' under Section 85 is critical because it extends criminal liability for offences under the IT Act beyond the company itself to every person who was in charge of and responsible for its conduct, meaning directors and officers can face personal prosecution, fines, or imprisonment. This prevents corporate entities from being used as shields against cyber-law violations and ensures that those who make decisions about data security, digital services, and electronic transactions bear direct legal accountability.

Legal text: As used in the Information Technology Act, 2000, 'company' means any body incorporated under the Companies Act and includes a firm or other association of individuals. In the context of Section 85, a company is a legal entity that can commit offences under the Act and whose directors, managers, secretaries, or other officers can be held personally liable for such offences.

definitions.definition: Compensation, as used in the Information Technology Act, 2000, means damages payable in money by a person who has committed a contravention or act of negligence under the Act to the person so affected by such contravention or negligence, awarded by way of civil remedy to make good the wrongful loss or injury suffered. Such liability to pay damages by way of compensation arises under Sections 43, 43A, and 45, and is adjudicated by an adjudicating officer appointed under Section 46.
definitions.plain_english: Compensation under the IT Act is money that a wrongdoer must pay to the victim who has been harmed by an illegal or negligent act involving computers, data, or digital systems. It is not a fine paid to the government — it goes directly to the person or organisation that suffered the loss. The amount is decided by a government-appointed officer (called an adjudicating officer) or a court, depending on how large the claim is.
real_world_examples: A hacker in Bengaluru gains unauthorised access to a startup's cloud server and steals its customer database; the affected company files a claim before the adjudicating officer and is awarded compensation for the business loss and reputational damage suffered.

A Noida-based BPO company fails to implement adequate security measures for the sensitive personal data (Aadhaar-linked information) it processes, leading to a data breach; the individuals whose data was exposed are entitled to claim compensation from the body corporate under Section 43A.

An e-commerce platform in Mumbai deliberately charges one customer's saved payment details to another customer's account by manipulating its computer system; the wrongly charged customer can seek compensation for the financial loss caused.

A disgruntled IT employee in Hyderabad deletes critical project files from his employer's server before resigning, causing project delays and financial loss; the employer approaches the adjudicating officer and obtains a compensation order against the former employee under Section 43.

A cyber cafe owner in Delhi knowingly allows a user to introduce a virus into a client's USB drive, corrupting the client's business data; the affected client claims and receives compensation for the damage caused to the computer resource.

A software vendor contravenes a regulation made under the IT Act by failing to maintain prescribed logs, causing wrongful loss to a service recipient; the affected party obtains up to Rs. 25,000 as compensation under the residuary provision of Section 45.
what_it_covers: Money awarded to a person whose computer, computer system, or computer network was damaged, accessed without permission, or disrupted under Section 43.
Damages payable by a body corporate that was negligent in implementing reasonable security practices and procedures, resulting in wrongful loss or wrongful gain to any person, under Section 43A.
A monetary award not exceeding Rs. 25,000 payable to a person affected by contravention of any rule or regulation under the Act where no separate penalty is prescribed, under Section 45.
Claims adjudicated by an adjudicating officer where the amount does not exceed Rs. 5 crore, and by a competent court where the claim exceeds Rs. 5 crore, under Section 46.
what_it_excludes: Criminal fines or penalties imposed by a court as punishment payable to the State, which are distinct from compensation awarded to the aggrieved individual.
Punitive or exemplary damages beyond the actual loss suffered, as the Act frames compensation as damages for the harm actually caused to the affected person.
Compensation claims arising from contractual disputes or tortious acts that have no nexus with a computer resource, computer system, or computer network governed by the IT Act.
Penal amounts levied on Certifying Authorities or other regulated entities under separate penalty provisions of the Act that are deposited with the government rather than paid to an affected person.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether this definition applies determines whether an aggrieved person can invoke the adjudicatory mechanism under Section 46 to obtain a binding monetary award directly from the wrongdoer, rather than pursuing a longer civil suit; it also determines whether the obligations under Sections 43, 43A, and 45 — including the liability of body corporates for data protection failures — are triggered against the defaulting party.

definitions.definition: "computer" means any electronic, magnetic, optical or other high-speed data processing device or system which performs logical, arithmetic, and memory functions by manipulations of electronic, magnetic or optical impulses, and includes all input, output, processing, storage, computer software or communication facilities which are connected or related to the computer in a computer system or computer network.
definitions.plain_english: A computer is any electronic or similar high-speed device that can process data by performing logical operations, calculations, and storing information using electrical, magnetic, or optical signals. This includes not just the main device itself but also everything connected to it — like keyboards, screens, printers, storage drives, and software — that together form part of the system. In simple terms, it covers any machine that takes in data, processes it, and gives out a result.
real_world_examples: A desktop PC or laptop used by a bank employee in Mumbai to process customer transactions — both the hardware and the banking software installed on it fall within this definition.
An ATM machine operated by SBI or HDFC Bank, which processes electronic impulses to authenticate PINs and dispense cash, qualifies as a computer under the Act.
A server rack at a data centre in Hyderabad hosting cloud services for Indian government e-governance portals is a computer, along with all its connected storage and network equipment.
A point-of-sale (POS) terminal used by a Reliance Retail store in Delhi to process UPI or card payments — being an electronic data processing device — is covered under this definition.
A smartphone used to access internet banking on the BHIM app may be treated as a computer when it performs data processing functions, especially in conjunction with the broader IT Act framework.
A supercomputer used by ISRO for satellite trajectory calculations at its Bengaluru facility, including all input devices and storage systems connected to it, falls squarely within this definition.
what_it_covers: Desktop computers, laptops, and workstations used in offices, homes, or government departments that process data electronically.
Servers and mainframes housed in data centres that store, process, and transmit large volumes of data using magnetic or optical media.
All peripheral devices — such as keyboards, monitors, printers, and external hard drives — that are connected or related to a computer as part of a computer system or network.
ATM machines and POS terminals that perform electronic data processing functions including authentication and transaction execution.
Embedded computing devices in industrial or governmental infrastructure (such as electronic voting machines or SCADA control systems) that perform logical and arithmetic data processing.
what_it_excludes: Basic electronic calculators that are not programmable and cannot be used in conjunction with external files, as they do not meet the high-speed data processing and logical function threshold.
Purely mechanical data processing devices or analogue machines that do not operate through electronic, magnetic, or optical impulses.
Simple electronic devices such as digital clocks, basic thermostats, or non-programmable household appliances that do not perform logical, arithmetic, and memory functions in an integrated manner.

Communication devices such as cell phones acting purely as voice communication tools, to the extent they do not function as data processing systems (though they may qualify under 'communication device' separately).
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a device qualifies as a 'computer' under the IT Act determines whether offences such as unauthorised access (Section 43), tampering with computer source code (Section 65), and hacking (Section 66) can be invoked — no prosecution under these provisions is possible unless the targeted device meets this definition. It also triggers the territorial jurisdiction provisions under Section 75 and the applicability of evidence and liability rules throughout the Act.

definitions.definition: "Computer contaminant" means any set of computer instructions that are designed— (a) to modify, destroy, record, transmit data or programme residing within a computer, computer system or computer network; or (b) by any means to usurp the normal operation of the computer, computer system, or computer network.
definitions.plain_english: A computer contaminant is any set of instructions (code) deliberately designed to interfere with a computer or network — either by tampering with its data and programs, or by taking over and disrupting how it normally works. Think of it as a broad category covering malicious software that either steals or corrupts data, or hijacks a system's normal functioning. It is wider than a computer virus, encompassing any harmful code with such intent.
real_world_examples: A hacker in Bengaluru deploys a keylogger that silently records banking credentials typed by users on their computers and transmits them to a remote server — this qualifies as a computer contaminant because it records and transmits data residing on the computer system.

A ransomware attack on an Indian hospital's network encrypts all patient records and demands payment, modifying and effectively destroying access to data stored on the computer system, thereby constituting a computer contaminant.

A state-sponsored group introduces malware into India's power grid control systems (critical infrastructure) that disrupts normal SCADA operations — this usurps the normal operation of the computer system and constitutes a computer contaminant under Section 66F for cyber terrorism purposes.

A disgruntled employee at a Mumbai-based IT firm plants a logic bomb — code that activates on a specific date to delete all client databases — into the company's servers; this is a computer contaminant as it is designed to destroy data residing within the computer network.

Spyware bundled with a free mobile application downloaded from a third-party Indian app store that secretly transmits the user's contacts, messages, and location data to an external server constitutes a computer contaminant by recording and transmitting data from the device.

A botnet agent introduced into government computers through a phishing email that causes those machines to send spam and participate in DDoS attacks, thereby usurping their normal operation, qualifies as a computer contaminant under the Act.
what_it_covers: Ransomware that encrypts or destroys data residing on a computer system or network.
Spyware or keyloggers designed to record and transmit data (such as passwords or personal information) from a computer resource without authorisation.
Logic bombs or backdoors that are programmed to usurp normal computer operations or delete data at a triggered event.
Worms that propagate across a computer network and modify or corrupt programmes and data stored therein.
Remote Access Trojans (RATs) that allow an attacker to take control of a computer system, thereby usurping its normal operation.
what_it_excludes: A computer virus as such is separately defined under Section 43 and, while overlapping, is a distinct statutory category — a contaminant is broader and does not require the self-replicating or performance-degrading characteristics specific to a computer virus.

Legitimate system administration or security testing scripts (e.g., authorised penetration testing tools) that modify or monitor data with the owner's permission, as the design must be for unauthorised harmful purposes.
Hardware-level physical damage to a computer system (e.g., overheating caused by deliberate physical tampering), which does not constitute a 'set of computer instructions'.
Accidental software bugs or coding errors that cause data loss or disruption, since the definition requires the instructions to be 'designed' (i.e., intentionally crafted) to cause such effects.
Authorised monitoring or data-collection software deployed by the Government under Section 69B, which is expressly permitted by the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether code qualifies as a 'computer contaminant' directly determines civil liability for compensation under Section 43 and criminal liability under Section 66 (imprisonment up to three years) and Section 66F (imprisonment up to life for cyber terrorism); it also triggers the Central Government's surveillance and monitoring powers under Section 69B for national cyber security purposes.

definitions.definition: "computer data base" means a representation of information, knowledge, facts, concepts or instructions in text, image, audio, video that are being prepared or have been prepared in a formalised manner, and is intended to be processed, is being processed or has been processed in a computer system or computer network, and may be in any form (including computer printouts, magnetic or optical storage media, punched cards, punched tapes) or stored internally in the memory of the computer; being a structured or organised collection of such data accessible by a computer.
definitions.plain_english: A computer database is an organised collection of information stored in a computer system or network in a structured way so that it can be accessed, managed, and updated electronically. Think of it like a digital filing cabinet where records such as customer details, financial transactions, or employee information are stored and retrieved by a computer. It is distinct from random data in that it is systematically arranged for efficient access and use.
real_world_examples: A bank's core banking system storing account holder details, transaction histories, and loan records of millions of customers across India — accessing or tampering with this without permission attracts liability under Section 43.

The Aadhaar database maintained by UIDAI containing biometric and demographic information of Indian residents, which if accessed or extracted without authorisation constitutes a violation under the IT Act.

An e-commerce company like Flipkart maintaining a structured database of registered users, their purchase histories, addresses, and payment information, which if copied or damaged by an unauthorised party triggers Section 43 penalties.

A hospital management information system in India storing patient medical records, diagnostic reports, and prescription histories — unauthorised downloading or destruction of this database would constitute an offence under the IT Act.

A State Government's land records database (such as the Maharashtra Land Records system) storing ownership, mutation, and survey details of land parcels — any unauthorised access or alteration of such a database falls under Section 43.
what_it_covers: A relational database (e.g., MySQL or Oracle) hosted on a server storing customer or financial records of an Indian enterprise.
A government e-governance portal's backend database containing citizen service requests, identity details, and status records.
A cloud-hosted NoSQL database used by an Indian startup storing structured user profile information, preferences, and activity logs.
An airline's reservation system database in India storing passenger booking, flight schedule, and payment information.
A stock exchange's trading database recording buy/sell orders, transaction timestamps, and broker details.
what_it_excludes: Unstructured raw data files (e.g., a loose collection of text files or images not organised into any retrievable schema) that do not constitute a formalised, organised database.
Physical paper-based filing systems or card indexes maintained manually without any computer processing or storage element.
A single standalone document or spreadsheet file containing incidental data, not organised as a systematically retrievable database for computer processing.
Computer programmes or software code themselves, which are separately categorised under 'computer programme' or 'computer source code' and not as a database.
Temporary cache or buffer data in transit within a computer network that has not been prepared in a formalised manner for structured storage or retrieval.
definitions.why_it_matters: Under Section 43 of the IT Act, any person who without permission accesses, downloads, copies, extracts, disrupts, denies access to, or introduces a computer contaminant into a computer database is liable to pay compensation to the affected party; the classification of information as a 'computer data base' is therefore critical because it determines whether the civil penalty and compensation provisions of Section 43 are triggered, and also whether the asset qualifies as a 'computer resource' attracting broader protections under the Act.

definitions.definition: "Computer database" as used in Section 66F of the Information Technology Act, 2000 refers to a structured collection of data, information, or records stored in or accessible through a computer resource, which may be restricted for reasons of the security of the State or foreign relations, and unauthorised access to or extraction of which may cause injury to the sovereignty, integrity, or security of India or its relations with foreign States.
definitions.plain_english: A computer database is an organised collection of information stored on a computer system — think of it like a digital filing cabinet containing records, files, or data that can be searched and retrieved. In the context of this law, it particularly refers to sensitive collections of data that the government or authorised bodies have restricted because making them public or allowing unauthorised access could harm national security or India's relations with other countries. If someone breaks into such a database without permission, it can amount to cyber terrorism under Indian law.
real_world_examples: A hacker based abroad gains unauthorised access to the National Intelligence Grid (NATGRID) database containing records of Indian citizens' travel, financial, and immigration data, and extracts classified profiles for a foreign intelligence agency — this constitutes accessing a restricted computer database under Section 66F.

A disgruntled insider at the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) copies classified missile programme specifications stored in DRDO's internal computer database and transmits them to a foreign nation, triggering the cyber terrorism provisions of Section 66F.

An organised group penetrates the Ministry of External Affairs' computer database containing sensitive diplomatic communications and treaty negotiations with neighbouring countries, intending to destabilise India's foreign relations.

Attackers compromise the Indian Space Research Organisation's (ISRO) database holding satellite launch vehicle designs and encrypted communications data, obtaining restricted technical information that could give a strategic advantage to a hostile foreign power.

A cybercriminal infiltrates the Border Security Force's personnel and deployment database, extracting information about troop positions and border surveillance schedules that could be used to aid infiltration attempts.

definitions.definition: "computer network" means the inter-connection of one or more computers or computer systems or communication device through the use of satellite, microwave, terrestrial line, wire, wireless or other communication media; and terminals or a complex consisting of two or more interconnected computers or communication device whether or not the inter-connection is continuously maintained.
definitions.plain_english: A computer network is any setup where two or more computers, computer systems, or communication devices are linked together through some form of communication medium — such as the internet, Wi-Fi, satellite, or physical cables. The connection does not need to be permanent or always active to count as a network. This includes everything from a small office Wi-Fi setup to large national broadband infrastructure.
real_world_examples: A corporate office in Mumbai where all employee desktops, laptops, and printers are connected via an internal LAN (Local Area Network) using Ethernet cables — this entire setup constitutes a computer network under the Act.

BSNL's national broadband infrastructure linking millions of subscribers across India through fiber-optic terrestrial lines and satellite uplinks qualifies as a computer network, making unauthorised access to it punishable under Section 43.

A university in Delhi providing Wi-Fi access across its campus to students' mobile phones and laptops — the wireless interconnection of those devices through the university's router forms a computer network, and any tampering with it triggers liability under Section 66.

An ATM network operated by a bank such as SBI, where ATM terminals across India are connected to the bank's central servers via leased lines and satellite links, constitutes a computer network; hacking it attracts penalties under Sections 43 and 66.

A hospital in Chennai using a Hospital Management System (HMS) where patient records are shared between doctors' workstations, nursing stations, and pharmacy terminals over a local wireless network — this forms a computer network whose data protection is governed by the Act.

India's National Knowledge Network (NKN) connecting research institutions, universities, and government laboratories across the country through high-speed optical fiber links is a computer network, and any unauthorised intrusion into it is an offence under Section 66.
what_it_covers: A Wi-Fi network in a café, hotel, or airport that connects multiple users' devices to the internet through a common router — even temporarily.
A Wide Area Network (WAN) connecting branch offices of a bank across multiple Indian cities through leased terrestrial lines or satellite links.
A mobile telecommunications network where communication devices (smartphones) are interconnected through wireless media such as 4G/5G towers.
A home network where a broadband router connects multiple devices — laptops, smart TVs, phones — via Wi-Fi, regardless of whether the connection is continuously maintained.
Government e-governance networks such as NIC's (National Informatics Centre) infrastructure linking central and state government departments across India.
what_it_excludes: A standalone, single computer or computer system that is not connected to any other device or communication medium — it may qualify as a 'computer' or 'computer system' but not a 'computer network'.
A non-programmable calculator or similar device that performs arithmetic functions but is not interconnected with any computer system or communication device.

A simple point-to-point direct cable connection used purely for data transfer between two devices without any network protocol or communication infrastructure (e.g., a USB tethering cable used solely for one-time file transfer, depending on context).
Physical postal or courier infrastructure used to transmit printed data or storage media, even if the content originated from a computer.
A Bluetooth pairing between two devices solely for audio output (e.g., a phone connected to a wireless speaker) where no computer network protocol or data processing network is involved.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a system qualifies as a 'computer network' determines whether offences such as unauthorised access (Section 43), hacking (Section 66), tampering with computer source code (Section 65), and extraterritorial jurisdiction (Section 75) can be invoked — without meeting this definition, acts involving interconnected systems may fall outside the Act's penal and compensatory provisions. It also defines the scope of lawful and unlawful access, directly determining civil liability for damages and criminal prosecution thresholds.

definitions.definition: "Computer programme" means a set of instructions expressed in words, codes, schemes or in any other form, including a machine readable medium, capable of causing a computer to perform a particular task or achieve a particular result. Though not separately defined in Section 2, it is used consistently in the Act to mean any executable set of instructions designed to be processed by a computer system.
definitions.plain_english: A computer programme is a set of coded instructions written for a computer to follow in order to carry out a specific task. Think of it as a recipe that tells a computer exactly what steps to perform and in what order. Examples include mobile apps, operating systems, antivirus software, and banking applications. It is any software code that can be loaded into and executed by a computer.
real_world_examples: A developer at an Indian IT firm in Bengaluru writes source code for a payroll management application; this source code and its compiled executable both constitute a computer programme under the Act.

An employee of a Mumbai-based bank tampers with the core banking software to alter transaction records — the banking software being tampered with is a computer programme, making the act an offence under Section 65 of the IT Act.

A student in Hyderabad creates a Python script that automatically scrapes and copies proprietary data from a competitor's website without authorisation; the script is a computer programme whose misuse attracts liability.

A cybercriminal distributes a ransomware executable (such as those seen in attacks on AIIMS Delhi) that encrypts hospital data and demands payment; the ransomware is a computer programme and its deployment constitutes an offence under the IT Act.

An e-commerce company in Pune deploys a machine-learning algorithm (a programme) to process customer orders and manage inventory — tampering with or stealing this programme triggers protections under the Act.

A government contractor in Delhi modifies the source code of the GSTN filing software to introduce backdoors; the GSTN software is a computer programme and unauthorised alteration is punishable under Section 65.
what_it_covers: Operating systems such as Windows or Linux installed on a government server that enable the computer to function.
Mobile applications (APKs or iOS apps) developed by Indian fintech companies for digital payments such as UPI apps.
Compiled executable files (.exe, .jar, .py scripts) and their corresponding human-readable source code used in enterprise software.
Malicious programmes including viruses, trojans, ransomware, and spyware designed to harm or exploit computer systems.
Embedded firmware programmes stored in ROM or flash memory that control hardware devices connected to a computer system.
Scripts and automation tools (shell scripts, macros, SQL stored procedures) that instruct a computer to perform specific data operations.
what_it_excludes: Raw data files such as spreadsheets, PDFs, or image files that contain information but do not instruct a computer to execute any task.
Hardware components of a computer system such as processors, memory chips, or circuit boards, which are physical rather than instructional in nature.
Printed or handwritten algorithmic descriptions or flowcharts that have not been translated into a machine-readable or executable form.
Pure mathematical formulae or abstract algorithms existing only in theoretical form without expression as code capable of being processed by a computer.
Electronic records and databases (data storage) that are merely repositories of information without any executable instructional logic embedded in them.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether something qualifies as a 'computer programme' is central to Section 65 of the IT Act, which makes it a criminal offence (punishable with up to three years imprisonment or a fine up to two lakh rupees) to knowingly or intentionally conceal, destroy, or alter the source code of a computer programme when required to be maintained by law; without this classification applying, no offence under Section 65 can be established. It also determines the scope of protections available under other provisions concerning unauthorised access, damage, and tampering with computer resources.

definitions.definition: "computer resource" means computer, computer system, computer network, data, computer data base or software.
definitions.plain_english: A computer resource is a broad term that covers any computer, a group of connected computers (network), the data stored in them, the databases they contain, or the software running on them. Essentially, it refers to all digital assets and infrastructure that store, process, or transmit information electronically. If something is a digital tool or a collection of digital information, it likely qualifies as a computer resource under this law.
real_world_examples: A server farm operated by a Mumbai-based bank storing customer account data and running core banking software constitutes a computer resource, and any unauthorised access to it attracts liability under Section 43 and Section 66 of the IT Act.

The National Informatics Centre's (NIC) government network interconnecting Central and State ministries across India is a computer resource, and any attempt to disrupt it could be prosecuted under Section 66F (cyber terrorism) or Section 70 (protected systems).

A smartphone application and its backend database used by an Indian e-commerce company like Flipkart to store user purchase histories, addresses, and payment details qualifies as a computer resource, making its protection mandatory under Section 43A.

An Aadhaar-linked biometric database maintained by UIDAI, along with the software used to process authentication requests, is a computer resource, and any breach or tampering would attract criminal liability under Sections 43, 66, and 66B of the Act.

A cloud storage service offered by an Indian IT company storing client business documents and proprietary software qualifies as a computer resource, and blocking or denying access to it without authorisation would constitute damage under Section 43.

The Election Commission of India's electronic voting machine (EVM) management software and the associated data on voter rolls stored in a networked system constitutes a computer resource protected under the IT Act.
what_it_covers: A standalone personal computer, laptop, tablet, or server used for data processing or storage.
A computer network such as a corporate intranet, the internet backbone, or a government Wide Area Network (WAN) interconnecting multiple offices across India.
Data stored electronically, including financial records, personal information, medical records, or any digital representation of information residing on a computer or network.
A computer database such as a customer relationship management (CRM) database, an SQL database containing banking transactions, or a government citizen registry.
Software applications, operating systems, firmware, and computer programmes installed on or running across any device or network.
Cloud computing environments and virtualised infrastructure hosted by Indian or foreign service providers where Indian entities store or process data.
what_it_excludes: Non-programmable calculators, as these are explicitly excluded from the definition of 'computer system' which forms part of 'computer resource', and they cannot perform the requisite logical or storage functions.
Purely analogue communication devices or traditional telephony hardware that do not involve digital data processing, storage, or logical functions.
Physical, non-digital records such as paper files, printed documents, or physical storage media that have not been processed or stored in an electronic or digital form.
Human intellectual resources, physical office infrastructure, or organisational processes that operate independently of any computer, network, data, database, or software.
Electronic devices such as basic feature phones used solely for voice calls with no data processing, storage, or programmable capability beyond their core communication function.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an asset qualifies as a 'computer resource' is the threshold question for applying virtually all major offences and obligations under the IT Act — including liability for unauthorised access (Section 43), data theft (Section 66B), cyber terrorism (Section 66F), and the government's power to intercept or block information (Sections 69, 69A, 69B) and to declare protected systems (Section 70). If an item falls outside this definition, none of these penal provisions, compensation obligations, or regulatory powers can be lawfully invoked against acts affecting it.

definitions.definition: "Computer source code" means the listing of programmes, computer commands, design and layout and programme analysis of computer resource in any form.
definitions.plain_english: Computer source code refers to the human-readable instructions, commands, and structural blueprints written by programmers that tell a computer what to do. It includes not just the lines of code but also the design diagrams, layout specifications, and analytical documentation of how a software or computer resource is built. Essentially, it is the foundational blueprint of any software, app, or computer-based system in any format it may exist.
real_world_examples: A disgruntled software engineer at a Bengaluru IT company deletes the proprietary source code of a banking application before leaving the organisation, destroying years of development work — this constitutes tampering with computer source code under Section 65.

A startup founder in Mumbai deliberately conceals the source code of a government-mandated tax-filing software from regulators who are legally entitled to inspect it, violating the requirement to maintain source code under Section 65.

A cybercriminal in Delhi steals and alters the source code of an e-commerce platform's payment gateway to introduce a backdoor for siphoning funds, attracting liability under Section 43(j) and criminal punishment under Section 66.

An employee at a Pune software firm covertly copies the proprietary source code — including design layouts and programme analysis documents — of a competitor's product and sells it to a rival company, constituting theft of computer source code under Section 43.

A government contractor tasked with developing a public health portal in Hyderabad intentionally modifies the programme analysis documents and design specifications of the portal's source code to cover up fraudulent billing, triggering offences under Sections 65 and 66.
what_it_covers: The written lines of programming instructions in any language (e.g., Java, Python, C++) that constitute the logic of a software application.
Design and layout documents, including architectural diagrams and UI/UX specifications that form part of the programme's structural plan.
Programme analysis reports and documentation that describe how the computer resource functions, regardless of the medium or format they are stored in.
Computer commands associated with any computer resource, whether stored in digital files, printed on paper, or embedded in removable storage media.
Source code in any form — whether in compiled pre-release form, partial draft listings, or complete final versions — as long as it relates to a computer resource.
what_it_excludes: Compiled binary or executable files (object code) that are the machine-readable output of source code, not the human-readable source listing itself.
Raw data, databases, or electronic records that are outputs or inputs of a programme, rather than the instructions constituting the programme itself.
General user manuals, help documentation, or end-user guides that do not contain programme commands, design layouts, or programme analysis of the computer resource.
Hardware schematics or firmware specifications of physical devices that are not part of the software programme's listing, commands, design, or analysis.
Business process documents or workflow charts that describe organisational procedures without constituting programme commands or programme analysis of a computer resource.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a document or file qualifies as 'computer source code' is determinative of criminal liability under Section 65 (tampering with computer source documents, punishable with up to three years' imprisonment and/or fine up to two lakh rupees) and civil liability under Section 43(j) for compensation; it also triggers Section 66 where such acts are done dishonestly or fraudulently, escalating punishment to up to three years' imprisonment and/or fine up to five lakh rupees.

definitions.definition: "computer system" means a device or collection of devices, including input and output support devices and excluding calculators which are not programmable and capable of being used in conjunction with external files, which contain computer programmes, electronic instructions, input data and output data, that performs logic, arithmetic, data storage and retrieval, communication control and other functions.
definitions.plain_english: A computer system is any single device or group of connected devices—like a desktop, laptop, server, or smartphone setup—that can run programs, store and retrieve data, and perform calculations or communication tasks. It must be programmable and work with external files. Basic non-programmable calculators are specifically excluded from this definition.
real_world_examples: A bank's core banking server cluster at State Bank of India's data centre in Mumbai, which processes millions of transactions daily, qualifies as a computer system under the Act.
An ATM machine operated by HDFC Bank, which runs software, processes input from the user's card and PIN, and retrieves account data, constitutes a computer system.
A government e-filing portal server used by the Income Tax Department of India for receiving and processing tax returns is a computer system.
A CCTV surveillance network in Delhi Metro stations where recorded footage is stored and retrieved through connected recording devices constitutes a computer system.
A hospital's electronic health records (EHR) setup at AIIMS New Delhi, consisting of interconnected workstations and storage servers handling patient data, qualifies as a computer system.
A point-of-sale (POS) terminal used at a Reliance Retail store that processes card payments, stores transaction data, and communicates with the payment gateway is a computer system.
what_it_covers: A single desktop or laptop computer running an operating system and capable of processing and storing files.
A collection of interconnected servers forming a data centre used for cloud services by Indian IT companies.
An ATM machine that accepts input, runs embedded software, retrieves bank account data, and dispenses cash.
A programmable industrial control system used in a power plant or manufacturing facility in India.
A government e-governance terminal or kiosk that processes citizen data and connects to central databases.
what_it_excludes: Basic non-programmable calculators that perform only fixed arithmetic functions and cannot be connected to external files.
Standalone analog devices or purely mechanical computing instruments that do not process electronic instructions or store data.
A simple digital clock or timer device that does not execute programmes, store retrievable data, or communicate with external files.
Purely passive storage media such as a blank hard drive or USB drive that contains no processing capability on its own.

It also governs the territorial jurisdiction of the Act under Section 75 and the scope of protected systems under Section 70.

definitions.definition: "Computer virus" means any computer instruction, information, data or programme that destroys, damages, degrades or adversely affects the performance of a computer resource or attaches itself to another computer resource and operates when a programme, data or instruction is executed or some other event takes place in that computer resource.
definitions.plain_english: A computer virus is any piece of code, data, or program that harms or slows down a computer or device, or that copies and spreads itself to other computers when triggered by running a program or some other action. It can delete files, corrupt data, or make the computer work poorly. In simple terms, it is a harmful digital agent that infects and damages computer systems.
real_world_examples: A hacker in Mumbai sends a phishing email to employees of a private bank; when an employee opens the attachment, a virus installs itself, encrypts all customer account files, and renders the bank's core banking system inoperable — constituting introduction of a computer virus under Section 43(c).

A student in Bengaluru downloads pirated software from a torrent website; hidden within the installer is a virus that attaches itself to system files and, upon each reboot, degrades the laptop's performance and transmits stored passwords to a remote server.

A disgruntled former IT employee of a Delhi-based e-commerce firm remotely introduces a virus into the company's order-management server before leaving, causing the system to crash and delete thousands of orders — triggering both civil liability under Section 43 and criminal punishment under Section 66.

Attackers deploy the 'WannaCry'-style ransomware virus targeting AIIMS New Delhi's hospital management system, causing it to attach to backup files and corrupt patient records, leading to disruption of critical healthcare services across the institution.

A malicious USB drive planted in a government office in Hyderabad auto-executes a virus upon insertion that degrades the performance of the NIC network terminals by consuming 100% CPU resources, qualifying as a computer virus under the Act.
what_it_covers: Ransomware programs that attach to files in a computer resource and encrypt or destroy data when executed, adversely affecting system performance.
Worms or trojans that replicate by attaching themselves to other computer resources on a network and activate upon a trigger event such as a system login or scheduled task.
Malicious scripts or instructions embedded in email attachments or downloads that, once run, degrade the operating speed or corrupt the data of the host computer system.
Boot-sector viruses that operate when the computer starts up, overwriting or damaging the master boot record of the computer resource.
Spyware code that attaches itself to browser processes and, upon execution of a web session, degrades browser performance while transmitting user credentials externally.
what_it_excludes: Legitimate antivirus or security software that modifies or quarantines files, as it does not adversely affect performance or destroy data but rather protects the computer resource.

Software bugs or unintentional coding errors that cause system crashes or performance issues, since a computer virus requires it to be a deliberate instruction, data or programme designed to cause harm.

Computer contaminants that are designed solely to usurp normal operation or modify data without attaching to another resource or operating on execution of a program — these fall under the separate definition of 'computer contaminant' rather than 'computer virus'.
Hardware malfunctions or physical damage to a computer system, which are not instructions, information, data, or programmes and therefore outside the scope of this definition.

Authorised penetration testing tools used by a certified ethical hacker with the owner's permission to test system vulnerabilities, as their use is consensual and not 'without permission' as required for liability under Section 43.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a piece of code qualifies as a 'computer virus' determines civil liability for compensation under Section 43(c) against any person who introduces or causes it to be introduced into a computer system without permission, and criminal culpability under Section 66 — which prescribes imprisonment up to three years or a fine up to five lakh rupees — when such introduction is done dishonestly or fraudulently.

definitions.definition: Conspiracy, as used in Section 84B of the Information Technology Act, 2000, refers to an agreement between two or more persons to do or cause to be done an illegal act or a legal act by illegal means, where an offence under this Act is committed in pursuance of such agreement. An act is said to be committed in pursuance of a conspiracy when it is carried out in execution of the concerted plan or agreement that constitutes the abetment.
definitions.plain_english: Conspiracy means a secret plan or agreement between two or more people to commit a crime together under the IT Act. When people plan together to carry out an illegal act — such as hacking, fraud, or spreading malware — and one of them actually does it, all of them can be held equally responsible. You don't have to physically commit the crime yourself; being part of the planning is enough to attract punishment.
real_world_examples: A group of individuals in Delhi plan together over encrypted messaging apps to hack into the servers of a government e-governance portal and steal citizen data; even those who only participated in the planning but did not execute the hack are liable under Section 84B read with the conspiracy provision.

Two employees of a Bengaluru-based IT company secretly agree to introduce a computer virus into their employer's computer network before resigning, and one of them executes the plan; both are guilty of conspiracy to commit an offence under the IT Act.

A gang in Mumbai collectively plans a phishing campaign targeting customers of a nationalised bank — designing fake websites, drafting fraudulent emails, and setting up collection accounts — and at least one member carries it out; all conspirators face punishment equal to the principal offender.

A person in Hyderabad coordinates with accomplices abroad to carry out a ransomware attack on critical information infrastructure in India; the coordinator who never directly accessed the systems is still liable as a conspirator under Section 84B.

Members of an online forum in Kolkata agree to collectively publish obscene material involving children on a shared server, and at least one member uploads the content; all who were part of the agreement are punishable as conspirators under the IT Act.
what_it_covers: A prior agreement or plan between two or more persons to commit an offence under the IT Act, even if only one person ultimately executes it.
Situations where an offence under the IT Act (such as unauthorised access, data theft, or spreading computer viruses) is committed in pursuance of a pre-arranged scheme among multiple individuals.
Remote or indirect participants who planned the offence but did not physically carry out the act, making them equally liable as conspirators.
Conspiracies formed through electronic communications such as encrypted chats, emails, or online forums, where the agreement itself is digital in nature.
what_it_excludes: Accidental or uncoordinated individual actions that happen to result in the same outcome without any prior agreement between the parties.
Mere knowledge of another person's intention to commit an offence without any active agreement or participation in the planning.
Offences committed entirely on a person's own initiative without any prior concert or agreement with another person.
Situations where an offence is committed through instigation or aid alone, without the element of a mutual agreement, which fall under separate limbs of abetment.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as conspiracy under Section 84B determines whether all participants in a criminal plan — not just the person who physically commits the offence — can be punished with the same penalty as the principal offender under the IT Act. Establishing conspiracy triggers joint criminal liability and allows prosecution of planners, organizers, and financiers even if they never directly accessed a computer system or committed the cyber offence themselves.

definitions.definition: A contract formed through electronic means, wherein the communication of proposals, the acceptance of proposals, the revocation of proposals and acceptances are expressed in electronic form or by means of an electronic record, and which shall not be deemed to be unenforceable solely on the ground that such electronic form or means was used for that purpose.
definitions.plain_english: A contract is a legally binding agreement between two or more parties. Under the IT Act, a contract formed online or through electronic messages is just as valid and enforceable as a paper-based contract. The law ensures that simply using email, a website, or other electronic means to agree on something does not make the agreement legally invalid.
real_world_examples: A freelance software developer in Bengaluru accepts a project offer from a Mumbai-based startup by clicking 'I Agree' on an online service agreement sent via email — this constitutes a valid enforceable contract under Section 10A.

An e-commerce platform like Flipkart displays terms and conditions and a buyer in Chennai completes a purchase by clicking 'Place Order', forming a binding contract electronically between the buyer and the seller.

A company in Delhi sends a purchase order to a supplier in Ahmedabad through an ERP system using electronic records, and the supplier accepts via the same system — the resulting agreement is a valid contract not invalidated by its electronic nature.

A lending fintech platform in Pune disburses a personal loan after a borrower digitally accepts the loan agreement via a mobile app using an OTP-based e-signature — this electronic acceptance constitutes a lawful contract.

Two parties enter into a non-disclosure agreement by exchanging signed PDF documents over email — the electronic transmission of proposals and acceptance forms a legally enforceable contract under the IT Act.
what_it_covers: Contracts formed entirely through email exchanges where offer and acceptance are communicated as electronic records.
Online clickwrap or browsewrap agreements on e-commerce or software-as-a-service platforms where users accept terms electronically.
Electronic purchase orders and acceptances exchanged between businesses through EDI systems or ERP platforms.
Loan agreements, service agreements, or NDAs executed digitally through mobile apps or web portals using electronic signatures.
Revocation of proposals communicated electronically before acceptance, forming part of the contract negotiation process.
what_it_excludes: Contracts that by law must be executed on physical stamp paper or registered in writing, such as sale deeds for immovable property under the Registration Act, 1908, are not rendered valid merely by Section 10A.
Contracts for the creation of powers of attorney, wills, or negotiable instruments that require physical signatures or specific formalities under other applicable Indian laws.

Oral contracts or verbal agreements that are neither expressed in electronic form nor backed by any electronic record, as Section 10A specifically requires electronic expression of proposals and acceptances.
Contracts where the underlying subject matter is illegal or against public policy — Section 10A validates the electronic medium, not the legality of the contract's subject matter.
definitions.why_it_matters: Section 10A determines whether an electronically formed agreement is legally enforceable, preventing a party from escaping contractual liability simply by arguing that no physical paper contract existed. It also triggers the applicability of Section 72A, under which disclosure of personal information obtained while providing services under a lawful contract is a punishable offence carrying imprisonment up to three years.

definitions.definition: The term 'contravention' is not formally defined in the Information Technology Act, 2000, but is used throughout the Act to denote any act or omission that violates, breaches, or fails to comply with any provision of this Act, or any rule or regulation made thereunder, for which civil liability in the form of penalty or compensation may be imposed, as distinct from a criminal offence punishable under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: A 'contravention' means breaking or not following the rules set out in the IT Act or its regulations, in a way that attracts a civil penalty rather than criminal punishment. Think of it as a regulatory violation — similar to jumping a traffic signal — where you face a fine rather than going to jail. The government-appointed Adjudicating Officer has the power to decide whether a contravention occurred and impose compensation or penalty accordingly.
real_world_examples: A Certifying Authority in Mumbai fails to maintain the security standards prescribed under the IT Act for issuing Digital Signature Certificates, thereby contravening the regulations framed under the Act and becoming liable to pay a penalty adjudicated by the Adjudicating Officer.

An e-commerce company based in Bengaluru collects sensitive personal data from customers without obtaining proper consent as required under IT (Reasonable Security Practices) Rules, 2011 — this constitutes a contravention of the Act's provisions attracting compensation liability under Section 43A.

A cyber café owner in Delhi fails to maintain and submit the prescribed user log records to the authorities as required under the Cyber Café Rules framed under the IT Act, constituting a contravention investigated by the Controller under Section 28.

A subscriber in Hyderabad provides false information to a Certifying Authority while applying for an Electronic Signature Certificate, contravening the provisions of Chapter VI of the IT Act and making himself liable to penalty proceedings before the Adjudicating Officer under Section 46.

An intermediary (social media platform operating in India) fails to observe due diligence while publishing third-party information on its platform, thereby contravening the IT (Intermediary Guidelines) Rules and attracting civil liability under the adjudication mechanism.

A company director in Chennai knowingly allows his firm to process and transmit user data in an unsecured manner, contravening body corporate obligations under Section 43A, making the company liable for compensation to affected persons.
what_it_covers: Any act or omission by a person that violates a specific provision of the IT Act, such as unauthorised access to a computer system under Section 43.

Failure to comply with rules or regulations framed under the IT Act, such as a body corporate not implementing reasonable security practices under the IT (Reasonable Security Practices and Procedures) Rules.
Violations committed outside India by any person that are covered under the Act's extraterritorial application under Section 1(2), including data breaches affecting Indian residents.
Actions by a Certifying Authority that breach its prescribed obligations under Chapter VI or VII of the Act, such as failing to publish accurate certification practice statements.
Acts by a cyber café or intermediary that violate the conditions and requirements prescribed under rules framed under the IT Act.
what_it_excludes: Criminal offences explicitly listed under Chapter XI of the IT Act (Sections 65–74), such as hacking or publishing obscene material, which attract prosecution and imprisonment rather than civil penalty proceedings.
Contractual disputes or private civil wrongs between parties that do not specifically breach a provision, rule, or regulation of the IT Act.
Acts or omissions relating to documents or transactions specifically excluded under the First Schedule to the IT Act, such as negotiable instruments (other than cheques) and wills.
Mere technical or procedural errors that do not amount to a breach of any substantive provision, rule, or regulation under the Act.
Actions that constitute 'abetment' or 'conspiracy' to commit an offence under the Act, which are treated as criminal matters rather than contraventions subject to civil adjudication.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes a 'contravention' determines whether the matter is adjudicated civilly by the Adjudicating Officer (with power to award compensation and impose penalty under Section 46) rather than prosecuted criminally before a court; it also triggers the Controller's investigative powers under Sections 28 and 29, the Appellate Tribunal's jurisdiction under Section 57, and corporate director liability under Section 85.

definitions.definition: "Critical Information Infrastructure" means the computer resource, the incapacitation or destruction of which, shall have debilitating impact on national security, economy, public health or safety.
definitions.plain_english: Critical Information Infrastructure refers to computer systems and digital resources that are so essential to the country that if they were damaged, shut down, or destroyed, it would seriously harm India's national security, economy, public health, or public safety. Think of it as the backbone digital systems that keep the nation running — like power grids, banking networks, or hospital systems. The government officially identifies and protects these systems under the law.
real_world_examples: The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) systems managing UPI and RTGS transactions — a cyberattack disabling these would cripple India's entire digital payment economy, qualifying them as Critical Information Infrastructure.
ISRO's satellite command and control computer networks — disruption or destruction of these systems would have a direct debilitating impact on national security and scientific infrastructure.

The Indian Railways computerised reservation and traffic management systems — a successful cyber intrusion causing widespread disruption to train operations would threaten public safety and the national economy.

Power grid control systems operated by entities like Power Grid Corporation of India — hacking into SCADA systems controlling electricity distribution across states could cause mass outages threatening public health and safety.
Computer systems of the Reserve Bank of India governing monetary policy operations and banking supervision — incapacitation would have a severe debilitating impact on India's economy.

AIIMS Delhi's hospital information management systems — as demonstrated in the 2022 ransomware attack, disruption of such systems directly threatens public health and patient safety on a national scale.
what_it_covers: Computer resources controlling power generation and distribution networks whose incapacitation would cause nationwide or regional electricity failure threatening public safety.
Banking and financial sector IT systems such as RBI core systems or interbank settlement platforms whose destruction would cause a debilitating impact on the national economy.
Defence and national security command-and-control computer systems whose compromise would directly undermine the security of the State.
Telecommunications backbone infrastructure and internet exchange systems that, if destroyed, would disable communications essential to national security and emergency services.
Public health IT infrastructure such as national disease surveillance systems or hospital networks where incapacitation would pose a debilitating risk to public health.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary private commercial computer systems or business IT networks that, while important to individual enterprises, do not have a debilitating impact on national security, economy, public health, or safety if incapacitated.
Personal computers, individual user devices, or small-scale local networks of private citizens or small businesses, which fall outside the scope of 'critical' national infrastructure.

Computer resources that affect only a localised or non-essential service, such as a single municipal office's administrative system, where disruption would not produce a debilitating national-level impact.
Computer systems already excluded from government notification under Section 70, i.e., those not formally declared as protected systems by the appropriate Government in the Official Gazette.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a computer resource qualifies as Critical Information Infrastructure determines whether an attack on it constitutes cyber terrorism under Section 66F, potentially attracting punishment up to imprisonment for life, and whether it can be designated a 'protected system' under Section 70, making unauthorised access a separate offence punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment. It also triggers the protective mandate of the national nodal agency under Section 70A.
