definitions.definition: "cyber cafe" means any facility from where access to the internet is offered by any person in the ordinary course of business to the members of the public.
definitions.plain_english: A cyber cafe is any physical place or establishment where a business owner allows members of the general public to use the internet, typically for a fee. This includes browsing centres, internet kiosks, and similar commercial setups. The key aspect is that internet access is provided as a regular business activity to anyone who walks in, not just to a restricted or private group.
real_world_examples: A small shop in a Delhi market with five desktop computers where customers pay Rs. 20 per hour to browse the internet, check email, or fill out online government forms — this is a classic cyber cafe covered under the definition.
A railway station kiosk in Mumbai that provides public internet terminals for travellers to book tickets, check PNR status, or send emails constitutes a cyber cafe under the Act.

An internet browsing centre in a tier-2 city like Patna or Ranchi that offers paid internet access and is registered with the local police under cyber cafe regulations falls squarely within this definition.

A PCO (Public Call Office) shop in Chennai that has added internet-access computers to its services and charges customers per session qualifies as a cyber cafe, subjecting the owner to applicable IT Act obligations.
A college canteen in Pune that installs pay-per-use Wi-Fi terminals accessible to any student or visitor for a fee would be considered a cyber cafe in the ordinary course of business.
A Jio Point outlet or BSNL Common Service Centre in a rural area of Uttar Pradesh that offers public internet access to local residents as a business service meets the definition of a cyber cafe.
what_it_covers: A paid internet browsing shop open to any member of the public, operating commercially on a per-hour or per-session basis.
An internet kiosk in a shopping mall, railway station, or airport that offers public internet access as a business service.
A PCO or STD booth that has expanded its services to include pay-per-use internet terminals accessible to walk-in customers.
A Common Service Centre (CSC) or government-designated e-governance kiosk that charges the public for internet-enabled services in the ordinary course of business.
A hotel business centre offering paid internet access terminals to guests and non-guests alike as a commercial service.
what_it_excludes: A private office or corporate workplace that provides internet access solely to its own employees and not to the general public.
A home internet connection used by a household for personal use, even if occasionally shared with neighbours, since it is not offered in the ordinary course of business.
A university computer lab that provides internet access exclusively to enrolled students and faculty, as access is restricted and not offered to members of the public at large.
A library that provides free internet access only to registered members with institutional credentials, not open to the general public on a walk-in commercial basis.
An individual's personal mobile hotspot shared with friends or family, as it is not a facility offered in the ordinary course of business to the public.
definitions.why_it_matters: Establishments that fall within the definition of 'cyber cafe' are subject to specific regulatory obligations under the IT Act and rules framed thereunder, including maintenance of user logs, identity verification of users, and cooperation with law enforcement during investigations — failure to comply can attract penalties and liability. The definition also determines whether an entity must adhere to the Cyber Cafe Rules (notified under the IT Act) and can be held accountable for facilitating offences such as those under Sections 66, 67, or 69 of the Act committed through its terminals.

definitions.definition: The term 'cyber incident' is not formally defined in the Information Technology Act, 2000, but as used in Section 70B, it refers to any event or occurrence that actually or potentially adversely affects the security, integrity, availability, or confidentiality of a computer resource, computer network, or information system, including unauthorised access, data breaches, malware attacks, denial-of-service attacks, and other disruptions to cyber infrastructure. Such incidents are subject to collection, analysis, dissemination, forecasting, alerting, and coordinated response activities by the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In).
definitions.plain_english: A cyber incident is any harmful or suspicious event that happens on a computer, network, or digital system — such as a hacking attempt, virus attack, data theft, or a service being knocked offline. It is the kind of digital emergency or security problem that the government agency CERT-In is set up to handle and respond to. When such an event occurs, CERT-In collects information, issues warnings, and coordinates the response to minimise damage.
real_world_examples: A ransomware attack on the servers of the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi in 2022 that encrypted patient data and disrupted hospital services for several weeks, requiring CERT-In coordination and response.
A Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack on the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) infrastructure causing disruption to UPI transactions across millions of users in India.

Unauthorised intrusion into the computer network of a major Indian public sector bank leading to theft of customer financial data, which is reported to CERT-In for analysis and issuance of advisories to other banks.

Deployment of malware (such as a computer virus) into the Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems of a power distribution company in Mumbai, causing partial grid failure and triggering CERT-In emergency response measures.

A phishing campaign targeting Indian government employees' email accounts resulting in credential theft and unauthorised access to sensitive e-governance portals, prompting CERT-In to issue vulnerability notes and advisories.
what_it_covers: Ransomware or malware attacks on any computer resource or computer network that compromise data availability or integrity.
Unauthorised access or intrusion into government, corporate, or critical information infrastructure systems.
Denial-of-service or distributed denial-of-service attacks that disrupt the functioning of information systems or digital services.
Data breaches involving theft or exposure of sensitive personal data or information from body corporates or intermediaries.
Phishing, spoofing, or social engineering attacks that result in credential compromise or fraudulent transactions through electronic means.
what_it_excludes: Physical damage to hardware or computer equipment caused without any digital or cyber element, such as theft or vandalism of servers without network exploitation.
Mere software bugs, system malfunctions, or technical failures that arise from internal errors rather than any intentional or externally caused security event.
Disputes over electronic contracts, e-commerce transactions, or digital signature validity that do not involve any security breach or hostile digital act.
Violations of data privacy or intermediary due diligence obligations that do not involve an actual or attempted breach of security or disruption of a computer resource.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an event qualifies as a cyber incident determines whether CERT-In's statutory mandate under Section 70B is triggered, including its powers to call for information from service providers, intermediaries, data centres, and body corporates, and to issue binding directions — non-compliance with which carries criminal liability of up to one year's imprisonment or a fine of up to one lakh rupees. It also governs whether CERT-In's emergency coordination, advisories, and reporting obligations apply to the affected entities.

definitions.definition: The Cyber Regulations Advisory Committee is a statutory committee constituted by the Central Government under Section 88 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, consisting of a Chairperson and such number of official and non-official members representing affected interests or having special knowledge of the subject-matter as the Central Government deems fit. It advises the Central Government on rules made under the Act and assists the Controller in framing regulations under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: The Cyber Regulations Advisory Committee is a government-appointed body set up under the IT Act to provide expert advice on making rules and regulations related to cyber law in India. It includes a Chairperson and a mix of government officials and outside experts who have relevant knowledge of information technology and related fields. The Committee guides both the Central Government when creating rules and the Controller of Certifying Authorities when drafting regulations. Non-official members receive travelling and other allowances fixed by the Central Government for their participation.
real_world_examples: When the Controller of Certifying Authorities in India sought to frame regulations specifying conditions for recognising foreign Certifying Authorities (such as those from the USA or UK) under Section 19, the Cyber Regulations Advisory Committee was consulted before the regulations were notified in the Official Gazette.

Before the Central Government issued rules prescribing the manner in which electronic records must be authenticated under the IT Act, the Cyber Regulations Advisory Committee, including IT industry representatives and legal experts, was convened to provide its recommendations.

When the Controller proposed regulations setting out the terms and conditions for granting licences to Indian Certifying Authorities under Section 21, the Cyber Regulations Advisory Committee reviewed the draft regulations and offered its expert opinion before Central Government approval was sought.

An IT policy expert nominated as a non-official member of the Cyber Regulations Advisory Committee attended a meeting in New Delhi where the Committee advised the Central Government on updating rules related to electronic signature standards, and subsequently claimed travelling allowances fixed by the government for the journey from Mumbai.

The Cyber Regulations Advisory Committee was consulted when the Controller drafted regulations requiring Certifying Authorities to disclose specific information to subscribers under Section 34, ensuring that both government and industry perspectives were incorporated into the final regulations.
what_it_covers: A body constituted by the Central Government comprising a Chairperson and a mix of official (government) and non-official (industry/expert) members appointed to advise on cyber law matters.
Advisory functions directed at the Central Government regarding the framing of rules under the IT Act and any other connected purpose under the Act.
Advisory functions directed at the Controller of Certifying Authorities specifically for framing regulations under the IT Act.
Non-official members who represent interests principally affected by the Act or who possess special knowledge of information technology, cybersecurity, or related subject-matter.
Entitlement of non-official members to receive travelling and other allowances as fixed by the Central Government for attending committee proceedings.
what_it_excludes: Adjudicatory or quasi-judicial functions — the Committee has no power to decide disputes, impose penalties, or adjudicate contraventions under the IT Act.
Executive or enforcement powers — the Committee cannot issue directives, licences, or orders binding on Certifying Authorities, intermediaries, or individuals.

Legislative authority — it cannot independently make, amend, or repeal rules or regulations; its role is purely advisory and its recommendations are not binding on the Central Government or the Controller.
Bodies or committees constituted under other statutes (e.g., TRAI, SEBI advisory panels, or committees under the Companies Act) even if they deal with technology-related matters.
Permanent regulatory commissions or tribunals such as the Appellate Tribunal constituted under Section 48 of the IT Act, which exercises independent adjudicatory jurisdiction.
definitions.why_it_matters: The requirement under Section 89 that the Controller must consult the Cyber Regulations Advisory Committee before making any regulation means that regulations framed without such consultation may be legally challenged as ultra vires or procedurally defective, potentially rendering them invalid. The Committee's advisory role acts as a mandatory procedural safeguard ensuring that regulations governing Certifying Authorities, electronic signatures, and cyber security practices reflect expert and stakeholder input before they acquire binding legal force.

definitions.definition: "Cyber security" means protecting information, equipment, devices, computer, computer resource, communication device and information stored therein from unauthorised access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification or destruction.
definitions.plain_english: Cyber security refers to all measures taken to keep digital information, computers, devices, and networks safe from people who should not access or tamper with them. This includes preventing hackers from breaking in, stopping unauthorised people from reading or changing data, and ensuring systems cannot be disrupted or destroyed by malicious actors. Essentially, it is the practice of defending everything digital from threats, misuse, or damage.
real_world_examples: The National Informatics Centre deploying firewalls and intrusion detection systems to protect sensitive government e-governance portals such as the UIDAI Aadhaar database from unauthorised access by external hackers.
A leading Indian bank such as SBI implementing multi-factor authentication, encryption, and real-time fraud monitoring to prevent cybercriminals from accessing customer accounts and financial data.

CERT-In (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team) issuing advisories and coordinating responses when ransomware attacks disrupt operations of Indian hospitals or critical infrastructure, thereby protecting stored patient records from destruction.

An Indian IT company securing its client data centres located in Bengaluru or Hyderabad through access controls, endpoint protection, and regular vulnerability assessments to prevent disclosure or modification of proprietary software and databases.

A state electricity board implementing cyber security protocols to protect its SCADA systems from unauthorised manipulation that could disrupt power supply across the grid, as highlighted in the 2020 Mumbai power outage investigations.
what_it_covers: Measures to prevent unauthorised access to computer systems, networks, and devices, including firewalls, encryption, and access control mechanisms.
Protection of information stored in communication devices, computer databases, and servers from unauthorised disclosure, modification, or destruction by malicious actors.

Actions taken to prevent disruption of computer resources and connected equipment, including safeguarding against ransomware, denial-of-service attacks, and cyber sabotage targeting critical information infrastructure.
Organisational policies, security audits, and technical safeguards implemented by body corporates to comply with reasonable security practices under the Act.
Government-mandated protective measures enforced through CERT-In under Section 70B to respond to and mitigate cyber incidents affecting national security or public services.
what_it_excludes: Physical security measures that do not relate to digital information or computer systems, such as locks, guards, or CCTV protecting a building's physical premises unconnected to any computer resource.
Authorised access, use, or modification of data and systems by legitimate users acting within their permissions, since the definition is concerned only with protection from unauthorised acts.

Intellectual property protection or copyright enforcement against lawful but commercially unauthorised use of software, which falls under separate IP legislation rather than cyber security under this Act.

Regulation of content legality or obscenity on the internet, which is addressed by other provisions of the IT Act and is distinct from protecting equipment and information from unauthorised access or destruction.

Privacy rights or data protection obligations arising from lawful processing of personal data, which are governed separately and are not inherently covered by the concept of cyber security as defined here.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of cyber security is the foundational basis for the mandate and functions of the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) under Section 70B, which is empowered to issue guidelines, coordinate responses, and impose obligations on service providers and intermediaries in furtherance of cyber security. Whether an act or protective measure qualifies as cyber security determines the scope of CERT-In's jurisdiction, the obligations of body corporates to maintain security practices, and the applicability of offences related to unauthorised access, damage, and disruption under Sections 43, 66, and 70 of the Act.

definitions.definition: "Damage" means to destroy, alter, delete, add, modify or rearrange any computer resource by any means.
definitions.plain_english: Damage, under the IT Act, refers to any act that changes, destroys, removes, adds to, or reorganises data or systems stored in or forming part of a computer resource. It does not require physical harm — even silently altering a database entry or rearranging files counts as damage. The definition is intentionally broad to capture all forms of unauthorised interference with digital assets.
real_world_examples: A disgruntled employee at a Bengaluru IT firm deletes critical source code files from the company's internal server before resigning, destroying data that took months to develop.
A hacker targeting an e-commerce platform based in Mumbai modifies product prices in the database, altering records to sell items at near-zero cost and causing financial loss to the business.
A cybercriminal introduces ransomware into the computer network of a Delhi hospital, which rearranges and encrypts patient records, making them inaccessible to doctors and staff.
An insider at a Hyderabad financial services company adds fictitious loan entries to the core banking system, modifying records to fraudulently disburse funds to dummy accounts.
A competitor's agent remotely accesses a Chennai logistics company's fleet management system and deletes route optimisation data, disrupting operations and causing service failures.
what_it_covers: Deleting files, folders, or database entries from a computer system or network without authorisation.
Altering or modifying existing data records, programme code, or configurations stored in a computer resource.
Adding malicious or spurious data, instructions, or entries into a computer resource to corrupt its integrity.
Rearranging the structure of a database or file system in a way that diminishes its utility or usability.
Destroying the entire contents of a computer resource, such as wiping a server's storage through a destructive attack.
what_it_excludes: Physical destruction of hardware (e.g., smashing a laptop or server rack), which is governed by general property damage laws rather than this definition.

definitions.definition: "data" means a representation of information, knowledge, facts, concepts or instructions which are being prepared or have been prepared in a formalised manner, and is intended to be processed, is being processed or has been processed in a computer system or computer network, and may be in any form (including computer printouts magnetic or optical storage media, punched cards, punched tapes) or stored internally in the memory of the computer.
definitions.plain_english: Data refers to any information, facts, or instructions that have been put into a structured or formal format so that a computer can work with them. This includes anything stored on a computer's memory, on storage devices like CDs or USB drives, or printed out from a computer. Essentially, if something has been prepared for, is being used by, or has come out of a computer system, it counts as data under this law.
real_world_examples: A customer's bank account details, transaction history, and balance stored on the servers of a State Bank of India branch constitute 'data' under the IT Act, and unauthorised access to such data attracts criminal liability under Section 66.
An Aadhaar-linked biometric record (fingerprint or iris scan) stored in UIDAI's database qualifies as data, and any tampering or theft of such records is a punishable offence under the IT Act.

A private company's sales figures, employee payroll records, and client contracts stored on an internal ERP system are data; a disgruntled employee who copies or deletes these files commits an offence under Section 66.
CCTV footage recorded and stored on a digital video recorder at a Delhi metro station is data within the meaning of the Act, making its unauthorised duplication or destruction an offence.

An income tax return filed electronically through the Income Tax e-filing portal and stored on government servers is data, and any fraudulent alteration of such records attracts liability under Section 66 read with other provisions.
WhatsApp messages, call logs, and contact lists stored on a smartphone seized during a CBI investigation constitute data, and their extraction and analysis are governed by the IT Act's framework.
what_it_covers: Text files, spreadsheets, and databases stored on a computer hard drive or cloud server, such as financial records maintained by a company on its servers.
Computer printouts of information that was generated or processed by a computer system, such as printed bank statements produced from a banking application.
Information stored on magnetic or optical storage media including CDs, DVDs, magnetic tapes, and USB drives containing processed records.
Instructions in the form of computer programmes or scripts that have been formalised and are intended to be executed by a computer system or network.
Data internally stored in the RAM or ROM of a computer, including temporarily cached information during active processing sessions.
Biometric records, digital images, audio files, and video files that have been processed or are intended for processing through a computer system or network.
what_it_excludes: Raw, unstructured information that has not been prepared in any formalised manner and is not intended for processing by any computer system, such as handwritten notes in a personal diary.
Oral or spoken communications that have never been captured, digitised, or processed through any computer system or network.
Physical documents such as paper contracts, printed maps, or handwritten letters that have never been scanned, digitised, or otherwise processed through a computer system.
Information stored purely in analogue formats (such as audio on a cassette tape or video on a VHS tape) that has not been converted into any form processed by a computer.
Abstract mental knowledge or concepts existing solely in human memory that have not been reduced to any formalised, computer-processable representation.

Whether a corporate espionage act, a cybercrime investigation, or a data breach compensation claim succeeds or fails often hinges on whether the information in question meets this statutory definition.

definitions.definition: "data base" means a representation of information, knowledge, facts, concepts or instructions in a formalised manner, organised and stored in a computer system or computer network, which is intended to be accessed, retrieved or processed by a computer resource. The term is used in Section 26 of the Act in the context of protecting proprietary databases maintained by Certifying Authorities.
definitions.plain_english: A database is an organised collection of information stored in a computer system so that it can be easily accessed, managed, and updated. Think of it like a digital filing cabinet where data is stored in a structured way — for example, a company's customer records or a bank's account details stored on servers. In the IT Act, it specifically includes databases maintained by Certifying Authorities that issue digital signature certificates.
real_world_examples: A Certifying Authority like (n)Code Solutions in India maintaining a structured database of all Digital Signature Certificates issued to subscribers, including their public keys and validity periods, which falls under Section 26 protections.
A bank such as State Bank of India storing its customer KYC records, account numbers, and transaction histories in an organised relational database on its central servers in Mumbai.
An e-commerce platform like Flipkart maintaining a product catalogue database containing millions of entries with item descriptions, prices, and inventory levels stored on cloud servers in India.
The Income Tax Department of India maintaining a centralised database of PAN card holders, their filed returns, and tax payment records accessible through the TRACES portal.

A hospital chain like Apollo Hospitals maintaining an electronic health records database containing patient diagnoses, prescriptions, and medical histories stored in a structured format on its internal servers.
what_it_covers: A structured collection of Digital Signature Certificate records maintained by a licensed Certifying Authority in India, as referenced in Section 26 of the IT Act.

Any organised set of data stored in a computer system or computer network in a formalised manner that is intended to be accessed and processed, such as a government e-governance portal's citizen records database.
Proprietary databases owned by body corporates or service providers containing customer information, transaction logs, or other business-critical data stored electronically.
Databases forming part of 'computer resource' as defined under the IT Act, including those stored on cloud infrastructure or distributed computer networks within India.
what_it_excludes: Unstructured or informal collections of data that are not organised in a formalised manner, such as a random folder of miscellaneous files on a personal computer.
Physical or paper-based filing systems and manually maintained registers, even if they contain the same type of information as an electronic database.
Data that exists only as transient input in a computer's processing pipeline and is never stored, organised, or made retrievable in a structured format.
Simple standalone documents such as a single Word file or PDF report, which contain information but are not organised as a structured, retrievable database.
definitions.why_it_matters: Under Section 26 of the IT Act, every Certifying Authority is legally obligated to ensure the accuracy of information in its database and to publish its repository; failure to maintain or protect such a database can attract penalties and affect the validity of Electronic Signature Certificates issued. Additionally, unauthorised access to, modification of, or damage to a database constitutes an offence under Sections 43 and 66 of the Act, making the classification of a system as a 'data base' critical to determining criminal and civil liability.

definitions.definition: The term 'data centre' is not formally defined in the Information Technology Act, 2000, but is used in Section 70B to denote a facility or infrastructure operated by a service provider or body corporate that hosts, stores, processes, or manages electronic data, computer resources, and information systems, and which is subject to directions and information requests issued by the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team in the context of cyber security incident response.
definitions.plain_english: A data centre is a physical facility or establishment where large amounts of digital data are stored, processed, and managed using computer servers, networking equipment, and related infrastructure. In everyday terms, think of it as a large, secure warehouse filled with computers that store information for businesses, governments, or internet services. Under the IT Act, data centres are required to cooperate with India's national cybersecurity agency (CERT-In) during cyber incidents.
real_world_examples: A Reliance Jio or Tata Communications data centre in Navi Mumbai that stores customer data and cloud services being directed by CERT-In to provide logs following a major ransomware attack on Indian banking infrastructure.

An NIC (National Informatics Centre) government data centre in Hyderabad hosting e-governance portals being asked by CERT-In to report details of a cyber intrusion affecting state government websites.

An Amazon Web Services (AWS) or Microsoft Azure facility located in Pune providing cloud hosting to Indian enterprises, receiving CERT-In directions to share incident-related traffic data after a large-scale DDoS attack on Indian financial institutions.

A co-location data centre in Chennai operated by CtrlS or Nxtra Data, where multiple corporate clients host their servers, being required to furnish information about a security breach affecting one of its tenants under Section 70B(6).

A private hospital chain's on-premise data centre in Delhi storing patient health records, directed by CERT-In to comply with vulnerability disclosure guidelines after a data leak affecting sensitive personal data.
what_it_covers: Commercial co-location facilities that rent server space and computing infrastructure to multiple businesses, such as those operated by NTT, CtrlS, or STT GDC India.
Government-owned data centres such as those operated by NIC or STPI that host e-governance applications and public digital services.
Private enterprise data centres maintained by banks, insurance companies, telecom operators, or large corporations for managing their own internal data and digital operations.
Cloud infrastructure facilities operated by domestic or foreign cloud service providers within Indian jurisdiction that store or process data of Indian users.
Disaster recovery and backup data centres that mirror primary data for business continuity purposes.
what_it_excludes: Individual personal computers, laptops, or home servers used by private individuals that do not constitute a commercial or institutional data hosting facility.
A simple office server room with minimal infrastructure that does not function as a dedicated, purpose-built data hosting or processing facility at an organisational scale.
Cyber cafes, which are separately defined and governed under the IT Act, and do not serve the function of storing or processing large-scale organisational data.
Mobile devices or edge computing nodes that temporarily process data but do not serve as centralised data storage or management infrastructure.

Intermediaries such as social media platforms or e-commerce portals whose primary function is information exchange or commerce, not infrastructure hosting, unless they also independently operate a data centre.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as a 'data centre' under Section 70B determines whether it is legally obligated to respond to CERT-In's information requests and directions during a cyber security incident; failure to comply exposes the data centre operator to criminal liability including imprisonment up to one year and/or a fine up to one lakh rupees under Section 70B(7).

definitions.definition: The term 'default' is not formally defined in the Information Technology Act, 2000, but is used in Section 47 to denote any failure, non-compliance, or wrongful act committed by a person in contravention of the provisions of the Act, which gives rise to liability for compensation as adjudged by the adjudicating officer. It encompasses the conduct or omission that results in unfair gain to the defaulter or loss to another person, and includes repetitive instances of such non-compliance.
definitions.plain_english: A 'default' under this Act means a failure or wrongful act by a person that breaks the rules or obligations set out in the IT Act. It is the underlying misconduct or breach that causes harm to someone else or gives an unfair benefit to the person who committed it. When someone defaults, an adjudicating officer can decide how much compensation must be paid, taking into account the gain made, the loss caused, and whether the person has done it before.
real_world_examples: A payment gateway company in Mumbai fails to implement adequate security measures for customer financial data as required under the IT Act, resulting in a data breach that exposes thousands of users' credit card details — this failure constitutes a default for which compensation can be assessed.

An e-commerce platform based in Bengaluru repeatedly collects and sells users' sensitive personal data without their consent in violation of data protection provisions of the IT Act, and the repetitive nature of this conduct is treated as a default when computing compensation.

A Certifying Authority in Delhi issues Digital Signature Certificates without following the prescribed verification procedures, causing a subscriber to suffer financial loss due to fraudulent transactions — the CA's non-compliance is a default under the Act.

A cyber café owner in Hyderabad fails to maintain logs of user activity as mandated under the IT Act rules, enabling a user to carry out an unauthorised access incident that harms a third party — the owner's omission amounts to a default.

An intermediary in Chennai does not take down unlawful content within the required timeframe after receiving a complaint, thereby gaining commercial advantage from continued hosting — this inaction is treated as a default when the adjudicating officer determines compensation.
what_it_covers: Failure by a body corporate to maintain reasonable security practices, leading to unauthorised disclosure of sensitive personal data.
Non-compliance by a Certifying Authority with prescribed procedures for issuing or revoking Digital Signature Certificates, resulting in loss to a subscriber.
Repeated violations by an intermediary of its due diligence obligations under the IT Act, causing harm to users or third parties.
An individual's deliberate or negligent act of accessing a computer resource without authorisation, causing damage to data or systems.
Omission by a service provider to preserve or disclose electronic records as required under the Act, resulting in disadvantage to another party.
what_it_excludes: Procedural defaults before the Appellate Tribunal, such as non-appearance of a party leading to ex parte proceedings under Section 58, which constitute a different procedural concept unrelated to substantive compensation liability.
Criminal offences under Chapters IX and XI of the IT Act, which are governed by penal provisions and prosecution rather than the compensation framework triggered by a default under Chapter IX.

Defaults or breaches under other laws (e.g., the Indian Penal Code or the Companies Act) that may arise from the same facts but are adjudicated under separate statutory regimes outside the IT Act's adjudication mechanism.
Mere technical errors or system failures not attributable to any failure of duty, obligation, or wrongful act on the part of a person.
Acts that are expressly authorised or exempted under the IT Act or under a lawful contract, which cannot constitute a default even if they cause incidental loss.
definitions.why_it_matters: The characterisation of conduct as a 'default' under Section 47 is the foundational trigger for the adjudicating officer's power to award compensation under Chapter IX of the IT Act — without a default, no compensation liability arises. The adjudicating officer must assess the quantum of compensation by reference to the gain made from the default, the loss caused by it, and whether it is repetitive, making the nature and gravity of the default directly determinative of the financial penalty imposed.

definitions.definition: A Deputy Controller is an officer appointed by the Central Government under Section 17 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, who performs functions assigned by the Controller of Certifying Authorities under the general superintendence and control of the Controller, and may be authorised in writing by the Controller to exercise any of the Controller's powers under Chapter VI of the Act. The Deputy Controller is deemed to be a public servant within the meaning of Section 21 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
definitions.plain_english: A Deputy Controller is a senior government official appointed by the Central Government to assist the Controller of Certifying Authorities in overseeing digital signatures and certifying authorities in India. They work under the direction of the Controller and can be given authority to exercise the Controller's powers when delegated in writing. Because they are considered public servants, they are held to the same legal accountability standards as other government officials.

definitions.definition: "digital signature" means authentication of any electronic record by a subscriber by means of an electronic method or procedure in accordance with the provisions of section 3.
definitions.plain_english: A digital signature is a secure, electronic way for a person to sign or authenticate a digital document, similar to a handwritten signature but done using a specific technology described in Section 3 of the IT Act. It verifies that the document was signed by a specific person and that the content has not been altered after signing. In India, it is legally recognised and carries the same weight as a physical signature for most official and commercial purposes.
real_world_examples: A company director in Mumbai digitally signs the annual financial returns filed on the Ministry of Corporate Affairs portal (MCA21) using a DSC (Digital Signature Certificate) issued by a licensed Certifying Authority such as eMudhra or (n)Code Solutions.

A taxpayer in Delhi uses a digital signature to authenticate and submit their Income Tax Return on the Income Tax Department's e-filing portal, ensuring the return is legally valid and attributable to them.

A government contractor in Bengaluru digitally signs a tender bid document uploaded on the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) portal, satisfying the requirement for authenticated submission without the need for physical presence.

A licensed advocate in Chennai electronically files a petition on the e-Courts platform using a digital signature, which the court system recognises as a valid and authenticated submission under the IT Act.
A bank in Hyderabad digitally signs electronic loan sanction letters and statements of account sent to customers, ensuring the authenticity and integrity of the documents during digital transmission.
what_it_covers: Authentication of any electronic record by a subscriber using the hash function and asymmetric crypto system procedure prescribed under Section 3 of the IT Act.
A Digital Signature Certificate issued by a licensed Certifying Authority under Section 35, used by a subscriber to generate a digital signature via a private key.
Digitally signed government forms, tax filings, company registrations, and court submissions where a subscriber authenticates the electronic record using a procedure conforming to Section 3.
Electronic contracts and agreements signed using a valid DSC, where the digital signature establishes the identity of the signatory and the integrity of the document content.
Digitally signed export-import documents, bank instruments, and procurement bids submitted through government or regulatory portals using a Section 3-compliant procedure.
what_it_excludes: A scanned image or photograph of a handwritten signature embedded in a PDF, as it does not involve an electronic method or procedure in accordance with Section 3.

An OTP-based or biometric-based authentication method that falls under the broader category of 'electronic signature' per the Second Schedule but does not comply with the specific asymmetric crypto system procedure of Section 3.
A simple typed name at the end of an email or electronic document, which lacks the cryptographic authentication mechanism required under Section 3.
Authentication performed by a person who is not a 'subscriber' as defined under the IT Act, such as an unauthorised third party using someone else's credentials.
Electronic marks or stamps applied by automated systems without a subscriber's direct invocation of the Section 3 procedure, as there is no identifiable human subscriber authenticating the record.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an authentication qualifies as a 'digital signature' under this definition determines whether it carries legal validity and evidentiary presumptions under Sections 3, 15, and 85B of the IT Act, including the presumption of the subscriber's intent and the record's integrity. It also determines eligibility for rights and obligations tied to Digital Signature Certificates under Sections 35 and 36, and triggers liability under Section 73 for publication of false Digital Signature Certificates.

definitions.definition: "Digital Signature Certificate" means a Digital Signature Certificate issued under sub-section (4) of section 35.
definitions.plain_english: A Digital Signature Certificate (DSC) is an official electronic document issued by a licensed Certifying Authority in India that confirms the identity of the holder and links them to their digital signature. It works like a digital version of a passport or identity card, allowing people to sign documents electronically in a legally recognized way. When you use a DSC, the recipient can verify that the signature genuinely belongs to you and that the document has not been tampered with.
real_world_examples: A company director in Mumbai obtains a Class 3 Digital Signature Certificate from a licensed Certifying Authority like eMudhra or Sify to file annual returns electronically on the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA21) portal.
A chartered accountant in Delhi uses a Digital Signature Certificate to digitally sign and file income tax returns on behalf of their corporate clients on the Income Tax e-filing portal.
A government contractor in Bengaluru uses their DSC to participate in and submit bids on the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) or Central Public Procurement Portal (CPPP) for tenders.

A registered exporter in Chennai uses their Digital Signature Certificate to submit shipping bills and customs documents electronically through the ICEGATE portal of the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs.
A property buyer in Hyderabad uses a DSC for executing and registering a sale deed electronically through the state's online land registration system.
A startup founder in Pune uses a Digital Signature Certificate during the online incorporation process of a company through the SPICe+ form on the MCA portal.
what_it_covers: A certificate issued by a licensed Certifying Authority under sub-section (4) of section 35 of the IT Act, 2000, binding a subscriber's identity to their public key.

Certificates of any class (Class 1, Class 2, or Class 3) issued by licensed Certifying Authorities such as eMudhra, NSDL e-Governance, Sify, or the Controller of Certifying Authorities itself, to individuals or organizations.
Certificates used by subscribers to affix digital signatures on electronic records for purposes such as e-filing, e-tendering, e-procurement, and electronic contracts.
A renewed or re-issued DSC granted under section 35(4) following expiry or revocation of a prior certificate, provided the new issuance complies with prescribed procedures.
Certificates issued to government entities, statutory bodies, or public sector undertakings enabling them to authenticate electronic communications and records officially.
what_it_excludes: An Electronic Signature Certificate issued under section 35 that is based on non-digital electronic signature techniques specified in the Second Schedule — such certificates are Electronic Signature Certificates but are not Digital Signature Certificates unless they specifically involve digital signature technology.
A self-signed or privately generated cryptographic certificate not issued by a licensed Certifying Authority under section 35(4), regardless of the technology used.
An expired, suspended, or revoked Digital Signature Certificate, as such certificates lose their legal validity and cannot be used to create valid digital signatures after the relevant event.
Any physical or paper-based signature certificate, seal, or notarial attestation, even if it purports to authenticate identity for digital transactions.
A certificate issued by a foreign Certifying Authority that has not been recognized or granted equivalence under the IT Act or any bilateral arrangement, unless explicitly notified by the Controller.
definitions.why_it_matters: Possession of a valid Digital Signature Certificate is a prerequisite for a subscriber to create a legally valid and enforceable digital signature under the IT Act, 2000; without it, electronically signed documents may lack legal recognition under sections 3, 5, and related provisions. Obligations and liabilities under sections 36–42 — including duties of the Certifying Authority upon issuance, the subscriber's duty to protect the private key, and grounds for suspension or revocation — are triggered only with respect to a valid Digital Signature Certificate, making its precise definition critical for determining legal rights and penalties.

definitions.definition: "director", in relation to a firm, means a partner in the firm. In relation to a company, a director refers to any director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company whose consent, connivance, or neglect is attributable to a contravention of any provision of the Act or any rule, direction or order made thereunder.
definitions.plain_english: A 'director' under this Act refers to a key person in a company or firm who holds a position of authority and responsibility. In the case of a regular company, this includes directors, managers, secretaries, and other officers. For a firm (like a partnership), a 'director' means any partner of that firm. This definition matters because such individuals can be held personally liable if their company breaks the rules of this Act.
real_world_examples: A Managing Director of a Bengaluru-based IT company approves the collection and storage of user data without adequate security measures, leading to a data breach. Under Section 85, he can be personally prosecuted because his decisions enabled the contravention.

A partnership firm running a cyber cafe in Mumbai allows customers to access and distribute obscene content. Each partner of the firm is treated as a 'director' and can be held personally liable for the firm's violation of the IT Act.

The Company Secretary of a Delhi-based e-commerce company knowingly signs off on a policy that fails to comply with prescribed data protection regulations. Being an 'officer of the company', the secretary qualifies as a director under this provision and faces personal liability.

A senior manager at a Hyderabad-based body corporate deliberately ignores repeated warnings about unlicensed software and hacking tools being used by employees. His neglect renders him liable as a 'director' equivalent under Section 85(2) of the IT Act.

Two partners of a Chennai-based IT consultancy firm collude to tamper with electronic records of a client. Both partners, treated as 'directors' under the IT Act, are deemed guilty and liable to be punished individually alongside the firm.
what_it_covers: A partner in a partnership firm, who is treated as a 'director' for the purposes of Section 85 when the firm commits a contravention under the IT Act.
A named director on the board of a body corporate whose consent or connivance contributed to the company's violation of the IT Act or any rule or order made thereunder.
A manager, company secretary, or other officer of a company whose neglect is found to be attributable to a contravention committed by the company under the IT Act.
A Managing Director or Chief Executive Officer of an incorporated company who was in a position of authority and responsible for the conduct that led to the breach of the Act.
Any officer of a company who actively participated in or facilitated a contravention, regardless of their formal job title, as long as they fall within the category of 'other officer of the company'.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary employees or staff of a company who do not hold managerial, secretarial, or directorial positions and are not responsible for the conduct of the company's business.
A shareholder or investor in a company who does not hold any officer-level position and has no operational control over the company's business or decision-making.
A nominee director who had no knowledge of the contravention and can demonstrate that the contravention occurred without their knowledge and that they exercised all due diligence to prevent it.
A sleeping or dormant partner in a firm who took no part in the conduct of the business and had no knowledge of the contravention at the time it was committed.
Third-party consultants or advisors engaged by the company who do not hold any formal officer or directorial position within the company itself.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'director' directly determines who can be held personally criminally liable when a company or firm violates the IT Act — extending prosecution beyond the corporate entity to individuals who consented, connived in, or were negligent about the contravention. Without this definition, partners in firms would not automatically be captured under the corporate liability provisions, creating a significant enforcement gap for non-incorporated business entities.

definitions.definition: The word 'dishonestly' shall have the meaning assigned to it in section 24 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860), which defines it as doing anything with the intention of causing wrongful gain to one person or wrongful loss to another person.
definitions.plain_english: Acting 'dishonestly' means doing something with the deliberate intention of unfairly gaining something of value for yourself or someone else, or unfairly causing someone else to lose something of value. The gain or loss must be of property or something that can be owned or possessed. It does not require deception — just the intention to cause such an unfair gain or loss.
real_world_examples: A hacker in Bengaluru breaks into a company's server and copies proprietary source code with the intention of selling it to a competitor, thereby causing wrongful loss to the original company — this constitutes a dishonest act under Section 66.
An employee in Mumbai unauthorisedly accesses his company's payroll database and inflates his own salary figures to receive excess payments, intending to gain wrongfully at the company's expense.

A person in Delhi uses stolen login credentials of another individual to access their net banking portal and transfers funds to his own account, constituting dishonest use of a unique identification feature under Section 66C.

A fraudster in Chennai receives a stolen laptop knowing it contains sensitive corporate data, retaining it to extract confidential business information for financial gain, attracting liability under Section 66B.

A cybercriminal in Hyderabad installs a keylogger on a public computer at a cyber café to capture passwords of unsuspecting users, intending to use those credentials to gain wrongful access to their bank accounts.
what_it_covers: Acts performed with the intention of causing wrongful gain to any person, including oneself, through unauthorised use of computer resources or communication devices.
Acts performed with the intention of causing wrongful loss to any person by accessing, damaging, or misusing computer systems, electronic records, or digital credentials without authorisation.
Retention or receipt of stolen computer resources or communication devices where the person knows or has reason to believe they are stolen and intends to benefit from or exploit such resources.
Unauthorised use of another person's electronic signature, password, or unique identification feature with the intention of gaining something of value or causing loss to the rightful owner.
what_it_excludes: Acts done in good faith or under a bona fide belief of entitlement, even if they accidentally result in gain or loss to any party, as there is no dishonest intent.
Accidental or negligent access to computer systems or data where there is no intention to cause wrongful gain or wrongful loss — mere carelessness does not satisfy the dishonesty standard.
Acts done fraudulently, which are governed separately by Section 25 of the IPC and involve deceit rather than the property-focused gain/loss intention that defines dishonesty.
Actions taken by authorised personnel within the scope of their legitimate duties, even if those actions incidentally benefit them, as there is no wrongful gain or loss intended.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act is done 'dishonestly' is a critical element of liability under Sections 66, 66B, and 66C of the IT Act — without proof of dishonest intent, a computer-related act cannot attract criminal punishment including imprisonment up to three years and fines up to five lakh rupees. Establishing or negating dishonesty directly determines whether a person is criminally liable for computer-related offences or merely subject to civil penalties under Section 43.

definitions.definition: The Act does not formally define 'due diligence,' but as used in Section 79(2)(c) and Section 85(1), it refers to the standard of reasonable care, caution, and active compliance measures that an intermediary or company officer is required to observe while discharging duties under the Act, including adherence to prescribed guidelines issued by the Central Government, so as to qualify for exemption from liability.
definitions.plain_english: Due diligence means taking all reasonable and responsible steps to prevent something harmful or illegal from happening. For an online platform or company, it means actively following the rules, putting proper systems in place, and not being careless or negligent. If a platform or company officer can prove they did everything reasonably expected of them, they may be protected from legal punishment.
real_world_examples: A large Indian social media platform like ShareChat regularly publishing its community guidelines, providing a grievance redressal mechanism with a named Grievance Officer, and promptly removing flagged illegal content within 36 hours, thereby satisfying due diligence requirements under Section 79 and the IT (Intermediary Guidelines) Rules.

A web hosting company based in Bengaluru, upon receiving a government notice that a website it hosts is being used to spread child sexual abuse material, immediately disabling access to the offending content without deleting server logs, as part of its due diligence obligations under Section 79(3)(b).

The Managing Director of a Delhi-based e-commerce company demonstrating due diligence under Section 85 by proving that the company had a documented internal compliance programme, employee training on IT Act obligations, and periodic audits, thereby seeking to avoid personal liability for a data breach contravention committed by a rogue employee.

A Mumbai-based cloud service provider maintaining detailed access logs, conducting regular security audits, appointing a Nodal Contact Officer for law enforcement coordination, and displaying clear terms of service prohibiting unlawful use — collectively constituting due diligence to claim safe harbour protection under Section 79.

An Indian Internet Service Provider (ISP) implementing automated filtering systems for known child pornography hashes, training customer support staff on recognising and escalating unlawful content reports, and maintaining records of all takedown actions — demonstrating ongoing due diligence to regulatory authorities during an inspection.
what_it_covers: An intermediary that has published terms of service, appointed a Grievance Officer, and established a functional takedown mechanism in compliance with Central Government guidelines.
A company director who can affirmatively prove they implemented internal controls, conducted employee training, and maintained audit trails to prevent contraventions of the IT Act.
A platform that, upon receiving actual knowledge of unlawful content through a government notification, expeditiously removes or disables access to the material without tampering with evidence.
Ongoing periodic review and updating of security policies, content moderation procedures, and user reporting systems by an intermediary to meet evolving prescribed guidelines.
Maintaining transparent records of compliance actions such as content removal logs, government request responses, and user grievance resolution timelines.
what_it_excludes: Passive or retroactive compliance — an intermediary that only acts after damage is done and has no pre-existing systems or policies in place does not satisfy the due diligence standard.

An intermediary that conspired in, abetted, or induced the commission of an unlawful act, regardless of any other precautions taken, as such conduct is explicitly excluded from safe harbour protection under Section 79(3)(a).

A company officer who was unaware of a contravention solely because they deliberately ignored red flags or failed to put any monitoring mechanism in place — wilful blindness does not constitute due diligence.
Mere display of terms of service without any operational enforcement mechanism or grievance redressal system, which falls short of the active standard required.
Actions taken only after a formal court order where the intermediary had previously ignored multiple government agency notifications about unlawful content on its platform.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an intermediary has observed due diligence under Section 79 is the decisive factor in determining if it qualifies for exemption from liability for third-party content — failure to demonstrate due diligence exposes the platform to full civil and criminal liability for such content. Under Section 85, proof of due diligence by a company officer is the primary statutory defence against personal criminal liability for a company's contravention of the IT Act.

definitions.definition: The term 'e-commerce' is not formally defined in the Information Technology Act, 2000. Based on its use in Section 84A, e-commerce refers to the buying, selling, or exchange of goods, services, or information conducted through electronic medium, including transactions carried out via computer networks, the internet, or other digital communication channels, facilitated by secure electronic means.
definitions.plain_english: E-commerce means doing business online — buying or selling products and services over the internet or other electronic networks. This includes everything from ordering groceries on an app to paying bills online or purchasing software digitally. The IT Act recognises e-commerce as a key activity that the government wants to make safe and secure by prescribing encryption standards.
real_world_examples: A customer in Mumbai purchasing a mobile phone on Flipkart or Amazon India using a debit card — the entire transaction from browsing to payment occurs electronically.
A small business owner in Jaipur selling handmade textiles through an online marketplace like Meesho, receiving payments via UPI or net banking.
An Indian consumer booking train tickets on IRCTC's website, completing payment through an encrypted payment gateway, and receiving an e-ticket via email.
A software company in Bengaluru licensing its enterprise software to a client in Delhi through a digital subscription portal, with invoicing and delivery entirely in electronic form.
A farmer in Punjab selling agricultural produce directly to buyers via an agri-tech platform like DeHaat, with contracts, payments, and delivery confirmations all handled electronically.
what_it_covers: Online retail transactions conducted through platforms like Amazon India, Flipkart, or Myntra where goods are ordered and paid for electronically.
Digital services purchased and delivered over the internet, such as streaming subscriptions, cloud storage, and online software licensing.
Business-to-business (B2B) transactions conducted electronically, including procurement, invoicing, and supply chain management through digital portals.
Financial transactions such as online banking, UPI-based payments, electronic fund transfers, and digital wallet transactions that constitute commercial activity.
Cross-border digital trade where Indian businesses sell goods or services to international buyers through electronic channels.
what_it_excludes: Traditional physical commerce conducted entirely offline — such as purchasing goods in a brick-and-mortar store using cash — even if the business also has an online presence.

E-governance activities of the government that are non-commercial in nature, such as filing taxes, applying for licences, or accessing public services online, which fall under 'e-governance' rather than 'e-commerce'.
Purely informational or content-sharing websites that do not involve any buying, selling, or exchange of goods, services, or monetary value.
Internal organisational electronic communications or data transfers within a company that do not constitute a commercial transaction between parties.
definitions.why_it_matters: The inclusion of 'e-commerce' in Section 84A empowers the Central Government to prescribe mandatory encryption modes and methods specifically to protect commercial transactions conducted online, thereby determining which encryption standards businesses must comply with to lawfully operate secure digital commerce platforms. Non-compliance with prescribed encryption norms could expose e-commerce operators to liability under the IT Act, while compliance provides a safe and legally recognised framework for conducting electronic transactions.

definitions.definition: The term 'e-governance' is not formally defined in the Information Technology Act, 2000, but is used in Section 84A to denote the use of electronic medium and digital processes by the Government for delivering public services, administering governance functions, and conducting official transactions. It encompasses the application of information technology by governmental bodies to enhance transparency, efficiency, and accessibility in public administration and service delivery.
definitions.plain_english: E-governance means the use of computers, the internet, and digital tools by the government to provide services and run official processes electronically instead of through paper-based or in-person methods. Examples include filing taxes online, applying for government certificates digitally, or accessing public records through a government website. It essentially brings government services to citizens through electronic channels, making them faster, more accessible, and more transparent.
real_world_examples: A citizen applying for a caste certificate or income certificate through the MeeSeva or DigiLocker portal in India, without visiting a government office in person.
The Income Tax Department's e-filing portal allowing taxpayers across India to submit their income tax returns electronically, with digital acknowledgements issued instantly.

The Government of India's UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app aggregating hundreds of central and state government services—such as EPFO passbook access, Aadhaar-based services, and Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana applications—on a single mobile platform.
The Ministry of Corporate Affairs' MCA21 portal enabling companies to electronically file incorporation documents, annual returns, and regulatory filings with digitally authenticated records.

State governments conducting land record mutations and property registrations through digital platforms like Maharashtra's iSarita or Andhra Pradesh's CARD system, replacing manual ledger entries with secure electronic records.
what_it_covers: Electronic filing of government forms, applications, and returns by citizens or entities through official government portals, such as GST filings or passport applications via Passport Seva.
Digital issuance and authentication of government certificates, licences, permits, and official documents using electronic signatures or digital signatures.
Online delivery of welfare scheme benefits, subsidies, and entitlements through government electronic platforms, including direct benefit transfers linked to Aadhaar.
Electronic record-keeping and maintenance of public registers, land records, court filings, and regulatory databases by governmental bodies.
Secure government-to-citizen and government-to-business communications conducted through encrypted electronic mediums as facilitated under Section 84A.
what_it_excludes: Private sector digital commerce or transactions between businesses and consumers, which fall under e-commerce rather than e-governance, even if conducted over the same electronic medium.
Internal private corporate governance processes or board-level digital decision-making by companies, which are not governmental in nature.
Purely informal digital communications between government employees (such as personal emails or instant messages) that do not constitute official government transactions or public service delivery.
Non-governmental organisations or civil society bodies providing digital services, even if those services complement or assist government programmes.
Digital activities of foreign governments or international organisations operating outside the ambit of Indian governmental administration.
definitions.why_it_matters: Section 84A empowers the Central Government to prescribe mandatory modes or methods of encryption specifically to promote e-governance and e-commerce over electronic mediums; whether a particular activity qualifies as e-governance determines whether the Central Government's encryption standards are applicable and whether the use of a non-prescribed encryption method may constitute non-compliance. This directly affects the legal validity and security obligations attached to electronic records and communications used in government service delivery.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of the Information Technology Act, 2000, the expression 'electronic cheque' shall have the same meaning as assigned to it in section 6 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (26 of 1881), and the provisions of this Act apply to electronic cheques subject to such modifications and amendments as the Central Government may, in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India, notify in the Official Gazette.
definitions.plain_english: An electronic cheque is a digital version of a traditional paper cheque that is issued and transmitted electronically, carrying the same legal standing as a physical cheque. It is defined by reference to the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, which governs how cheques work in India. The IT Act, 2000 ensures that all its digital and cybersecurity-related rules also apply to electronic cheques, making them legally valid and enforceable instruments.
real_world_examples: A business in Mumbai sends an electronic cheque to its supplier in Chennai through a bank-approved digital payment platform, and the transaction is processed without any physical paper being exchanged.
An employer in Bengaluru issues electronic cheques to its employees for salary payment through a banking software system that generates digitally signed instruments compliant with RBI guidelines.

A customer of an Indian scheduled commercial bank authorises an electronic cheque via net banking for payment of a large invoice, and the instrument is transmitted to the payee's bank electronically for clearing through the image-based cheque truncation system.

A corporate borrower in Delhi makes a loan repayment by issuing an electronic cheque to its lending bank, which is processed under the framework jointly notified by the Central Government and the Reserve Bank of India under the IT Act.

A real estate developer in Hyderabad accepts post-dated electronic cheques from home buyers as security for instalment payments, relying on the legal enforceability guaranteed under the Negotiable Instruments Act read with the IT Act.
what_it_covers: A cheque issued and transmitted entirely in electronic form through a bank-approved digital channel, carrying the same legal obligations as a paper cheque under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.

Electronic instruments that are digitally signed or authenticated and meet the requirements set out in section 6 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 as adapted by Central Government notifications.
Digital cheque instruments processed through RBI-approved clearing systems, including image-based and electronic clearing mechanisms used by Indian scheduled commercial banks.
Corporate or individual payment instructions transmitted electronically that satisfy the formal requirements of a cheque as defined in Indian banking law and RBI guidelines.
what_it_excludes: A scanned photocopy or digital photograph of a traditional paper cheque that is merely shared electronically but not issued as a native electronic instrument under the prescribed framework.
Online fund transfer instructions such as NEFT, RTGS, or IMPS transactions, which are electronic payment orders but do not constitute cheques under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
Demand drafts or pay orders issued in electronic form, which are separate instruments under the Negotiable Instruments Act and are not classified as cheques.

Digital payment instruments issued outside the framework notified by the Central Government in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India, which would not qualify as legally recognised electronic cheques under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an instrument qualifies as an electronic cheque determines whether the dishonour and criminal liability provisions of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (including the offence under section 138) apply to its issuer, and whether the IT Act's cybersecurity, authentication, and evidentiary rules govern its validity and enforceability in legal proceedings.

definitions.definition: "Electronic form" with reference to information, means any information generated, sent, received or stored in media, magnetic, optical, computer memory, micro film, computer generated micro fiche or similar device.
definitions.plain_english: Electronic form refers to any information that exists in a digital or electronically stored format — such as files on a computer, data on a hard drive, emails, or records stored on optical discs. It is the opposite of a paper-based or physical document. Essentially, if information is created, transmitted, or kept using any kind of electronic or magnetic storage technology, it is in 'electronic form'.
real_world_examples: A taxpayer filing their Income Tax Return on the Income Tax Department's e-filing portal — the return submitted and stored on government servers qualifies as information in electronic form under the IT Act.
A bank in Mumbai sending a loan sanction letter to a customer via email — the email and its attachment are information generated and sent in electronic form.
A hospital in Delhi storing patient medical records in its hospital management software on a magnetic hard drive — those records are maintained in electronic form.

A company in Bengaluru executing a business contract through an e-signing platform like DocuSign or SignDesk, with the signed document stored on cloud servers — the contract document exists in electronic form.
A government department publishing a gazette notification on the National Informatics Centre's portal — the notification made available digitally constitutes information in electronic form.
A WhatsApp message or SMS sent between two parties in a commercial dispute, later produced as evidence — such messages are information received or stored in electronic form.
what_it_covers: Information stored on magnetic storage devices such as hard disk drives, floppy disks, and magnetic tapes used by businesses or government agencies in India.
Information stored on optical media such as CDs, DVDs, and Blu-ray discs, including archived government records or digitised legal documents.
Data held in computer memory (RAM or ROM), including transient processing data in a running application.
Emails, digital messages, and electronically transmitted documents generated and received over the internet or private networks.
Microfilm and computer-generated microfiche records used by archival institutions, courts, or banks for long-term storage.
Information stored on cloud servers or data centres, including documents uploaded to government e-governance portals like MCA21 or DigiLocker.
what_it_excludes: Information recorded on paper, whether handwritten, typed, or printed — physical documents do not fall within electronic form.
Verbal or oral communications, such as in-person conversations or telephonic discussions that are not recorded or stored electronically.
Physical objects or tangible artefacts, such as printed photographs, physical seals, or rubber-stamp impressions on paper documents.
Information engraved or inscribed on non-electronic physical media, such as stone inscriptions or metal plates.
Purely mechanical recordings not involving electronic processing, such as traditional film photography negatives (unless digitised).
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether information qualifies as being in 'electronic form' is foundational to the operation of the IT Act — Sections 4, 6, and 7 grant legal recognition, government filing validity, and retention rights specifically to information in electronic form, while Sections 67, 67A, and 67B impose criminal liability for publishing or transmitting obscene or sexually explicit material only when it is in electronic form. If information does not meet this definition, none of these rights, obligations, or offences under the IT Act are triggered.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 79A, 'electronic form evidence' means any information of probative value that is either stored or transmitted in electronic form and includes computer evidence, digital audio, digital video, cell phones, digital fax machines.
definitions.plain_english: Electronic form evidence is any digital information that can help prove or disprove something in a court case or legal proceeding. This includes data stored on computers, recordings, videos, mobile phone data, and digital fax records. Essentially, if information exists in a digital or electronic format and is relevant to a legal matter, it qualifies as electronic form evidence.
real_world_examples: A WhatsApp chat history stored on a mobile phone submitted as evidence in a cyberstalking case before a Delhi court qualifies as electronic form evidence.
CCTV digital video footage from a Mumbai bank showing a fraudulent ATM transaction presented before a magistrate constitutes electronic form evidence.
Call detail records (CDRs) retrieved from a telecom server and produced before the CBI during a terror investigation in Bengaluru count as electronic form evidence.
An email trail between corporate executives stored on a company's mail server, submitted during a commercial dispute arbitration in the Bombay High Court, is electronic form evidence.
A digital audio recording of an extortion call captured on a victim's smartphone and produced before a sessions court in Hyderabad qualifies as electronic form evidence.
A digital fax transmission record showing fraudulent insurance claims filed with an IRDAI inquiry authority in Chennai is treated as electronic form evidence.
what_it_covers: Data stored on computers, laptops, servers, or cloud systems that has relevance to a legal proceeding, such as spreadsheets showing financial fraud.
Digital audio recordings, including voice messages and recorded phone calls stored on mobile devices or servers.
Digital video files from CCTV cameras, smartphone cameras, or body-worn devices capturing incidents relevant to a case.
Cell phone data including call logs, SMS messages, GPS location records, and app data stored or transmitted through a mobile device.
Digital fax machine transmission records that carry probative value in a dispute or investigation.
Computer evidence such as browser history, system logs, metadata, and emails stored or transmitted across networks.
what_it_excludes: Physical or paper-based documents, even if they originated from a digital print, as they are no longer in electronic form.
Oral testimony or witness statements, which carry probative value but are not stored or transmitted in electronic form.
Analogue audio or video recordings (such as VHS tapes or analogue CCTV tapes) that have not been converted to a digital format.
Information that lacks probative value, meaning data with no relevance to proving or disproving a fact in a legal proceeding.
Physical objects such as hard drives or USB drives themselves — the definition covers the information contained therein, not the storage medium as a physical artifact.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of material as 'electronic form evidence' determines whether a notified Examiner of Electronic Evidence under Section 79A can be called upon to provide expert opinion on it before a court or authority, making such expert testimony legally admissible and credible. Without this classification, the evidentiary value and the mechanism for expert validation of digital material in Indian courts would remain uncertain, potentially affecting the outcome of cybercrime, fraud, and digital dispute proceedings.
