definitions.definition: "Electronic Gazette" means the Official Gazette published in the electronic form.
definitions.plain_english: The Electronic Gazette is the official government publication — the same as the traditional printed Official Gazette — but made available in digital or electronic format. It is the authoritative online version of government notifications, laws, rules, and orders published by the Central or State Governments. When a notification appears in the Electronic Gazette, it carries the same legal weight as if it were printed in the physical gazette.
real_world_examples: The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology publishes an amendment to the IT (Amendment) Rules on the e-Gazette portal (egazette.nic.in), and this digital publication is treated as the official legal notification for the amendment to take effect.

The Central Government notifies a new list of 'protected systems' under Section 70 of the IT Act, 2000 by uploading the notification to the Electronic Gazette, making it legally enforceable from the date of such electronic publication.

A State Government issues a notification declaring certain cybersecurity standards mandatory for state-owned enterprises through the Electronic Gazette, eliminating the need for physical print distribution to all departments.

Under Section 8 of the IT Act, when the Central Government publishes any rule or regulation in the Electronic Gazette, it constitutes valid and legally sufficient publication, satisfying the requirement of gazetting under various statutes.

The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) notifies e-commerce policy amendments via the Electronic Gazette, and businesses are expected to comply from the date of such electronic publication without waiting for a physical printed copy.
what_it_covers: The Official Gazette of India (or any State Government) published and made available in electronic form through authorised digital platforms such as egazette.nic.in.
Any statutory notification, rule, regulation, or order that the Central or State Government is required by law to publish in the Official Gazette, when such publication is done in electronic form.
Electronic publication of appointments, amendments, commencement dates, and directions issued under the IT Act, 2000 when released through the digital gazette system.
Official government proclamations or declarations required to be gazetted under any Indian statute, where the government chooses or is authorised to publish them electronically.
what_it_excludes: The physical or printed version of the Official Gazette, even if it contains identical content — that is simply the 'Official Gazette' and not the 'Electronic Gazette' as defined.

Unofficial or third-party digital reproductions or summaries of gazette notifications published on news websites, legal databases, or commercial portals that are not the authorised electronic publication of the government.
Internal government circulars, departmental memoranda, or office orders published online that do not constitute a formal gazette notification issued through the authorised electronic gazette system.
Electronic communications such as emails or press releases issued by government ministries announcing policy changes, even if widely circulated, as these do not constitute the Electronic Gazette.
definitions.why_it_matters: Under Section 8 of the IT Act, 2000, any rule, regulation, or notification required to be published in the Official Gazette may be published in the Electronic Gazette, and such electronic publication is deemed to constitute valid legal publication — this means the date of online publication triggers commencement of legal obligations, penalties, or rights under the relevant Act or rule. If a notification does not appear in either the Official Gazette or the Electronic Gazette, it may be legally challenged as not having been properly promulgated.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 66A, 'electronic mail' means a message or information created or transmitted or received on a computer, computer system, computer resource or communication device including attachments in text, image, audio, video and any other electronic record, which may be transmitted with the message.
definitions.plain_english: An electronic mail (email) is any message or piece of information that is created, sent, or received using a computer or electronic device, and can include text, images, audio clips, videos, or any other file attached to it. It covers messages sent through traditional email services as well as other electronic messaging platforms. Essentially, it is any digitally transmitted communication exchanged between a sender and one or more recipients via electronic systems.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai repeatedly sends emails through Gmail to a business competitor containing false claims about the competitor's products, intending to mislead customers about the origin of those communications — this constitutes an 'electronic mail' under Section 66A.

An individual in Delhi sends a threatening email with an audio recording attached to a former colleague, causing criminal intimidation — both the message body and the audio attachment together form the 'electronic mail' covered under this definition.

A fraudster in Bengaluru sends bulk emails to bank customers falsely claiming to be from the Reserve Bank of India, with fake PDF documents attached, to deceive recipients about the origin of the message — this falls squarely within the definition of electronic mail.

A Kolkata resident sends an email containing an obscene video file to an ex-partner with the intent to cause annoyance and harassment — the message along with the video attachment constitutes an 'electronic mail' as defined under Section 66A.

A user sends a WhatsApp message or a message through a webmail portal with a forged sender address to mislead the recipient about who sent it — because it is created and transmitted on a communication device or computer resource, it qualifies as an electronic mail under this provision.
what_it_covers: Traditional email messages sent via platforms such as Gmail, Yahoo Mail, or Outlook, including any text, image, audio, or video attachments transmitted along with them.
Messages created or received on a computer resource or communication device that are designed to deceive the recipient about their origin, even if they use spoofed or forged sender addresses.

Webmail-based messages, messages through corporate email servers, or electronically transmitted communications over any computer network, including those with embedded electronic records such as PDFs or multimedia files.

Any information in electronic form — whether a written note, a forwarded image, an audio clip, or a video — that is attached to or transmitted as part of a digital message on a computer system or communication device.
what_it_excludes: Physical or paper-based letters, postcards, or traditional postal communications, even if their content is later digitised, since they are not created or transmitted on a computer resource or communication device.
Voice calls made over a telephone network (non-data-based) where no electronic message, attachment, or data record is created or transmitted in the course of communication.

Purely verbal or oral in-person communication, even if the content is offensive or threatening, as there is no electronic creation, transmission, or receipt involved on any computer or communication device.
Automated system-generated logs or internal process records within a computer system that are not intended to be transmitted as messages to an addressee or recipient.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a communication qualifies as an 'electronic mail' under Section 66A determines whether sending it with offensive, false, or deceptive intent attracts criminal liability including imprisonment of up to three years and a fine; if the communication does not meet this definition, Section 66A cannot be invoked to prosecute the sender. Note that Section 66A was struck down by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) as unconstitutional, but the definition retains documentary and interpretive relevance.

This covers not just traditional emails but also messages sent through various digital communication platforms. The content can be in any format such as text, pictures, audio clips, videos, or other digital files.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai sends a threatening email to a business rival via Gmail containing false allegations about the rival's company, intending to damage his reputation and cause him mental distress.
A WhatsApp message with an attached audio clip containing abusive content is sent repeatedly by an individual in Delhi to a former colleague with the intention of causing annoyance and harassment.

An individual in Bengaluru sends a bulk email campaign containing fabricated news about a political candidate, disguising the origin of the email to mislead recipients into believing it comes from a legitimate news source.
A student in Chennai uses a spoofed email address to send obscene video attachments to a professor, deliberately masking the true origin of the message to deceive the recipient.
A fraudster in Hyderabad sends phishing emails posing as a bank official to thousands of account holders, attaching fake PDF forms requesting sensitive banking credentials under a false pretext.
what_it_covers: A standard email sent through services like Gmail or Yahoo Mail containing offensive text or false information intended to harass the recipient.

Bulk or persistent electronic messages sent to cause annoyance, inconvenience, or criminal intimidation to the recipient.
what_it_excludes: Physical letters or postal communications, even if they contain offensive content, as they are not created or transmitted via a computer resource or communication device.
Verbal or oral communications made over a telephone call where no electronic message or attachment is created, stored, or transmitted in electronic form.

Electronic messages sent for lawful, non-offensive purposes such as legitimate business correspondence or official government communications, which do not meet the threshold of causing annoyance, deceit, or harm under Section 66A.
Messages where no digital device or computer resource is involved in their creation or transmission, such as handwritten notes passed in person.
Automated system-generated alerts or transactional notifications sent by banks or service providers for legitimate operational purposes without any intent to deceive or cause annoyance.

definitions.definition: The term 'electronic means' is not formally defined in the Information Technology Act, 2000, but as used in Section 6A, it refers to the delivery, communication, or performance of services, transactions, or functions through the use of electronic, digital, or computerised systems, networks, or devices, including internet-based platforms, computer terminals, and other digital infrastructure established or maintained by authorised service providers.
definitions.plain_english: Electronic means refers to using computers, the internet, digital devices, or other technology-based systems to provide or receive services, rather than doing things in person or on paper. For example, applying for a government certificate online instead of visiting an office counts as using electronic means. It covers any method of delivering or accessing services through digital or computerised channels.
real_world_examples: A citizen applying for a caste certificate through the Maharashtra government's Aaple Sarkar portal instead of visiting the tehsildar's office in person.
A service provider like CSC (Common Service Centre) collecting utility bill payments on behalf of state government utilities through a digital kiosk terminal in a rural village.
Renewal of a driving licence via the Parivahan Sewa portal (parivahan.gov.in) operated by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways without physically visiting an RTO.

Filing of income tax returns electronically through the Income Tax Department's e-filing portal (incometax.gov.in), with the service being delivered and processed entirely through digital infrastructure.
A state government authorising an IT company to provide birth and death certificate services through an online portal, allowing citizens to upload documents and receive certificates via email.
what_it_covers: Delivery of government services through internet portals operated by authorised private or public service providers under Section 6A.
Collection of service charges by authorised service providers via digital payment gateways or computerised billing systems.
Setting up and maintaining computerised kiosks or online platforms by service providers to facilitate citizen services such as certificate issuance, licence renewal, or utility payments.
Communication and processing of proposals, acceptances, or contractual communications expressed through digital or electronic records as envisaged under Section 10A.
Upgradation and operation of digital infrastructure by authorised service providers to ensure efficient public service delivery.
what_it_excludes: Physical or in-person delivery of government services at counters, offices, or brick-and-mortar service centres.
Services delivered exclusively through traditional postal or courier methods without any digital or computerised component.
Verbal or telephonic communication not routed through a digital or computer network, such as purely voice-based helpline services with no electronic record generation.
Manual paper-based transactions or form submissions even if the subject matter relates to technology or IT services.
Unauthorised or unofficial digital platforms not notified or authorised by the appropriate Government under Section 6A.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a service is delivered through 'electronic means' determines whether an authorised service provider can legally collect, retain, and appropriate service charges under Section 6A, and whether contracts formed during such delivery are enforceable under Section 10A. If this condition is not met, the service provider's authority to charge fees and the legal validity of electronically formed contracts may be challenged.

definitions.definition: The term 'electronic medium' is not formally defined in the Information Technology Act, 2000, but as used in Section 84A, it refers to any digital or network-based channel, platform, or infrastructure through which electronic data, communications, transactions, or governance services are transmitted, processed, or delivered, including the internet, computer networks, and digital communication systems. definitions.plain_english: The 'electronic medium' simply means any digital channel or platform used to send, receive, or process information electronically — such as the internet, mobile networks, or computer systems. Think of it as the digital highway on which emails, online banking, government portals, and digital transactions travel. The government uses this concept to ensure that encryption rules keep these channels safe and trustworthy for citizens and businesses.
real_world_examples: A citizen filing income tax returns through the Income Tax Department's e-filing portal (incometax.gov.in) is using the electronic medium, and the Central Government's prescribed encryption standards under Section 84A protect this data in transit.

A merchant on Flipkart or Amazon India processing a payment via UPI or net banking is transacting over the electronic medium, requiring secure encryption modes mandated by the government to prevent data theft.

State government departments delivering services through the Common Service Centres (CSCs) across rural India — such as issuing caste certificates or ration cards digitally — operate over the electronic medium, making encryption compliance under Section 84A directly applicable.

A hospital in Mumbai sharing patient records with a specialist in Delhi via a secure health information exchange platform is transmitting sensitive data over the electronic medium, necessitating encryption protocols prescribed by the Central Government.

A bank conducting Know Your Customer (KYC) verification through video calls and digital document submission for opening a savings account is using the electronic medium, and the encryption of such communications falls under the regulatory scope of Section 84A.
what_it_covers: The internet and World Wide Web used for accessing government portals, banking services, and online marketplaces in India.
Mobile networks and digital platforms through which SMS, app-based transactions, and digital payments (UPI, NEFT, IMPS) are conducted.
Computer networks and intranet systems used by government departments for inter-departmental communication, e-governance, and public service delivery.
Cloud-based platforms and data centres used by businesses and government agencies to store, process, and transmit electronic records.
Email systems, digital signature platforms, and secure messaging services used for official and commercial communications.
what_it_excludes: Traditional postal or courier services used to deliver physical documents, letters, or printed materials, which are not electronic in nature.
Verbal or oral communications made through face-to-face meetings or telephone voice calls that are not digitally recorded or transmitted as data.
Physical paper-based records, transactions, or filings submitted in person at government offices or courts, which do not involve any digital transmission.
Broadcast media such as traditional AM/FM radio or analogue television signals that do not operate as data-driven digital communication networks.
Manual ledger books or physical registers maintained by businesses or government bodies without any electronic or digital component.

It also anchors the government's regulatory authority to ensure that digital infrastructure used for public services and commerce remains secure and trustworthy.

definitions.definition: "Electronic record" means data, record or data generated, image or sound stored, received or sent in an electronic form or micro film or computer generated micro fiche.
definitions.plain_english: An electronic record is any piece of information — such as text, images, audio, or data — that is created, stored, sent, or received using electronic means, including storage on microfilm or computer-generated microfiche. Think of it as the digital equivalent of a paper document. It includes emails, digital contracts, scanned files, database entries, and any other information handled by a computer or electronic device.
real_world_examples: An Aadhaar e-KYC XML file downloaded from UIDAI's portal and submitted to a bank as proof of identity constitutes an electronic record under the IT Act.
A GST invoice generated and stored on a business's accounting software and transmitted to a buyer via email is an electronic record for purposes of legal validity and admissibility.
A WhatsApp message or SMS sent between two parties in a commercial dispute, stored on a mobile phone, qualifies as an electronic record and can be produced as evidence in an Indian court.
A digitally signed PDF agreement executed between two companies on a DocuSign or NeSL platform is an electronic record that carries legal enforceability under Sections 4 and 10A of the IT Act.

Hospital patient data stored in an Electronic Health Record (EHR) system maintained by a private hospital in India constitutes an electronic record, and its unauthorised access or disclosure can attract liability under the IT Act.
A screenshot of a social media post or an archived webpage stored on a government server for cybercrime investigation purposes is treated as an electronic record admissible before a court.
what_it_covers: Emails, SMS messages, and instant messages sent or received on electronic devices.
Data entries, files, and databases generated or stored within computer systems or computer networks.
Digitally scanned documents stored on microfilm or computer-generated microfiche.
Audio and video recordings stored or transmitted in electronic form.
Digitally signed contracts, certificates, and government notifications published in the Electronic Gazette.
Log files, transaction records, and metadata generated by computer systems during processing.
what_it_excludes: Physical paper documents that have never been digitised or stored in any electronic medium.
Oral communications that are not recorded or stored in any electronic format.
Handwritten records or physical ledgers that exist solely in tangible, non-electronic form.
Data stored solely in non-electronic analogue formats (e.g., traditional photographic film not involving computer-generated microfiche).
Physical currency and paper-based negotiable instruments that have not been converted into electronic form.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether something qualifies as an electronic record determines its legal validity and enforceability under Sections 4 and 7 of the IT Act (legal recognition and retention of records), its admissibility as evidence in judicial proceedings, and whether offences such as tampering (Section 66), unauthorised access, or breach of privacy under Sections 66A–72 can be attracted. It also governs obligations around secure storage, digital signatures, and data protection imposed on bodies corporate and service providers.

Essentially, if information lives in a digital or electronic medium rather than on paper, it qualifies as an electronic record.
real_world_examples: An e-mail sent by a Mumbai-based company to its supplier in Delhi confirming a purchase order, stored on the company's email server, constitutes an electronic record under the IT Act.
A PDF of a signed contract exchanged between two parties via WhatsApp or email in India qualifies as an electronic record and can be produced as evidence in a civil dispute.
A digital photograph or CCTV footage stored on a hard disk at a bank branch in Bengaluru, capturing a transaction or incident, is an electronic record admissible in court proceedings.
An entry in a hospital's electronic health management system recording a patient's diagnosis and treatment in Chennai is an electronic record protected under the provisions of the IT Act.
An SMS or text message sent from one individual to another through a mobile network in India, stored on the recipient's device or telecom server, is treated as an electronic record.
Financial transaction logs generated and stored by a payment gateway such as Razorpay or Paytm during a UPI transfer constitute electronic records for audit and legal purposes.

Scanned documents stored as digital files, including microfilm and computer-generated microfiche reproductions.
Electronic government records such as digitally filed tax returns, e-court filings, and Aadhaar-linked data stored on government servers.
what_it_excludes: Physical paper documents, handwritten records, or printed materials that have not been digitised or stored in any electronic medium.
Oral communications or verbal agreements that were never recorded or stored in any electronic or digital format.
Physical microfilm reels or photographic films that are not computer-generated or not stored in an electronic or digital system.
Calculator outputs or data from non-programmable devices expressly excluded from the definition of 'computer' under the Act.
Pure analogue recordings (such as old magnetic tape audio not digitised) that exist solely in analogue form without digital conversion.

definitions.definition: "Electronic signature" means authentication of any electronic record by a subscriber by means of the electronic technique specified in the Second Schedule and includes digital signature.
definitions.plain_english: An electronic signature is a legally recognised way for a person to sign or authenticate a digital document using an approved electronic method. It works like a handwritten signature but in the digital world, confirming that a specific person has agreed to or verified the contents of an electronic record. Digital signatures are a specific, more secure type of electronic signature and are automatically included within this definition.
real_world_examples: A taxpayer in India using Aadhaar-based OTP authentication to e-file their Income Tax Return on the Income Tax Department portal — the OTP-based authentication qualifies as an electronic signature.

A company director signing board resolutions or annual filings on the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA21) portal using a USB-token-based Class 3 Digital Signature Certificate issued by a licensed Certifying Authority such as eMudhra or Sify.

A borrower signing a loan agreement digitally on a fintech lending platform like a bank's net banking portal using an Aadhaar eSign service, which is listed in the Second Schedule as an approved electronic technique.

A government employee in an e-procurement system (such as GeM — Government e-Marketplace) authenticating a purchase order electronically using their digital signature certificate to legally bind the government to the transaction.

A litigant or advocate submitting electronically signed affidavits or vakalatnamas through the eCourts filing system, where the electronic signature authenticates the identity of the signatory and gives the document legal validity.
what_it_covers: Digital signatures created using an asymmetric crypto system and a Digital Signature Certificate issued by a licensed Certifying Authority under section 35 of the Act.
Aadhaar-based eSign services where a subscriber uses biometric or OTP-based authentication linked to their Aadhaar number, as specified in the Second Schedule.
Any other electronic technique that the Central Government may notify in the Second Schedule as a recognised method for authenticating electronic records.
Authentication of electronic records submitted in e-governance applications, online contracts, and digital filings where the subscriber uses an approved Second Schedule method.
what_it_excludes: A scanned image or photograph of a handwritten signature pasted into a document, which is not an authentication by means of any electronic technique specified in the Second Schedule.

Authentication methods or techniques not listed or notified in the Second Schedule, even if they are electronic in nature, such as simple email-based consent or clicking an 'I agree' checkbox without a recognised cryptographic or biometric underpinning.
Signatures or marks made by a person who is not a 'subscriber' as defined under the Act — i.e., a person who has not been certified or enrolled under a recognised electronic signature scheme.
Handwritten wet-ink signatures on physical paper documents, which are governed by the Indian Contract Act, 1872 and the General Clauses Act, 1897, not by the IT Act, 2000.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a signature qualifies as an 'electronic signature' under this definition determines whether an electronic record is legally authenticated under section 5, giving it the same legal effect as a handwritten signature and making electronic contracts and documents enforceable. Forgery or fraudulent use of another person's electronic signature attracts criminal liability under sections 66C (identity theft) and 71 (misrepresentation), while improper issuance of Electronic Signature Certificates triggers liability under section 73.

definitions.definition: "Electronic Signature Certificate" means an Electronic Signature Certificate issued under section 35 and includes Digital Signature Certificate.
definitions.plain_english: An Electronic Signature Certificate is an official digital document issued by a licensed authority that links a person's identity to their electronic signature, confirming that the signature is genuine and trustworthy. It is the broader category of certificates used to authenticate electronic records in India, and it includes the more specific Digital Signature Certificate. Think of it as the digital equivalent of a government-issued identity card that proves your electronic signature belongs to you.
real_world_examples: A chartered accountant in Mumbai uses an Electronic Signature Certificate issued by a licensed Certifying Authority to digitally sign and file GST returns on the GSTN portal, ensuring the submission is legally authenticated.

A company director in Bengaluru uses an Electronic Signature Certificate to sign Memorandum of Association documents during online company incorporation through the Ministry of Corporate Affairs' MCA21 portal.

A government contractor in Delhi submits a digitally signed bid on the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) portal using an Electronic Signature Certificate, which authenticates her identity and the integrity of the tender document.
A bank in Hyderabad issues loan agreements to customers who sign them using Electronic Signature Certificates, making the agreements legally valid and enforceable under the IT Act, 2000.
A lawyer in Chennai uses an Electronic Signature Certificate to e-file court documents on the eCourts platform, satisfying the authentication requirements for electronic submission of pleadings.
what_it_covers: Digital Signature Certificates issued under sub-section (4) of section 35 of the IT Act, which are explicitly included within the definition.
Any certificate issued under section 35 by a licensed Certifying Authority using electronic techniques specified in the Second Schedule of the IT Act.
Certificates that bind a subscriber's public key to their identity, enabling verification of electronic signatures on digital documents such as tax filings, contracts, and government submissions.

Certificates issued using asymmetric crypto systems or any other electronic technique approved and notified under the Second Schedule, thereby covering future technology-neutral authentication methods.
what_it_excludes: Certificates issued by unlicensed entities not granted a licence under section 24 of the IT Act, as only licensed Certifying Authorities can issue valid Electronic Signature Certificates.
Simple username-password authentication mechanisms or OTP-based verifications, which are not certificates issued under section 35 and do not constitute Electronic Signature Certificates.
Physical or wet-ink signature verifications and notarised documents, which fall outside the electronic authentication framework governed by the IT Act.
Foreign digital certificates issued by overseas certification authorities unless specifically recognised or accepted under a bilateral agreement or notification under the IT Act.

Offences related to fraudulent issuance, misrepresentation, or misuse of Electronic Signature Certificates attract penal liability under sections 71, 73, and 74 of the IT Act.

definitions.definition: Encryption refers to the modes or methods prescribed by the Central Government for converting electronic data or information into a secure, unreadable format to protect it during transmission or storage over the electronic medium, for the purpose of secure use of the electronic medium and promotion of e-governance and e-commerce, as contemplated under Section 84A of the Information Technology Act, 2000.
definitions.plain_english: Encryption is the process of scrambling or converting readable digital data into a coded, unreadable format so that only authorised persons with the correct key can access or read it. The Indian government has the power to decide which encryption methods are acceptable and standard for use in digital transactions and government services. It is essentially a digital lock that protects your data from being read or misused by unauthorised parties.
real_world_examples: A citizen filing income tax returns on the Income Tax Department's e-filing portal — the data transmitted between the browser and the server is encrypted using SSL/TLS protocols to prevent interception by third parties.
A customer making a UPI payment via PhonePe or Google Pay — the transaction data, including bank account details and OTP, is encrypted end-to-end before being transmitted across the NPCI network.

A government hospital in Maharashtra using the National Health Mission's digital health records system — patient data stored and transmitted is encrypted to prevent unauthorised access by hospital staff or external hackers.

A law firm in Delhi using an encrypted email service to send sensitive client contracts and case strategies, ensuring that even if the email is intercepted, the contents remain unreadable to the attacker.

Aadhaar-based eKYC transactions performed by telecom operators such as Airtel or Jio — biometric and demographic data is encrypted before transmission to UIDAI servers to comply with security standards.
An e-commerce company like Flipkart encrypting stored customer credit/debit card data on its servers to prevent data breaches from exposing financial information of millions of Indian consumers.
what_it_covers: Modes and methods of converting plaintext electronic data into ciphertext to prevent unauthorised access during digital transactions.
Encryption standards mandated or prescribed by the Central Government for use in e-governance platforms such as DigiLocker, GSTN, or e-Courts.
End-to-end encryption of communications transmitted over computer networks, including emails, messaging services, and financial payment systems operating in India.
Encryption of sensitive personal data or information stored in data centres by body corporates and government agencies to comply with security obligations.
Protocols and algorithms (such as AES, RSA, or SSL/TLS) designated by the Central Government as acceptable encryption methods for secure electronic records and digital signatures.
what_it_excludes: Physical security measures such as locking servers in secure rooms or using hardware security modules that do not involve algorithmic transformation of electronic data.
Password protection of files or documents that merely restricts access without algorithmically transforming the underlying data into an unreadable encoded format.
Analogue or non-electronic encoding methods such as physical ciphers, invisible ink, or steganography in printed documents, which fall outside the scope of the electronic medium.
Encryption methods or standards that have not been prescribed or approved by the Central Government under Section 84A and applicable rules, which may not enjoy statutory recognition under the Act.
Authentication mechanisms such as OTPs, digital signatures, or biometric verification alone, which verify identity but do not by themselves encrypt or encode the underlying data content.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether government-prescribed encryption standards are followed determines the legal validity and security compliance of electronic records and e-governance transactions under the IT Act; non-compliance may expose organisations to liability under sections governing data protection, unauthorised access, and interception, while proper encryption may serve as a defence or mitigating factor in adjudication proceedings. Additionally, the government's power to prescribe encryption methods under Section 84A directly intersects with decryption obligations under Section 69, where failure to assist authorised agencies in decrypting data constitutes a punishable offence.

definitions.definition: The word 'fraudulent' shall have the meaning assigned to it in section 25 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860), which defines 'fraudulently' as doing a thing with intent to defraud, whether or not the defrauding is of a person. In the context of the IT Act, it connotes an act done with the intent to gain a wrongful advantage or to cause wrongful loss to another through deceit or deception in the electronic or digital domain.
definitions.plain_english: Acting 'fraudulently' means doing something with a deliberate intention to cheat or deceive someone for personal gain or to cause harm to another person. It goes beyond mere mistake or negligence — there must be a conscious, calculated intent to defraud. In simple terms, if you knowingly trick or deceive someone using digital tools or electronic certificates, you are acting fraudulently.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai creates a fake Digital Signature Certificate mimicking a government official's certificate and submits it on a public e-procurement portal to win a tender fraudulently — constituting publication for fraudulent purpose under Section 74.

A cybercriminal in Bengaluru publishes a forged Electronic Signature Certificate falsely attributed to a well-known bank to deceive customers into believing a phishing website is legitimate, thereby committing fraud under the IT Act.

An employee in Delhi deliberately creates and circulates a counterfeit electronic signature certificate purporting to be from the Income Tax Department to fraudulently authenticate fake tax refund notices sent to taxpayers.

A vendor in Hyderabad knowingly makes available a fabricated Electronic Signature Certificate on a marketplace platform to fraudulently validate fake invoices and siphon GST refunds from the government.

A fraudster in Chennai generates and publishes a fake Certifying Authority certificate online to trick users into installing malicious software, falsely representing it as certified and secure software.
what_it_covers: Knowingly creating or publishing a fake Electronic Signature Certificate with intent to deceive a third party or gain an unlawful advantage.
Using another person's electronic signature or unique identification feature with deliberate intent to impersonate and cause wrongful gain or loss.
Any act involving digital or electronic records, systems, or signatures carried out with a calculated intention to cheat, deceive, or cause financial or reputational harm to another person or entity.
Deliberately making available a forged certification document on a digital platform to facilitate an unlawful transaction or misrepresentation.
what_it_excludes: Acts done negligently or by mistake without any conscious intention to deceive or defraud — mere carelessness does not constitute fraudulent conduct.
Acts done in good faith, even if they result in loss to another party, as the element of deliberate deceptive intent is absent.
Unauthorised access or computer-related offences committed purely out of curiosity or mischief without any intent to gain wrongful benefit or cause wrongful loss to any specific party.
Technical errors or system malfunctions that result in incorrect issuance or publication of certificates, as these lack the mens rea (guilty mind) required for fraudulent conduct.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'fraudulent' is a critical determinant of criminal liability under Sections 66, 66C, and 74 of the IT Act — if established, it can attract imprisonment and monetary fines, elevating the offence from a civil contravention to a cognizable criminal offence. Without proof of fraudulent intent, an act may not cross the threshold required for prosecution under these provisions, significantly affecting whether criminal charges can be framed.

definitions.plain_english: Acting 'fraudulently' means doing something with a deliberate intention to cheat or deceive another person in order to gain an unfair advantage or cause harm. It is not enough to accidentally or negligently cause harm — there must be a conscious plan to deceive. The key element is the intent to defraud, which separates fraudulent conduct from mere mistakes or careless behaviour.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai creates a fake copy of a bank's website and tricks customers into entering their net banking credentials, then uses those credentials to transfer funds — this is fraudulent use of another's identity features under Section 66C.

An employee in a Bengaluru IT firm deliberately copies proprietary source code and sells it to a competitor, misrepresenting himself as the rightful owner — the act of misrepresentation with intent to gain constitutes fraudulent conduct under Section 66.

A cybercriminal in Delhi impersonates a government official by using a cloned digital signature to submit fraudulent e-tenders on a government procurement portal, intending to win contracts illegally.

A person in Hyderabad uses another individual's Aadhaar-linked OTP obtained through social engineering to fraudulently register a SIM card and access the victim's UPI accounts, constituting fraudulent misuse of a unique identification feature under Section 66C.

A scammer operating from Kolkata sends phishing emails mimicking the Income Tax Department, collects login credentials from taxpayers, and files false refund claims — all acts done with clear intent to defraud both the victims and the government.
what_it_covers: Using another person's electronic signature, password, or unique identification feature with a deliberate intention to deceive or gain unfairly, as in identity theft under Section 66C.
Intentionally and deceptively accessing or manipulating a computer system or data with a pre-planned scheme to cause wrongful loss to another or wrongful gain to oneself.
Knowingly submitting forged or manipulated electronic records with the purpose of misleading authorities, courts, or other persons for personal or financial benefit.
Deliberately impersonating another person online or in digital communications with the goal of deceiving the recipient and obtaining something of value or causing harm.
what_it_excludes: Accidental or negligent acts that result in harm without any deliberate intention to deceive or defraud — such as unintentional data breaches caused by poor security practices.
Acts done in good faith or under a bona fide belief of legal entitlement, even if they turn out to be incorrect or harmful to another party.
Mere unauthorised access to a computer system without any accompanying intent to deceive or gain an unfair advantage — which may be covered under other provisions but not as 'fraudulent' conduct.
Technical errors, software bugs, or system failures that cause data corruption or loss without any human intent to defraud.

definitions.definition: "function", in relation to a computer, includes logic, control, arithmetical process, deletion, storage and retrieval and communication or telecommunication from or within a computer.
definitions.plain_english: In the context of the IT Act, 'function' refers to any operation a computer can perform — such as performing calculations, storing or retrieving data, deleting information, controlling processes, or sending and receiving communications. It is a broad term that captures the full range of capabilities that a computer can carry out. Essentially, anything a computer 'does' internally or externally is a function.
real_world_examples: When a hacker based in Mumbai remotely deletes financial records stored on a bank's server in Pune, the act of deletion is a 'function' of the computer being unlawfully interfered with under the IT Act.
When an e-commerce platform like Flipkart processes an arithmetic calculation to apply a discount code during checkout, that arithmetical process constitutes a 'function' of their computer system.

When a government official in Delhi uses a computer to retrieve Aadhaar-linked data from the UIDAI database without authorisation, accessing the storage and retrieval function of that computer triggers liability under the Act.

When a malware program disrupts the control functions of SCADA systems managing a power grid in Maharashtra, interfering with the computer's 'control' function makes it a cyber-attack on critical infrastructure.

When an employee of an IT firm in Bengaluru sends confidential client data via email using the company's internal server, the communication function of the computer is engaged, and any unauthorised interception would constitute an offence under the Act.
what_it_covers: Logical operations performed by a computer, such as conditional processing and decision-making by software applications.
Arithmetical processes, including calculations performed during financial transactions, tax computations, or data analytics.
Deletion of data, files, or records stored in a computer system or computer network.
Storage and retrieval of data, encompassing database read/write operations, file saves, and data lookups.
Communication or telecommunication from or within a computer, including sending emails, transmitting files over a network, or internal inter-process communication.
what_it_excludes: Physical or mechanical operations of hardware that do not involve logical, arithmetical, or communicative processing, such as the act of physically powering on or off a device.
Functions performed by non-programmable calculators, which are explicitly excluded from the definition of 'computer' under the Act and therefore fall outside the scope of 'function' in this context.
Human cognitive or manual functions performed without the involvement of a computer, such as a person manually sorting paper records or performing mental arithmetic.
Operations of communication devices (like standalone telephony) that are not connected to or operating as part of a computer, computer system, or computer network.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'function' is critical because unauthorised interference with, or gaining entry into, any function of a computer determines whether an offence such as unauthorised access (Section 43), computer damage, or hacking (Section 66) has been committed. If an act does not engage a recognised 'function' of a computer, it may fall outside the purview of these offences and associated civil or criminal liability under the Act.

definitions.definition: An act or intended act is deemed to be done in 'good faith' under the Information Technology Act, 2000, when it is done honestly and without any fraudulent intent, in pursuance of the Act or any rule, regulation, or order made thereunder, even if done negligently. Section 84 extends this protection to the Central Government, State Government, the Controller, persons acting on behalf of the Controller, and adjudicating officers against any suit, prosecution, or other legal proceeding arising from such acts.
definitions.plain_english: Good faith means acting honestly and sincerely, without any intention to deceive or cause harm, while carrying out duties or powers given under the IT Act. If a government official or officer makes an honest mistake while doing their job under this law, they cannot be sued or prosecuted for it. It does not protect deliberate wrongdoing or fraud — only genuine, honest actions taken in the course of official duties.
real_world_examples: A Controller of Certifying Authorities in India suspends a digital certificate after receiving a complaint of compromise. Even if the suspension later proves unwarranted, as long as it was done honestly based on available information under the IT Act, the Controller is protected from a civil lawsuit by the certificate holder.

An adjudicating officer appointed under the IT Act passes an interim order freezing a company's electronic records during an investigation into a data breach. If the order is later found to be procedurally flawed but was made honestly and without malice, the officer cannot be prosecuted for the inconvenience caused to the company.

A state government official, acting on behalf of the Controller, issues a notice to a Certifying Authority in good faith based on a tip-off about fraudulent certificate issuance. Even if the tip turns out to be false, the official is protected from legal proceedings because the action was taken honestly in pursuance of the IT Act.

During a cybersecurity incident affecting critical infrastructure in Mumbai, an officer of the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team takes down a suspected malicious server hosted by an ISP. If the server later turns out to be legitimate but the action was taken honestly to protect national interests under the IT Act, the officer enjoys good faith protection.

A Central Government officer, while implementing a notification under the IT Act designating a protected system, inadvertently restricts access to a private company's legitimate operations. Since the act was done honestly in pursuance of the Act and without fraudulent intent, no legal proceedings can be maintained against that officer.
what_it_covers: An adjudicating officer who issues an erroneous penalty order while genuinely attempting to enforce the IT Act without any fraudulent or malicious intent.
The Controller of Certifying Authorities who revokes or suspends a Digital Signature Certificate honestly based on information available at the time, even if the decision is later overturned.
A Central or State Government official who, acting under a rule or regulation made under the IT Act, restricts access to certain electronic records or systems honestly and without corrupt motive.
Any person acting on behalf of the Controller who executes instructions under the IT Act in a sincere and honest manner, even if those instructions cause incidental harm to a third party.
what_it_excludes: Actions taken with a known fraudulent or dishonest motive, such as an adjudicating officer deliberately misusing powers under the IT Act for personal gain or to harass a specific party.
Acts committed outside the scope of the IT Act, its rules, regulations, or orders — meaning unofficial or ultra vires actions cannot claim good faith protection under Section 84.

Private individuals or intermediaries who are not acting on behalf of the Controller or the Government; good faith protection under Section 84 is limited to the specific enumerated persons and entities.
Deliberate suppression of evidence or intentional procedural violations by an adjudicating officer that go beyond honest mistake and amount to willful misconduct or mala fide action.
definitions.why_it_matters: The applicability of 'good faith' under Section 84 determines whether a suit, prosecution, or other legal proceeding can be maintained against government officials and adjudicating officers — if the act qualifies as done in good faith, no legal action lies against them, effectively blocking civil and criminal liability. Conversely, if an act is shown to be malicious, fraudulent, or outside the purview of the Act, the good faith shield falls away and the officer or authority becomes legally accountable.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 3(2), 'hash function' means an algorithm mapping or translation of one sequence of bits into another, generally smaller, set known as 'hash result' such that an electronic record yields the same hash result every time the algorithm is executed with the same electronic record as its input making it computationally infeasible— (a) to derive or reconstruct the original electronic record from the hash result produced by the algorithm; (b) that two electronic records can produce the same hash result using the algorithm.
definitions.plain_english: A hash function is a mathematical formula that converts any digital document or file into a unique, fixed-size code called a 'hash result' or 'hash value'. No matter how many times you run the same document through this formula, you always get the same code. It is practically impossible to reverse-engineer the original document from this code, and no two different documents should ever produce the same code — making it a reliable way to verify that a document has not been tampered with.
real_world_examples: When a taxpayer files an Income Tax Return electronically on the Income Tax Department's portal, the hash function processes the ITR document and generates a unique hash value that is embedded in the digital signature, ensuring the return cannot be altered after submission without detection.

A Mumbai-based company executing a major commercial contract via e-signing platform (such as eMudhra or SignDesk) relies on hash functions to lock the contract's content — any post-signature modification to even a single word changes the hash result, immediately invalidating the digital signature and alerting the parties.

When the Ministry of Corporate Affairs receives digitally signed incorporation documents filed on the MCA21 portal by a Chartered Accountant, the server uses the hash function to verify the document's integrity, confirming that the document received is identical to the one that was signed.

A software company in Bengaluru distributes a software update and publishes its SHA-256 hash result on its website; Indian customers can run the same hash function on the downloaded file to confirm it has not been tampered with or infected with malware during transit.

Courts admitting electronic records as evidence under the Indian Evidence Act rely on the hash function principle to establish that a digital document produced before the court is the same unaltered record that was originally created, satisfying the integrity requirement of electronic evidence.
what_it_covers: Standard cryptographic hashing algorithms such as SHA-256, SHA-1, or MD5 when used to produce a hash result from an electronic record for the purpose of digital signature creation or verification under the IT Act.

The process of mapping an arbitrarily large electronic record (such as a contract, government notification, or certificate) into a fixed-length hash result that uniquely represents that specific document.
The computational function applied within the asymmetric crypto system during the authentication of electronic records by a subscriber affixing a digital signature under Section 3.

Any algorithm used in conjunction with a private key to envelope and transform an initial electronic record into a digitally signed electronic record, satisfying the one-way and collision-resistance properties stated in Section 3(2).
what_it_excludes: Symmetric encryption algorithms that are designed to be reversible (i.e., where the original data can be recovered from the encrypted output), since a hash function must be computationally infeasible to reverse.

Simple checksums or cyclic redundancy checks (CRCs) used only for error detection in data transmission, which do not satisfy the collision-resistance and irreversibility requirements stipulated in the definition.

Encoding or compression techniques (such as Base64 encoding or ZIP compression) that convert data into another format but are fully reversible and not designed to produce a cryptographically secure fixed-length hash result.

Password hashing used solely for access control or authentication data storage that does not form part of the digital signature process or the enveloping and transformation of an electronic record under Section 3.
definitions.why_it_matters: The hash function is a mandatory technical component of a valid digital signature under Section 3 of the IT Act; if the algorithm used does not satisfy the properties of irreversibility and collision-resistance set out in the definition, the resulting signature may not constitute a legally valid 'digital signature', thereby undermining the legal enforceability of digitally signed electronic records and any obligations or rights that depend on authenticated electronic records under the Act.

definitions.definition: 'Indian Computer Emergency Response Team' means an agency established under sub-section (1) of Section 70B.
definitions.plain_english: The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) is an official government agency set up under the IT Act to handle cybersecurity threats and emergencies in India. It acts as the national nodal agency for responding to computer security incidents, coordinating cybersecurity efforts, and issuing guidelines to protect India's cyberspace. Think of it as the cyber equivalent of a national emergency response service, but specifically for digital and internet-based threats.
real_world_examples: When a major ransomware attack like NotPetya or WannaCry affects Indian hospitals, banks, and IT companies, CERT-In issues emergency advisories and coordinates with affected organisations to contain the damage and restore systems.

After a large-scale data breach at an Indian e-commerce platform exposing millions of customer records, the company is legally required to report the incident to CERT-In within six hours of becoming aware of it, as mandated under CERT-In directions.

When a critical vulnerability is discovered in widely used Indian government portals (such as those run by NIC), CERT-In coordinates with the concerned ministries and technical teams to patch the systems and disseminate advisories to other potentially affected agencies.

During a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack targeting Indian banking infrastructure, CERT-In works with the Reserve Bank of India, ISPs, and the affected banks to identify the attack source, mitigate damage, and publish threat intelligence to prevent further incidents.

A cybersecurity firm operating in India discovers a new malware strain targeting Indian telecom networks and reports technical indicators to CERT-In, which then validates the threat and circulates an alert to all critical sector organisations under its mandated framework.
what_it_covers: The statutory national nodal agency constituted by the Central Government under Section 70B(1) of the IT Act for cybersecurity incident response and coordination in India.

The body empowered to issue directions, guidelines, and advisories to service providers, intermediaries, data centres, and government organisations regarding cybersecurity practices and incident reporting obligations.
The agency authorised to call for information, conduct forensic analysis, and coordinate responses to cyber incidents affecting critical information infrastructure or any computer resource in India.
CERT-In as the authority to whom mandatory reporting of cybersecurity incidents (such as data breaches, ransomware attacks, DDoS attacks) must be made by covered entities within prescribed timelines.
what_it_excludes: State-level Computer Emergency Response Teams or sector-specific CERTs set up by individual ministries or private bodies, which are not the same legal entity as CERT-In established under Section 70B.
Private cybersecurity firms, incident response companies, or managed security service providers operating in India, even if they perform similar technical functions in the private sector.
International or foreign computer emergency response teams such as US-CERT or ENISA, which operate under foreign jurisdictions and have no statutory standing under the IT Act.

The National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC), which is a separate body established under Section 70A of the IT Act and serves a distinct protective mandate for critical infrastructure.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as or falls under the jurisdiction of the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team determines the applicability of mandatory incident reporting obligations, compliance with CERT-In directions, and liability for non-compliance under Section 70B of the IT Act. Directions issued by CERT-In carry statutory force, and failure to comply can attract penalties and enforcement action against service providers, intermediaries, and other covered entities.

definitions.definition: "information‖ includes data, message, text, images, sound, voice, codes, computer programmes, software and databases or micro film or computer generated micro fiche. (As defined under Section 2(1)(v) of the Information Technology Act, 2000.)
definitions.plain_english: Under the IT Act, 'information' is a very broad term that covers almost anything stored, sent, or processed electronically — including text messages, emails, images, audio, video, software code, and databases. It goes beyond just facts or data and includes computer programmes and even microfilm records. Essentially, if it can be digitally created, stored, or transmitted, it likely qualifies as 'information' under this law.
real_world_examples: A WhatsApp message sent by a Mumbai-based user containing a threat — the text of that message constitutes 'information' and can be the basis of prosecution under Section 66A (before it was struck down) or related provisions.

Aadhaar biometric and demographic records stored in UIDAI's central database qualify as 'information,' and unauthorised disclosure of such information triggers liability under Section 72 of the IT Act.

A Bollywood production house's unreleased film files, scripts, and soundtrack stored on a cloud server are 'information,' and hacking into that server to steal them constitutes unauthorised access to information under Section 43 and Section 66.

A bank's customer transaction logs, account numbers, and balance records stored in its core banking system are 'information' — any breach or leak of these records attracts obligations under the Act's data protection and cyber security provisions.
A government e-tender portal's uploaded bid documents, technical specifications, and financial offers are 'information,' and tampering with them can attract Section 65 or Section 66 penalties.

CCTV footage stored digitally at a Delhi Metro station constitutes 'information' (as it is sound and image stored in electronic form), making unauthorised copying or transmission of that footage a potential offence.
what_it_covers: Text messages, emails, and any written digital communication exchanged over computer networks or communication devices
Images, audio recordings, video files, and voice data stored or transmitted electronically
Computer programmes, software source code, and databases stored on any computer resource
Microfilm and computer-generated microfiche records
Codes and machine-readable instructions that form part of a computer system
Personal and sensitive data stored in government or private digital repositories
what_it_excludes: Physical, paper-based documents or records that have never been digitised or stored in any electronic form
Oral speech or conversations that are not recorded, transmitted, or stored through any electronic or digital medium
Documents or transactions specified in the First Schedule to the IT Act, to which the Act itself does not apply

definitions.definition: An 'information system' under the Information Technology Act, 2000 refers to a system that is programmed by or on behalf of an originator to operate automatically for the purpose of sending electronic records, as contemplated under Section 11. It encompasses any automated computing or electronic infrastructure configured to generate, process, store, or transmit electronic records without direct human intervention at the time of each operation.
definitions.plain_english: An information system is essentially an automated computer-based system that is set up and programmed to send or process electronic messages and records on its own, without a human pressing 'send' each time. Think of it as a pre-configured digital machine that carries out instructions automatically on behalf of the person or organisation that set it up. For example, a bank's server that automatically sends account statements to customers is an information system.
real_world_examples: An Indian bank's core banking software that automatically generates and dispatches monthly e-statements or OTP messages to customers without any manual intervention at the time of sending — the bank is the originator and the system acts on its behalf.
An e-commerce platform like Flipkart or Amazon India running automated order confirmation and invoice dispatch systems that send electronic records to buyers immediately upon purchase completion.

The Income Tax Department's automated systems that generate and electronically transmit income tax notices, refund intimations, and assessment orders to taxpayers through the e-filing portal without manual triggering for each record.
A GST-compliant ERP system deployed by a large Indian manufacturer that automatically generates and transmits e-invoices to the GST Network (GSTN) portal upon each sale transaction.
A hospital management system used by AIIMS or a private hospital chain that automatically sends appointment confirmations, discharge summaries, and billing records electronically to patients.
A stockbroking firm's trading platform that automatically sends electronic contract notes and settlement records to clients after each trade executed on NSE or BSE.
what_it_covers: Automated banking servers programmed to dispatch electronic statements, alerts, and notices on behalf of the bank (the originator) without per-message human action.

Government e-governance portals and backend systems programmed to automatically issue digitally signed certificates, notices, or orders — such as the MCA21 system issuing company incorporation certificates.
Enterprise ERP or CRM systems configured by a business entity to automatically generate and transmit electronic invoices, contracts, or acknowledgements to counterparties.
Automated email or SMS dispatch engines set up by an originator to send transactional electronic records like OTPs, confirmations, and legal notices in bulk.
IoT-based or SCADA systems programmed to automatically log and transmit electronic records to a central authority on behalf of the operating organisation.
what_it_excludes: A human operator who manually composes and sends an individual electronic record on behalf of the originator — that falls under personal or authorised-agent attribution, not information system attribution.
A general-purpose computer or device that has not been specifically programmed or configured to automatically send electronic records on the originator's behalf.
Third-party intermediaries or service providers who operate systems independently and not specifically programmed by or on behalf of the originator for that particular automated function.
Paper-based or purely offline systems that do not generate, process, or transmit electronic records in any form.
Systems operated solely for internal data storage with no outbound electronic record transmission programmed into them on behalf of an originator.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a system as an 'information system' under Section 11 determines whether an electronic record automatically generated and sent by that system can be legally attributed to the originator — a critical factor in establishing the authenticity and legal enforceability of electronically transmitted documents, notices, and contracts in disputes before courts or adjudicating officers. If the attribution under Section 11 is successfully established, the originator bears full legal responsibility for the content of records dispatched by the system, triggering obligations and liabilities under the Act.

definitions.definition: The term 'injury' is not formally defined in the Information Technology Act, 2000. As used in the Act, 'injury' means any harm, loss, or detriment caused to a person — whether to body, mind, reputation, property, or legal rights — arising from a contravention of the provisions of the Act, including harm caused by unauthorised access to computer resources, sending offensive or false information, or acts of cyber terrorism that threaten individuals or national interests.
definitions.plain_english: Injury refers to any kind of harm or damage suffered by a person as a result of someone else's illegal or wrongful act under this law. This can include physical harm, emotional distress, damage to reputation, financial loss, or harm to a country's security interests. It is the basis on which a victim can claim compensation or the government can take action against an offender.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based professional receives thousands of false and defamatory messages sent through a computer network by a former colleague, causing severe damage to her reputation and mental health — this constitutes injury warranting a compensation claim before the adjudicating officer under Section 46.

A hacker in Delhi gains unauthorised access to a Bengaluru hospital's patient database and leaks sensitive health records, causing injury to hundreds of patients whose private medical information is exposed publicly.

A cybercriminal sends repeated false messages to a Kolkata businessman's clients falsely claiming the businessman is bankrupt, causing financial injury by destroying business relationships and resulting in loss of contracts.

A state-sponsored cyber attack disrupts the SCADA systems of a power grid in Chennai, causing widespread power outage and physical injuries to persons dependent on life-support systems — constituting injury to persons under Section 66F on cyber terrorism.

A fraudulent phishing email campaign targeting HDFC Bank customers in Hyderabad tricks thousands of users into revealing their credentials, causing monetary injury through unauthorized withdrawal of funds from their accounts.

A social media harassment campaign carried out through a communication device sends menacing messages to a female journalist in Pune, causing psychological injury and compelling her to shut down her professional accounts.
what_it_covers: Financial loss suffered by an individual or organisation due to unauthorised access to their computer systems or data, qualifying the victim to claim compensation before the adjudicating officer.
Psychological or reputational harm caused by the sending of offensive, menacing, or false information through communication devices under Section 66A.
Physical harm or death caused to persons as a result of cyber terrorism acts under Section 66F, such as attacks on critical infrastructure disrupting essential services like hospitals or power grids.
Injury to national interests, sovereignty, or security of India caused by unauthorised access to restricted government or defence computer databases under Section 66F.
Harm suffered by a body corporate or its customers due to negligence in maintaining reasonable security practices, leading to data breaches and consequential financial or reputational damage.
what_it_excludes: Mere inconvenience, annoyance, or irritation that does not rise to the level of quantifiable harm or detriment, as such minor grievances are separately addressed in the Act without constituting compensable injury.

Contractual disputes or civil wrongs that do not arise from a contravention of the Information Technology Act or its rules and regulations, which fall outside the adjudicating officer's jurisdiction under Section 46.

Injury claims exceeding rupees five crore before the adjudicating officer, as jurisdiction for such claims is expressly vested in the competent court by Section 46(1A) and not within the adjudicating officer's power.
Hypothetical or speculative future harm that has not yet materialised as an actual or imminent consequence of a contravention of the Act.
Damage to inanimate property or infrastructure that does not result in harm to any person's legal rights, interests, or well-being as contemplated by the Act's compensation and penalty framework.
definitions.why_it_matters: The existence and quantum of 'injury' directly determines the jurisdiction of the adjudicating officer versus the competent court under Section 46(1A) — claims up to rupees five crore go to the adjudicating officer, while larger claims go to court. Establishing injury is also a prerequisite for awarding compensation to aggrieved persons and for prosecuting offences under Sections 66A and 66F, making it a foundational element of both civil and criminal liability under the Act.

definitions.definition: Instigation, within the meaning of Section 84B of the Information Technology Act, 2000, refers to the act of actively urging, encouraging, inciting, or provoking another person to commit an offence under the Act, such that the offence is committed in consequence of such instigation. It constitutes one of the modes by which abetment of an offence is established under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: Instigation means actively pushing, encouraging, or provoking someone else to commit a crime under the IT Act. It is not merely suggesting something passively — it involves a deliberate effort to get another person to do something illegal. If the other person actually commits the crime because of that encouragement, the person who instigated it can be punished just as severely as the one who actually did it.
real_world_examples: A cybercrime gang leader in Mumbai repeatedly pressures and encourages a junior member to hack into a bank's computer system, providing technical guidance and motivational threats, and the junior member eventually carries out the hack — the leader's conduct amounts to instigation.

An individual in Delhi sends repeated WhatsApp messages to a known hacker urging him to deface a government website and promises monetary reward; the hacker carries out the defacement — the sender has instigated the offence.

A disgruntled ex-employee in Bengaluru convinces a current employee via encrypted chat to introduce a computer virus into the company's database by assuring them they won't get caught, resulting in the virus being deployed — this constitutes instigation.

An online forum administrator in Chennai actively encourages members through private messages to publish obscene material on their platforms, and several members do so — the administrator's conduct qualifies as instigation of the obscenity offences committed by those members.

A fraudster in Hyderabad coaches and repeatedly urges an unsuspecting accomplice to use a stolen digital signature certificate to authenticate fraudulent electronic records, and the accomplice does so — the fraudster has instigated the offence.
what_it_covers: Actively urging, pressuring, or encouraging another person through any electronic communication medium to commit an offence under the IT Act, where the offence is subsequently committed.
Providing deliberate moral support, repeated persuasion, or explicit directions to a person to carry out an illegal act such as unauthorized access, data theft, or publishing obscene content online.
Coercing or threatening another person into committing a cyber offence, where such coercion causes the offence to be carried out in consequence of the instigation.
Inciting another person through social media, messaging apps, emails, or other digital platforms to engage in conduct that constitutes an offence under the IT Act.
what_it_excludes: Mere passive knowledge or awareness that another person is planning to commit an offence, without any active encouragement or provocation — this does not amount to instigation.
General statements, opinions, or discussions about cybercrime techniques made without any specific intent to encourage a particular individual to commit an offence.
Acts that constitute conspiracy or the provision of aid, which are separate and distinct modes of abetment under Section 84B and are not classified as instigation.
Situations where an offence is committed spontaneously without any causal connection to the alleged instigation — the instigation must be a direct cause of the offence being committed.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person's conduct qualifies as instigation determines whether they are liable for abetment of an IT Act offence under Section 84B, exposing them to the same punishment as the principal offender even if they never directly committed the act themselves. Establishing instigation is therefore critical to prosecuting individuals who orchestrate or encourage cybercrimes through others while maintaining apparent distance from the actual commission of the offence.
