definitions.definition: In case of a digital signature, 'signature creation data' means the private key of the subscriber. More broadly, signature creation data refers to the unique data, including cryptographic keys, which the signatory uses to create an electronic signature, and which must, at the time of affixing the signature, be under the exclusive control of the signatory and stored and affixed in such exclusive manner as may be prescribed.
definitions.plain_english: Signature creation data is the secret information — most commonly a private cryptographic key — that a person uses to create their electronic or digital signature. Think of it like a unique, secret password or seal that only you possess and use to sign documents electronically. For digital signatures in India, this is specifically the private key issued to you as part of a Digital Signature Certificate. The law requires that this data remain exclusively in your control to ensure the signature is genuinely yours.
real_world_examples: A chartered accountant in Mumbai uses a USB token (hardware security module) issued by a licensed Certifying Authority such as eMudhra or (n)Code Solutions, which stores their private key. When they digitally sign an income tax return on the Income Tax e-filing portal, the private key stored on that token is the signature creation data being used.

A company director in Bengaluru signs board resolutions and MCA filings using a Class 3 Digital Signature Certificate. The private key stored on their encrypted smart card, which they alone can access with a PIN, constitutes the signature creation data under the IT Act.

A government officer at a State Treasury in Hyderabad uses a DSC-enabled USB token to approve electronic fund transfers on the PFMS portal. The private key within that token — inaccessible to anyone else — is the signature creation data that authenticates each transaction.

A lawyer in Delhi electronically signs a vakalatnama submitted through an eCourt platform. The private key stored in their personal hardware token, issued after identity verification by a Certifying Authority, is the signature creation data that makes the signature legally valid under Section 15 of the IT Act.

An exporter in Chennai uses a Digital Signature Certificate to file a shipping bill on the ICEGATE customs portal. The private key stored in their password-protected DSC token is the signature creation data, and any compromise of that token could invalidate the security of the electronic signature.
what_it_covers: The private key of a subscriber in a public key infrastructure (PKI) system, as explicitly stated in Section 15 of the IT Act for digital signatures.

Any unique cryptographic data element linked exclusively to the signatory that is used in the process of generating a secure electronic signature under an approved technique listed in the Second Schedule.
Data stored in a hardware security module or smart card token that is used by a subscriber to affix their digital signature, provided it remains under their exclusive control.
Authentication data used by a signatory that is linked to that person alone and was under their exclusive control at the time of signing, satisfying the reliability conditions of Section 3A(2).
what_it_excludes: The public key of the subscriber, which is shared openly and used by others to verify the signature — not to create it.

The Digital Signature Certificate itself (the electronic credential issued by a Certifying Authority), which is a separate artifact that contains the public key and identity information rather than the secret signing data.
Shared or multi-user cryptographic keys that are not under the exclusive control of a single signatory, as these fail the exclusivity requirement under Section 15(1)(a).
Passwords or PINs used solely to access a device or application, which are not themselves the cryptographic data used to generate the electronic signature.
Authentication data used solely for the purpose of verifying identity (as distinct from signing), which is separately referred to in the Act as 'authentication data' under Section 3A.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether data qualifies as 'signature creation data' under Section 15 determines if an electronic signature achieves the status of a 'secure electronic signature', which carries a presumption of authenticity and integrity under Section 16 and shifts the burden of proof in disputes. Compromise, loss of exclusive control, or improper storage of signature creation data can invalidate this presumption and expose the subscriber to liability, while also affecting enforceability of electronically signed contracts and documents.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 5, 'signed', with its grammatical variations and cognate expressions, shall, with reference to a person, mean affixing of his hand written signature or any mark on any document, and the expression 'signature' shall be construed accordingly.
definitions.plain_english: In the context of the IT Act, 'signed' means that a person has physically written their signature or placed any identifying mark on a document by hand. This traditional understanding of signing is the baseline meaning, which Section 5 then extends to include electronic signatures as a legally equivalent alternative. So when any law says a document must be 'signed', it can now be satisfied either by a handwritten signature or a valid electronic signature.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based contractor physically signs a paper agreement for a government construction tender using a pen; this constitutes 'signed' under the traditional meaning recognised in Section 5.
A taxpayer in Delhi affixes a thumb impression (a mark) on a paper income tax return form because they are unable to write; this thumb mark qualifies as 'signed' under Section 5's definition.
A small trader in Chennai signs a promissory note by hand before submitting it to a moneylender; the handwritten signature satisfies the 'signed' requirement under the traditional limb of Section 5.

A property owner in Hyderabad uses a rubber stamp bearing their name and initials on a lease agreement as their identifying mark; this stamped mark may constitute 'signed' within the meaning of the section.
A pensioner in Kolkata puts a cross mark (X) on a bank withdrawal form in the presence of a bank officer; this mark on the document satisfies the definition of 'signed' for the purposes of Section 5.
what_it_covers: A handwritten signature in ink placed by a person on any document using their usual signature style.
Any mark made by a person on a document — including a thumb impression, cross mark, or initials — intended to authenticate it.
A rubber stamp or seal mark affixed personally by an individual as their identifying mark on a document.
The act of signing in vernacular scripts (e.g., Devanagari, Tamil, Bengali) where a person writes their name or mark by hand.
A signature placed on a document by a visually impaired or illiterate person using a distinctive mark witnessed and certified as per applicable law.
what_it_excludes: An electronic signature or digital signature affixed through electronic means — these are governed separately under the electronic signature provisions of the Act, not the traditional 'signed' definition.
A signature printed or typed using a computer or typewriter without any physical handwritten element, as this is not a handwritten signature or mark personally affixed.
The signature of an authorised agent or attorney acting on behalf of a person, unless it is the person themselves affixing the mark (the definition is person-specific — 'with reference to a person').
A scanned image of a signature that is merely attached to an electronic document without compliance with prescribed electronic signature procedures.
A verbal or oral affirmation of agreement, which does not involve affixing any handwritten signature or mark on any document.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition determines whether a document satisfies a statutory requirement to be 'signed' under any existing Indian law — if the handwritten signature or mark is absent and no valid electronic signature is used instead, the document may be legally unenforceable or non-compliant, triggering invalidity of contracts, filings, or instruments. It directly enables Section 5 to function as a bridge between the traditional paper-based signing requirement and the electronic signature regime introduced by the IT Act.

definitions.definition: A computer resource or communication device is 'stolen' within the meaning of Section 66B when it has been obtained through theft, misappropriation, or any unlawful taking from its rightful owner or lawful possessor without consent, such that the person receiving or retaining it does so dishonestly, knowing or having reason to believe that the said resource or device was so unlawfully obtained.
definitions.plain_english: Something is 'stolen' under this law when a computer resource (like data, files, or a computer system) or a communication device (like a mobile phone or SIM card) has been taken away from its rightful owner without their permission and in an unlawful manner. If you receive or keep such an item knowing it was taken illegally, you are treated as having handled stolen property. The law targets not just the person who steals, but also those who knowingly benefit from the theft.
real_world_examples: A person in Delhi buys a second-hand laptop at a suspiciously low price from an unknown seller, later found to contain confidential corporate data stolen from an IT company in Bengaluru — the laptop and its data qualify as stolen computer resources under Section 66B.

A cybercriminal in Mumbai sells stolen SIM cards and mobile handsets that were cloned or physically lifted from a telecom retailer in Pune; any person who purchases these devices knowing they are stolen is liable under Section 66B for retaining a stolen communication device.

An employee in Hyderabad copies proprietary source code from his employer's servers onto a USB drive and sells it to a competitor; the recipient company, having reason to believe the data was not legitimately sourced, is liable for dishonestly receiving a stolen computer resource.

A stolen smartphone seized in Chennai is found to contain a hacked e-banking application with stored credentials of multiple users; the individual in possession of this device, aware of its stolen origin, faces prosecution under Section 66B for retaining a stolen communication device.

A data broker in Kolkata purchases a hard drive containing a stolen customer database extracted from a major e-commerce platform's servers without authorisation; the broker's knowing retention of this stolen computer resource invites liability under Section 66B.
what_it_covers: A computer resource (data, database, computer system) that has been taken from its rightful owner without consent through theft or unlawful appropriation.
A communication device (mobile phone, SIM card, router) that has been physically stolen or fraudulently obtained and is being retained by someone who knows or has reason to believe it is stolen.
Digital data or software unlawfully extracted from a secured system and subsequently received or retained by a third party with knowledge of its stolen nature.
Cloned or duplicated SIM cards and devices obtained through fraudulent means from telecom operators, possessed by persons aware of their illicit origin.
Any computer resource received as consideration or as proceeds of an unlawful transaction where the receiver had reason to believe it was not legitimately obtained.
what_it_excludes: A computer resource or device received in good faith, without knowledge or reasonable cause to believe it was stolen, even if it later turns out to have been unlawfully obtained.
Data or devices that were lawfully purchased or transferred, even if the original owner disputes the sale, as the element of unlawful taking would be absent.

A law enforcement officer or authorised government agency that seizes and retains a stolen computer resource or communication device in the course of an official investigation, as such retention is authorised by law.
Inadvertent receipt of a stolen digital file through an email or network transfer where the recipient had no knowledge of or reason to suspect the stolen nature of the content.
Situations where the alleged 'taking' was done with the consent of the owner, such as licensed transfer or authorised remote access, which would not constitute the item being 'stolen'.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a computer resource or communication device qualifies as 'stolen' is the foundational threshold for triggering liability under Section 66B; if the element of the resource being stolen is not established, the offence of dishonestly receiving or retaining it cannot be made out, and the accused cannot face imprisonment of up to three years or a fine of up to one lakh rupees. It also determines whether the mental element of knowingly dealing with stolen property attaches, which is essential to distinguish criminal liability from innocent receipt.

definitions.definition: "Subscriber" means a person in whose name the Electronic Signature Certificate is issued, being a person who holds a private key corresponding to the public key listed in the Electronic Signature Certificate and is capable of using that private key to affix electronic signatures.
definitions.plain_english: A subscriber is any individual or entity in whose name a digital or electronic signature certificate has been officially issued by a Certifying Authority. This person holds a unique private key that allows them to digitally sign electronic documents and records. Think of a subscriber as someone who has been issued a digital equivalent of a personal seal or handwritten signature.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based chartered accountant who obtains a Digital Signature Certificate from a licensed Certifying Authority like eMudhra or NIC to file income tax returns and MCA forms electronically on behalf of clients.
A government official in Delhi who is issued an Electronic Signature Certificate to digitally sign official government communications and e-Gazette notifications under the e-governance framework.
An entrepreneur in Bengaluru who applies for and receives a Class 3 Digital Signature Certificate to participate in e-procurement tenders on the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) portal.

A bank employee in Chennai who holds an Electronic Signature Certificate issued by a Certifying Authority to authenticate and approve high-value NEFT or RTGS electronic fund transfer instructions on behalf of the bank.

A legal professional in Hyderabad who obtains a digital signature certificate to electronically file pleadings and affidavits before courts that accept e-filing under the digitisation initiatives of the Indian judiciary.
what_it_covers: An individual person who has been issued a Digital Signature Certificate by a licensed Certifying Authority under Section 35 of the IT Act and holds the corresponding private key.
A company or body corporate in whose name an Electronic Signature Certificate is issued, enabling authorised representatives to digitally authenticate electronic records on its behalf.
A government officer or public servant issued an Electronic Signature Certificate by a Controller-approved Certifying Authority for authenticating official electronic records and communications.

Any professional such as a company secretary, auditor, or advocate who has obtained an Electronic Signature Certificate for statutory electronic filings with regulatory bodies like MCA, SEBI, or Income Tax authorities.
what_it_excludes: A Certifying Authority itself — even though it issues certificates, it is not a subscriber under the Act but a licenced authority governed separately under Sections 21–34.

An intermediary such as an internet service provider or network service provider who merely transmits or stores electronic records but does not hold an Electronic Signature Certificate in their own name for authenticating records.
A person who merely uses or verifies an electronic signature or digital signature without holding a corresponding Electronic Signature Certificate and private key issued in their name.
The originator or addressee of an electronic record who sends or receives messages without having been issued a formal Electronic Signature Certificate by a licensed Certifying Authority.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a person as a 'subscriber' triggers specific legal duties under Sections 40, 40A, 41, and 42, including obligations to generate key pairs using secure systems, keep the private key secure, and exercise reasonable care to prevent unauthorised use, with liability for misrepresentation under Section 73 arising directly if the subscriber provides false information to the Certifying Authority. Obligations relating to generating and affixing digital and electronic signatures under Sections 3, 3A, 15, and 18 are legally meaningful only when performed by a duly recognised subscriber, making this definition central to the enforceability and legal validity of electronically signed documents in India.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 79, the expression 'third party information' means any information dealt with by an intermediary in his capacity as an intermediary.
definitions.plain_english: Third party information refers to any content, data, or communication that an intermediary (such as a website, social media platform, or internet service provider) handles on behalf of others, not on its own behalf. The information originates from users or external parties, not from the intermediary itself. The intermediary merely stores, transmits, or provides access to this information as part of its service.
real_world_examples: A user posts a defamatory message about a public figure on a social media platform like Facebook India or Twitter/X India — the post constitutes third party information hosted by the intermediary platform.
A WhatsApp message forwarded between users and routed through Meta's servers in India qualifies as third party information transmitted by WhatsApp as an intermediary.
A video uploaded by a content creator on YouTube India that allegedly infringes copyright is third party information stored and made available by YouTube acting as an intermediary.
An e-commerce marketplace like Flipkart hosting product listings and reviews created by sellers and buyers is handling third party information in its capacity as an intermediary.
An internet service provider like Jio or Airtel transmitting an email containing fraudulent content between two users is carrying third party information, as the ISP did not create the message.
A cloud storage service like DigiLocker or a private Indian cloud provider storing documents uploaded by its users holds third party information in its capacity as an intermediary.
what_it_covers: Posts, comments, videos, and images uploaded by users on social media platforms like Instagram, Twitter, or ShareChat operating in India.
Messages transmitted by users through messaging services such as WhatsApp, Telegram, or Signal, where the intermediary merely routes or stores the communication.
Product listings, reviews, and seller-generated content hosted on e-commerce platforms like Amazon India or Meesho acting as marketplace intermediaries.
Emails and attachments transmitted by internet service providers or web hosting companies on behalf of their subscribers.
Files, documents, and data uploaded and stored by end-users on cloud hosting or data centre services provided by Indian or foreign intermediaries operating in India.
what_it_excludes: Information created, authored, or originated by the intermediary itself in its own editorial or authorial capacity, as it would not be acting purely as an intermediary.
Information where the intermediary has initiated the transmission, selected the receiver, or modified the content, as such involvement removes the passive intermediary character.

Content that the intermediary has conspired to create, abetted, or induced, since active participation in unlawful content creation disqualifies it from being treated as mere third party information under the safe harbour.
Information that the intermediary continues to host after receiving actual knowledge or government notification that it is being used for an unlawful act and failing to remove it expeditiously.
Proprietary content, advertisements, or editorial material published by the platform on its own initiative and under its own authority, which is first-party content.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether content qualifies as 'third party information' under Section 79 determines whether an intermediary is shielded from civil and criminal liability for that content — if it qualifies and the intermediary meets the due diligence conditions, the intermediary is exempt from liability; if it does not qualify or the conditions are breached, the intermediary can be held liable for hosting or transmitting unlawful material under various provisions of the IT Act and other laws.

definitions.definition: "Traffic data" means any data identifying or purporting to identify any person, computer system or computer network or location to or from which the communication is or may be transmitted and includes communications origin, destination, route, time, data, size, duration or type of underlying service and any other information.
definitions.plain_english: Traffic data refers to the metadata or routing information associated with digital communications — essentially the 'envelope' details of a message rather than its content. It tells you who sent something, who received it, when, from where, through which path, and how big the communication was. Think of it as the call log on your phone: it records that a call was made, to whom, for how long, and from which tower — but not what was said during the call.
real_world_examples: CERT-In directing an Indian Internet Service Provider like BSNL or Jio to share the IP address logs, timestamps, and routing paths of communications associated with a suspected cyberattack on a government portal, enabling authorities to trace the origin of the intrusion.

An authorised government agency monitoring the source and destination IP addresses, packet sizes, and connection durations of data flows passing through a data centre in Mumbai to detect and prevent the spread of malware such as ransomware affecting critical banking infrastructure.

The National Cyber Coordination Centre (NCCC) collecting metadata from telecom operators like Airtel about the volume, timing, and routing of data packets during a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack targeting an Indian defence network, without accessing the actual content of communications.

Law enforcement authorities requesting an e-commerce platform like Flipkart or Amazon India to provide server logs showing the origin IP addresses, session timestamps, and network routes used by accounts suspected of conducting large-scale online fraud.

A government agency analysing traffic data from a cloud service provider operating in India to identify patterns of communication between devices forming part of a botnet suspected of spreading computer viruses across Indian banking systems.

CERT-In requiring a social media intermediary operating in India to furnish data on the size, frequency, and geographic routing of bulk message transmissions to identify coordinated inauthentic behaviour campaigns threatening national cyber security.
what_it_covers: IP addresses identifying the source and destination computers or networks involved in a digital communication.
Timestamps, session duration, and size of data packets transmitted across a computer network.
Routing paths and protocols through which a communication travels between nodes across the internet.
Type of underlying service used for communication, such as HTTP, FTP, VoIP, or email protocols.
Geographic or network location data purporting to identify the physical or logical origin point of a communication.
Any other metadata associated with a communication that identifies or purports to identify parties or pathways involved.
what_it_excludes: The actual content or substance of the communication itself, such as the body of an email, the text of a message, or the audio of a voice call.
Stored personal data unrelated to the routing or transmission of a communication, such as user profile information or transactional records not linked to a specific communication event.
Encryption keys or decryption data used to secure the content of communications, which are governed separately under Section 69 of the IT Act.
Computer source code or software programmes stored on a computer resource that are not generated as part of an active communication transmission.
Data relating to the internal processing or storage operations of a computer that do not involve any outgoing or incoming network communication.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether information qualifies as 'traffic data' under Section 69B determines whether an authorised government agency can lawfully compel an intermediary or computer resource operator to provide it for cyber security monitoring purposes; failure by an intermediary to furnish such data upon authorised request attracts criminal liability including imprisonment up to three years and a fine under Section 69B(4).

definitions.definition: The term 'transmit' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Information Technology Act, 2000; however, as used in Section 66E and read with the definition of 'communication device' under Section 2, it means the act of sending, dispatching, or conveying any text, video, audio, image, or electronic record from one person or device to another through any electronic, digital, or telecommunication medium. It encompasses any deliberate act of forwarding or broadcasting such content over a computer network, the internet, or any communication device.
definitions.plain_english: To 'transmit' means to send or pass along any content — such as a photo, video, or message — from one person or device to another using electronic or digital means, like the internet, mobile networks, or any other communication technology. It is essentially the act of pushing information out so that someone else can receive it. This can happen through apps, email, messaging platforms, or any device capable of sending digital data.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai uses WhatsApp to send a privately captured intimate photograph of another individual to a group of friends without that person's consent — this constitutes transmitting a voyeuristic image under Section 66E.
An individual in Delhi forwards a secretly recorded video of a person in a private space via email to multiple recipients across India, thereby transmitting the content electronically.
A user in Bengaluru uploads and shares a private image of another person on a social media platform like Instagram or Facebook, causing the image to be transmitted to all followers over the internet.
A person in Chennai uses a mobile phone to send an MMS containing a captured image of someone in a private area to contacts, constituting transmission via a communication device under the Act.

An employee in Hyderabad forwards confidential captured footage of a colleague taken without consent through a corporate messaging tool like Slack or Microsoft Teams to other employees, thereby transmitting it over a computer network.
what_it_covers: Sending a captured intimate image of another person via WhatsApp, email, or any messaging application over the internet.
Forwarding a privately recorded video through a mobile network or cellular communication device to one or more recipients.
Uploading and sharing electronic records containing images of a person's private area on social media platforms, causing broadcast transmission to multiple users.
Broadcasting digital content over a computer network, including peer-to-peer file sharing or cloud-based distribution of unlawfully captured material.
Transmitting any audio, video, or image through a combination communication device such as a smartphone using either cellular data or Wi-Fi connectivity.
what_it_excludes: Merely viewing or storing a captured image on a personal device without sending or forwarding it to any other person or system.

real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai sends obscene photographs via WhatsApp to multiple contacts — this act of sending constitutes 'transmitting' under Section 67 of the IT Act, 2000.

An individual in Delhi emails a link containing sexually explicit material involving adults to another person — the act of sending that email is a 'transmission' of obscene material under Section 67A.
A user on a social media platform in Bengaluru forwards a pornographic video clip to a group chat of 200 members — each act of forwarding amounts to 'transmitting' prohibited content.

A person in Chennai uses a mobile phone to send MMS containing obscene images to someone in Hyderabad — the use of the communication device to send such content qualifies as 'transmitting' under Sections 67 and 67A.

An accused in Kolkata uses a peer-to-peer file-sharing application to share sexually explicit content with other users across India — the act of seeding or sharing files through such a platform constitutes 'transmitting' electronically.

A cyber-criminal uses a bulk SMS gateway service to distribute links to obscene websites to thousands of phone numbers across India — this mass dissemination amounts to 'transmitting' under the IT Act.
what_it_covers: Sending obscene electronic content such as images, videos, or text via email, WhatsApp, SMS, or any messaging application over the internet.

Automated or bulk transmission of obscene content via bots, bulk messaging services, or email marketing platforms.
what_it_excludes: Merely viewing or accessing obscene content online without sending or forwarding it to any other person — passive consumption is not 'transmitting'.

definitions.definition: The expression 'truncated cheque' shall have the same meaning as assigned to it in section 6 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, being a cheque which is truncated during the course of a clearing cycle, either by the clearing house or by the bank whether paying or receiving payment, immediately on generation of an electronic image for transmission, substituting the further physical movement of the cheque in writing.
definitions.plain_english: A truncated cheque is a physical paper cheque that is stopped mid-way through the bank clearing process and replaced by a digital image of itself. Instead of the paper cheque physically travelling from one bank to another, a scanned electronic image of it is sent for processing and payment. The original paper cheque is retained at the point where it was scanned, and the digital image does all the work of completing the transaction.
real_world_examples: A customer deposits a physical cheque drawn on State Bank of India at an HDFC Bank branch in Mumbai; the HDFC branch scans the cheque and transmits its electronic image through the CTS (Cheque Truncation System) grid to SBI for clearing, and the paper cheque never physically moves to SBI — this is a truncated cheque in operation.

A Delhi-based company issues a cheque to a vendor who deposits it at a Punjab National Bank branch; PNB's branch scanner captures the cheque image, which is sent electronically to the RBI-operated clearing house for settlement, with the physical cheque retained at PNB — the cheque has been truncated.

An individual in Chennai deposits a cheque from a cooperative bank at Axis Bank; Axis Bank, acting as the presenting bank, truncates the cheque by generating its digital image and presenting it through the MICR-based CTS grid, avoiding physical dispatch of the paper instrument across cities.

A corporate treasury in Bengaluru receives hundreds of outstation cheques and deposits them at its Kotak Mahindra Bank branch; the bank scans each cheque under the CTS 2010 standard, transmits the images to respective drawee banks electronically, and retains all original paper cheques locally — each such cheque is a truncated cheque under the Negotiable Instruments Act framework extended by Section 81A of the IT Act.

During a high-volume salary disbursement cycle, a PSU issues paper cheques to contractors; when contractors deposit these at various Bank of Baroda branches across India, each branch truncates the cheques by capturing digital images and routing them through the National Clearing Cell, eliminating inter-city physical cheque movement.
what_it_covers: A physical paper cheque whose further movement is stopped and replaced by an electronic image during the clearing cycle by a clearing house or a bank.
Cheques scanned and transmitted via RBI's Cheque Truncation System (CTS) grids (Mumbai, Chennai, New Delhi) where the originating branch retains the paper instrument.
Situations where either the paying bank or the receiving bank generates and transmits an electronic image of the cheque in substitution of the physical instrument for settlement purposes.
Cheques processed under the CTS 2010 standard wherein both the MICR data and the image of the cheque front and back are transmitted electronically to the drawee bank.
Any cheque truncated by a clearing house (such as an RBI-operated clearing centre) at any point during the multi-bank clearing cycle before payment is made.
what_it_excludes: Electronic cheques that are created, issued, and signed digitally from the outset and never exist as a physical paper instrument — these fall under the separate definition of 'electronic cheque'.
NEFT, RTGS, IMPS, or UPI-based electronic fund transfers, which are not cheque instruments at all and do not involve truncation of any physical document.
A physical cheque that is physically transported in its paper form through the entire clearing cycle to the drawee bank without being scanned or imaged at any intermediate stage.
Demand drafts or pay orders that are processed physically without truncation, even if they are negotiable instruments under the Negotiable Instruments Act.
Post-dated cheques or cheques held by a party and not yet presented for clearing, as truncation is an event that only occurs during an active clearing cycle.
definitions.why_it_matters: The inclusion of truncated cheques under Section 81A of the IT Act means that all provisions of the IT Act — including those relating to authenticity, legal recognition, and evidentiary value of electronic records — apply to the electronic images generated during truncation, giving them the same legal standing as the physical cheque for purposes of dishonour and liability under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. Failure to comply with prescribed security and authentication standards for truncated cheque images could affect the enforceability of the payment instrument and expose banks or clearing houses to liability under both the IT Act and the Negotiable Instruments Act.

definitions.definition: "Under circumstances violating privacy" means circumstances in which a person can have a reasonable expectation that (i) he or she could disrobe in privacy, without being concerned that an image of his private area was being captured; or (ii) any part of his or her private area would not be visible to the public, regardless of whether that person is in a public or private place.
definitions.plain_english: This phrase describes situations where a person reasonably expects that their intimate body parts are not being photographed, filmed, or recorded without their knowledge or agreement. It covers both private settings like changing rooms and bathrooms, as well as public settings where a person still expects that their private areas will not be captured on camera. The key idea is the reasonable belief of the victim that their privacy would be respected, not simply whether the location was public or private.
real_world_examples: A hidden camera is installed in the women's changing room of a clothing store in Bengaluru, recording customers as they try on clothes — the victims reasonably expect complete privacy while disrobing, making this a clear violation.

A person at a crowded beach festival in Goa uses a smartphone tucked into a bag to film up a woman's skirt without her knowledge — even though she is in a public place, she has a reasonable expectation that her private area will not be captured.

A male employee in a Delhi office secretly places a camera in an attached bathroom used by female colleagues, recording them while they bathe — the victims have an unambiguous reasonable expectation of privacy while disrobing in such a setting.

A gym in Mumbai installs a concealed recording device in the locker room area, capturing images of members in various states of undress — members reasonably expect that they can change clothes without being filmed, triggering this provision.

A voyeur in a Chennai shopping mall uses a specially angled mirror device to photograph the private areas of women on escalators — despite being in a fully public space, the victims had a reasonable expectation that their undergarment-clad areas would not be made visible or captured.

A paying guest landlord in Hyderabad secretly records a female tenant through a pinhole camera while she dresses in her rented room — the tenant has a reasonable expectation of complete privacy in her own room, satisfying this circumstance.
what_it_covers: Recording or photographing a person in a changing room, bathroom, or toilet where they reasonably expect to disrobe without observation.

Capturing images of a person's private area in a public location, such as using a camera placed under clothing or at an upward angle on an escalator, where the victim still has a reasonable expectation that those areas remain unexposed.
Filming a person through a hidden camera in a hotel room, hostel dormitory, or rented accommodation where the occupant reasonably expects complete privacy.
Situations in gyms, swimming pool changing areas, or spa facilities where individuals undress and have a clear reasonable expectation that no recording is taking place.
Any setting, public or private, where a person's undergarment-clad or naked private areas are captured without consent and the person could not have anticipated or consented to such exposure.
what_it_excludes: Medical or clinical imaging of private areas conducted with the informed consent of the patient and for legitimate diagnostic or surgical purposes.
Consensual photography or filming of a person's private areas where the subject has expressly agreed to the capture and publication of such images.

Security camera footage incidentally capturing a person's private area in circumstances where no reasonable expectation of privacy exists, such as footage of a person who voluntarily exposed themselves in an open public space.
Journalistic or law-enforcement documentation undertaken under lawful authority and with appropriate procedural safeguards, where privacy is not being violated within the meaning of the section.
Accidental or inadvertent image capture where there is no intent and where the circumstances do not objectively give rise to a reasonable expectation of privacy being breached.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether conduct falls within 'circumstances violating privacy' is the decisive threshold element of Section 66E — only if these circumstances are established does the intentional or knowing capture, publication, or transmission of a private-area image become a cognizable criminal offence attracting imprisonment of up to three years or a fine of up to two lakh rupees, or both; without this element being satisfied, the provision is not triggered and no criminal liability under Section 66E attaches.

definitions.definition: The term 'unique identification feature' is not formally defined in the Information Technology Act, 2000, but as used in Section 66C, it denotes any electronic credential, biometric marker, token, identifier, or personal attribute uniquely associated with a specific individual that is used to authenticate, verify, or establish that individual's identity in an electronic or digital environment. It is used conjunctively with 'electronic signature' and 'password' to encompass all personal identifiers beyond those two specific categories that serve to singularly distinguish and authenticate a person in cyberspace.
definitions.plain_english: A 'unique identification feature' is any special digital marker or credential that belongs only to one person and is used to prove who they are online or on a device. This could be something like a fingerprint scan, an Aadhaar number used for digital login, a one-time PIN, a biometric ID, or any other personal digital token. If someone fraudulently uses another person's such feature, it is a crime under the IT Act.
real_world_examples: A fraudster in Mumbai obtains someone's Aadhaar-based biometric data through a skimming device and uses it to authenticate a mobile banking transaction, thereby misusing that person's unique biometric identification feature.

A cybercriminal in Delhi gains access to a government employee's GSTN login credentials — which include a unique taxpayer identification number — and files fraudulent GST returns on their behalf, constituting misuse of a unique identification feature.

An impersonator in Bengaluru uses another person's stored fingerprint template leaked from an HR database to clock in and out of a corporate attendance system, fraudulently using that individual's biometric unique identification feature.

A scammer in Hyderabad obtains a victim's DigiLocker PIN and the associated Aadhaar-linked unique identifier, logs into the victim's DigiLocker account, and downloads sensitive documents to impersonate the victim before a government authority.

An attacker intercepts the SIM-swap of a user in Chennai and uses the victim's mobile number — which serves as a unique identifier tied to their UPI account — to fraudulently authorise financial transactions without the victim's consent.
what_it_covers: Biometric identifiers such as fingerprints, iris scans, or facial recognition data used to authenticate a person in a digital system
Aadhaar numbers or Aadhaar-linked OTPs used as digital authentication credentials for government or banking services
Unique device-bound tokens, smart card PINs, or cryptographic keys assigned exclusively to an individual for identity verification
Mobile numbers registered as unique identifiers for UPI or banking authentication systems
Employee or citizen identification numbers (e.g., PAN, EPF UAN) used as digital login or verification credentials in electronic systems
what_it_excludes: Generic usernames or account names that are not uniquely assigned and can be shared among multiple users
Passwords, which are separately and explicitly enumerated in Section 66C and are therefore a distinct category from 'unique identification feature'
Electronic signatures and digital signatures, which are also separately named in Section 66C and governed under their own definitional framework in the Act
Physical identification documents such as a paper Aadhaar card or passport when not used as an electronic authentication credential
Shared or organisational credentials (e.g., a common departmental login) that do not uniquely identify a single natural person
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether something qualifies as a 'unique identification feature' determines whether fraudulent or dishonest use of it attracts criminal liability under Section 66C of the IT Act, which carries imprisonment of up to three years and a fine of up to one lakh rupees. A broader interpretation of this term expands the scope of identity theft offences, thereby protecting more categories of digital credentials and individuals from impersonation and fraud.

Examples: A fraudster in Mumbai obtains someone's Aadhaar-based biometric data through a skimming device and uses it to authenticate a mobile banking transaction, thereby misusing that person's unique biometric identification feature. | A cybercriminal in Delhi gains access to a government employee's GSTN login credentials — which include a unique taxpayer identification number — and files fraudulent GST returns on their behalf, constituting misuse of a unique identification feature. | An impersonator in Bengaluru uses another person's stored fingerprint template leaked from an HR database to clock in and out of a corporate attendance system, fraudulently using that individual's biometric unique identification feature. | A scammer in Hyderabad obtains a victim's DigiLocker PIN and the associated Aadhaar-linked unique identifier, logs into the victim's DigiLocker account, and downloads sensitive documents to impersonate the victim before a government authority. | An attacker intercepts the SIM-swap of a user in Chennai and uses the victim's mobile number — which serves as a unique identifier tied to their UPI account — to fraudulently authorise financial transactions without the victim's consent.

Tags: digital identity authentication, biometric credential misuse, electronic identity theft, personal authentication marker, fraudulent identity impersonation, cybercrime identity offence, unique personal digital identifier, non-password authentication feature, identity fraud liability, electronic credential protection

Covers: Biometric identifiers such as fingerprints, iris scans, or facial recognition data used to authenticate a person in a digital system; Aadhaar numbers or Aadhaar-linked OTPs used as digital authentication credentials for government or banking services; Unique device-bound tokens, smart card PINs, or cryptographic keys assigned exclusively to an individual for identity verification; Mobile numbers registered as unique identifiers for UPI or banking authentication systems; Employee or citizen identification numbers (e.g., PAN, EPF UAN) used as digital login or verification credentials in electronic systems

Excludes: Generic usernames or account names that are not uniquely assigned and can be shared among multiple users; Passwords, which are separately and explicitly enumerated in Section 66C and are therefore a distinct category from 'unique identification feature'; Electronic signatures and digital signatures, which are also separately named in Section 66C and governed under their own definitional framework in the Act; Physical identification documents such as a paper Aadhaar card or passport when not used as an electronic authentication credential; Shared or organisational credentials (e.g., a common departmental login) that do not uniquely identify a single natural person

Why it matters: Whether something qualifies as a 'unique identification feature' determines whether fraudulent or dishonest use of it attracts criminal liability under Section 66C of the IT Act, which carries imprisonment of up to three years and a fine of up to one lakh rupees. A broader interpretation of this term expands the scope of identity theft offences, thereby protecting more categories of digital credentials and individuals from impersonation and fraud.

(Information Technology Act, 2000)

definitions.definition: "verify" in relation to a digital signature, electronic record or public key, with its grammatical variations and cognate expressions means to determine whether— (a) the initial electronic record was affixed with the digital signature by the use of the private key corresponding to the public key of the subscriber; (b) the initial electronic record is retained intact or has been altered since such electronic record was so affixed with the digital signature.
definitions.plain_english: To 'verify' means to confirm that a digital signature on an electronic document is genuine and was created by the person who claims to have signed it, using their private key. It also means checking that the document has not been changed or tampered with after it was signed. This process uses the signer's public key to perform the check, ensuring both the identity of the signer and the integrity of the document.
real_world_examples: A company in Mumbai receives a digitally signed PDF contract from a vendor; their software uses the vendor's public key obtained from a Certifying Authority to verify that the digital signature is authentic and the contract content has not been altered in transit.

A government officer at the Ministry of Corporate Affairs verifies the digital signature on an e-filing submission on the MCA21 portal to confirm that the director who submitted the annual return is indeed the authorised signatory and that the form was not tampered with after signing.

An income tax assessee digitally signs their ITR on the Income Tax e-filing portal; the portal's backend system verifies the digital signature using the assessee's public key to confirm identity and document integrity before accepting the return.

A bank in Delhi receives a digitally signed electronic cheque; the bank's system verifies the digital signature of the account holder using the asymmetric crypto system to ensure the cheque was signed by the genuine account holder and has not been fraudulently modified.

A High Court e-filing system in Chennai verifies the digital signature on a petition submitted by an advocate to confirm it was filed by the registered advocate and the petition document remains unaltered since submission.

An e-commerce platform processes a digitally signed purchase order from a corporate buyer; the platform verifies the digital signature to authenticate the buyer's identity and ensure the order details have not been intercepted and changed.
what_it_covers: Determining whether a digital signature affixed to an electronic record was created using the private key corresponding to the signer's public key, thereby confirming the signer's identity.
Checking whether the electronic record has remained intact and unaltered since the digital signature was affixed, ensuring document integrity.

The process carried out by a relying party or recipient using the subscriber's public key to validate the authenticity of a digitally signed electronic record such as an e-contract, e-filing, or electronic cheque.
Verification performed by automated systems of Certifying Authorities or government portals to authenticate electronically signed documents submitted online.
Verification of a secure electronic signature to confirm it meets the security standards prescribed under the Act.
what_it_excludes: Manual or physical verification of handwritten signatures on paper documents, which falls outside the scope of this digital/electronic process.

Verification of the legal or substantive content, validity or enforceability of the underlying electronic record or contract itself — the process only covers authenticity and integrity, not legal merit.
Authentication processes that do not involve a digital signature or electronic signature as defined under the Act, such as username-password login or OTP-based authentication alone.
Verification of a public key or digital signature certificate that has been revoked, suspended, or issued by an entity not licensed as a Certifying Authority under section 24.
Physical identity verification of the subscriber's person, as 'verify' is strictly limited to the cryptographic validation of the digital signature and record integrity.
definitions.why_it_matters: The ability to successfully verify a digital signature is the legal foundation for establishing authenticity and integrity of an electronic record under the IT Act; if verification fails or is not possible, the digital signature cannot be relied upon to create binding obligations, and electronic records may not be admissible as evidence or enforceable as signed instruments. It directly governs the legal validity of transactions under sections 3, 35, and related provisions, and determines whether obligations of Certifying Authorities and subscribers have been discharged.

definitions.definition: The term 'wrongful gain' is not formally defined in the Information Technology Act, 2000, but is used consistently in Sections 43A and 72A to denote gain by unlawful means of property to which the person gaining it is not legally entitled, being gain achieved through negligent failure to protect data or through unauthorised disclosure of personal information in breach of a lawful contract. By reference to the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Section 23), 'wrongful gain' means gain by unlawful means of property to which the person gaining is not legally entitled.
definitions.plain_english: Wrongful gain means getting something of value — such as money, data, business advantage, or property — through illegal or improper means, specifically when that gain comes at the expense of someone else's rights or data. In the context of the IT Act, it refers to situations where a person benefits improperly because someone else failed to protect personal data or disclosed private information without consent. The gain must be something the person was not legally entitled to in the first place.
real_world_examples: A competitor company bribes an employee of a Bengaluru-based IT firm to disclose a client's confidential business data stored on the firm's servers; the competitor gains a wrongful commercial advantage by using that data to poach the client.

A data analytics startup in Mumbai negligently leaves its customer database unsecured; a fraudster accesses the personal financial information and uses it to take out loans in customers' names, thereby gaining funds he was not entitled to.

An intermediary providing cloud storage services in Hyderabad discloses sensitive personal data of users to a marketing firm without consent and in breach of the service contract; the marketing firm gains wrongful commercial benefit by targeting those users.

An employee of an e-commerce platform in Delhi, while handling customer order data under a lawful employment contract, sells purchase history and contact details of thousands of users to a rival firm for monetary consideration, enabling the rival to gain customers wrongfully.

A hospital's outsourced IT vendor in Chennai accesses patients' sensitive medical records and sells them to an insurance company, which uses the data to deny legitimate claims and gain financially by avoiding payouts it was otherwise obligated to make.
what_it_covers: Monetary profit obtained by a person who accesses or receives another's personal data through a body corporate's failure to implement reasonable security practices.
Commercial or business advantage gained by an intermediary or third party who receives personal information disclosed in breach of a lawful contract without the data subject's consent.
Financial gain obtained through identity theft or fraud enabled by unauthorised access to sensitive personal data or information negligently left unprotected by a body corporate.

Gain in the form of trade secrets, client lists, or competitive intelligence wrongfully acquired through disclosure of personal information by a service provider in violation of contractual obligations.
Any benefit — monetary, reputational, or positional — that a person accrues by exploiting personal data they were not legally entitled to access or use.
what_it_excludes: Lawful gain obtained through authorised access to data under a valid agreement or applicable law, even if the data is sensitive personal data or information.

Incidental or unintentional benefits that arise without any intent to cause wrongful gain and without negligence in security practices, where no breach of lawful contract or duty of care has occurred.
Gain derived from publicly available information that is not personal information or sensitive personal data or information as defined under the Act.
Benefits arising from legitimate competitive intelligence gathered through lawful and independent means unconnected to any breach of data security or contract.
Gain obtained by government authorities or law enforcement agencies acting under lawful authority and within the scope of their legal powers to access data.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes 'wrongful gain' is a key trigger for civil liability under Section 43A — requiring a body corporate to pay compensation — and for criminal liability under Section 72A, which prescribes imprisonment up to three years and/or a fine up to five lakh rupees for intentional disclosure of personal information in breach of a lawful contract; without establishing wrongful gain (or wrongful loss), neither the compensation remedy nor the penal sanction is attracted.

definitions.definition: The term 'wrongful loss' is not independently defined in the Information Technology Act, 2000, but is used in conjunction with 'wrongful gain' consistent with its meaning under the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Section 23): 'wrongful loss' means the loss by unlawful means of property to which the person losing it is legally entitled. In the context of the IT Act, it signifies the unlawful deprivation of a person's legally entitled property, data, financial asset, or right caused by negligent data protection failures or unauthorised disclosure of personal information.
definitions.plain_english: Wrongful loss means that someone has been illegally deprived of something they were legally entitled to keep or own. In the digital context, this could mean losing money, data, business opportunities, or other rights because of someone else's illegal or negligent actions online. The loss must be something the person had a rightful claim to, and it must have been caused unfairly or without legal justification.
real_world_examples: A Bengaluru-based e-commerce company fails to encrypt customer payment data, leading to a breach that drains funds from customers' linked bank accounts — the customers suffer wrongful loss of money they were legally entitled to retain.

A Mumbai hospital's negligent handling of patient health records results in sensitive data being leaked to an insurance company, causing the patient to be denied a policy they were otherwise eligible for, constituting wrongful loss of an insurable right.

An IT services employee in Hyderabad, while working under a lawful contract, discloses a client company's proprietary business data to a competitor, causing the client to lose a major government tender they were positioned to win — a wrongful loss of business opportunity.

A Delhi-based fintech intermediary fails to maintain reasonable security practices, resulting in a fraudster siphoning a user's wallet balance of ₹2 lakhs, directly causing wrongful loss to the user who had a legal entitlement to those funds.

A social media platform operating in India negligently exposes private user data including Aadhaar-linked information, enabling identity thieves to fraudulently transfer a user's fixed deposit — causing wrongful loss of the deposited amount.

An HR software provider in Pune leaks employee salary and bank account details due to poor security, leading to unauthorised deductions from employee accounts, constituting wrongful loss to each affected employee.
what_it_covers: Loss of money or funds from a bank account or digital wallet caused by a body corporate's failure to implement reasonable security practices protecting sensitive personal data.

Deprivation of a business opportunity, contract, or tender that a person was legally entitled to, resulting from unauthorised disclosure of confidential business information by an intermediary in breach of a lawful contract.

Loss of a legally held right or entitlement — such as insurance eligibility, employment, or credit access — caused by the wrongful exposure of sensitive personal data like medical records or financial information.
Unlawful depletion of a person's digital assets, intellectual property, or proprietary data to which they had legal ownership, resulting from a data security failure or unauthorised disclosure.
what_it_excludes: Losses that are accidental and not caused by any negligence in security practices or intentional disclosure — purely technical failures without a duty of care breach do not qualify as wrongful loss.
Losses stemming from lawful actions, such as a court-ordered disclosure of data or a regulator-mandated sharing of information, even if the person suffers financial disadvantage as a result.

Speculative or anticipated losses that a person was not yet legally entitled to, such as future profits not yet earned or business deals not yet concluded, which do not constitute 'wrongful loss' of something legally held.
Losses suffered by a person who had no legal entitlement to the property or right in the first place — wrongful loss requires the losing party to have been legally entitled to what was taken.
definitions.why_it_matters: The presence of 'wrongful loss' is a key trigger for civil liability under Section 43A, compelling a body corporate to pay compensation to the affected person for negligent data protection failures, and for criminal liability under Section 72A, where intentional or knowing disclosure of personal information causing such loss attracts imprisonment up to three years and/or a fine up to five lakh rupees. Without establishing wrongful loss (or wrongful gain), neither the compensation remedy nor the criminal punishment is activated.
